optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Implement a new kernel (e.g., mmid_prepare_sycl) that: 1) Each thread reads ids[iid1][id] and compares to target expert. 2) Use work-group-level scan (sycl::exclusive_scan_over_group) to compute per-expert prefix sums. 3) Write row_mapping and contiguous src1 in a single fused kernel. 4) Use device-side memory for expert bounds (no host copy). The CUDA mm_ids_helper kernel in ggml/src/ggml-cuda/mmid.cu (line 28) serves as a reference implementation. Key change: remove stream->wait() at line 2969 and the host-side ids_host vector entirely.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Requires a new kernel plus refactoring the dispatcher control flow. The CUDA implementation has been battle-tested, so the algorithm is proven. Risk is in the SYCL-specific implementation (atomic ordering, memory model differences). Must handle the case where expert counts are needed for dst buffer sizing — may need a two-pass approach (count first, then gather).

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace the ne12==1 path (lines 2994-3012) which launches O(n_ids * ne[1]) individual MUL_MAT calls with the batched compaction path (ne12>1 style). The ne12==1 path dispatches each token-expert pair as a separate matrix-vector product — for a typical MoE inference with 128 tokens and top-2 routing, this means 256 individual kernel launches (each launching DMMV or MMVQ internally). The batched path groups all tokens for the same expert into one matrix multiply, reducing kernel launches to 3 * n_active_experts.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-20x speedup for the ne12==1 path by reducing kernel launch count from O(n_ids * ne[1]) to O(n_active_experts). For 128 tokens with top-2 routing across 8 experts: from 256 GEMV launches to ~24 kernel launches (3 * 8 experts). Each batched GEMM is also more compute-efficient than individual GEMVs.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Unify both paths to always use the compaction approach. The ne12==1 case just means src1 has batch_size=1, but the compaction code handles this correctly already (it treats each iid1 as a separate token). Remove the ne12==1 special case entirely and always use the ne12>1 path. This also enables the mm_ids_helper optimization (opt_006_001) to cover all cases.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The ne12>1 path already handles all the indexing correctly for ne12==1 (the inner loop still iterates over iid1 and id). The main risk is if there's an edge case where ne12==1 requires different tensor layout assumptions — verify with the GGML_ASSERT checks on nb11 and nb1 at lines 3079-3080.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized 16-byte loads/stores (sycl::vec<float, 4>) in the gather (k_copy_src1_to_contiguous) and scatter (k_copy_dst_from_contiguous) kernels. Currently each thread copies one float (4 bytes) per loop iteration. With vec4, each thread would copy 4 floats (16 bytes) per iteration, reducing the number of memory transactions by 4x and better utilizing the memory bus.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 2-3x speedup for the copy kernels themselves. Since copy kernels are a fraction of total MUL_MAT_ID time (the GEMM dominates), overall impact is 5-10% reduction in MUL_MAT_ID latency. More impactful for large hidden dimensions (ne10 or ne0 = 4096+).
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace the scalar copy loop: `for (int i = tid; i < ne10; i += WG) { dst[i] = src[i]; }` with: `int vec_ne10 = ne10 / 4; for (int i = tid; i < vec_ne10; i += WG) { reinterpret_cast<sycl::vec<float,4>*>(dst)[i] = reinterpret_cast<const sycl::vec<float,4>*>(src)[i]; } // handle remainder`. Must verify 16-byte alignment of src1 and dst buffers. The contiguous buffers are pool-allocated and likely aligned; the original buffers depend on the allocator.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Straightforward vectorization of a copy loop. Must handle ne10 not divisible by 4 (tail elements). Alignment should be verified but pool-allocated buffers are typically well-aligned.

optimization_opportunities.description: Reduce wasted work-groups in k_copy_src1_to_contiguous by restructuring the launch. Currently the kernel launches ids->ne[1] * n_ids work-groups (one per token-expert pair), but most immediately early-exit because row_id_i != i02. For a model with 64 experts and top-2 routing, only ~2/64 = 3% of work-groups do useful work. Instead, use a two-phase approach: (1) a small kernel to scan ids and compute per-expert row lists, then (2) launch exactly num_src1_rows work-groups for the actual copy.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-20% reduction in gather phase latency by eliminating wasted work-group launches. More impactful for models with many experts (n_as=64) where 97% of WGs are no-ops. The actual improvement depends on the GPU's work-group scheduling overhead.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: This optimization naturally falls out of implementing the mm_ids_helper kernel (opt_006_001). If the helper kernel pre-computes the list of row indices for each expert, the copy kernel can be launched with exactly num_src1_rows work-groups, each knowing exactly which source row to copy. No early-exit needed.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: This is a natural consequence of opt_006_001. As a standalone optimization (without mm_ids_helper), it requires an extra scan kernel pass, which adds complexity. Better to implement as part of opt_006_001.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace dpct::atomic_fetch_add on global memory with a work-group-local atomic or scan-based row assignment in k_copy_src1_to_contiguous. Currently each matching work-group's thread 0 atomically increments a global counter. With many tokens routed to the same popular expert, this creates a serial bottleneck on the global atomic. Using sycl::atomic_ref<int, sycl::memory_order::relaxed, sycl::memory_scope::device, sycl::access::address_space::global_space> would be more correct, and using a scan-based approach would eliminate contention entirely.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-10% improvement in the gather phase for popular experts with many routed tokens. The global atomic creates a serialization point — with 128 tokens and top-2 routing, up to ~256/n_experts = 32 work-groups may contend on the same counter.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Option A (simple): Replace dpct::atomic_fetch_add with sycl::atomic_ref — more portable and allows relaxed memory ordering. Option B (better): Pre-compute the row index for each work-group using a prefix-sum scan of the ids tensor (part of opt_006_001), eliminating the runtime atomic entirely. Option C (intermediate): Each work-group determines its own row index without atomics by counting the number of matching rows with iid1 < current_iid1 or (iid1 == current_iid1 && id < current_id) — deterministic ordering without atomics.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The dpct::atomic_fetch_add is already functionally correct — the change is for performance and code quality. sycl::atomic_ref is the standard SYCL way. The scan-based approach requires more refactoring but eliminates the serialization point.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use sycl::access::fence_space::local_space in the barrier call (line 2918) instead of the default global fence. The DPCT1065 comment at line 2913-2917 correctly identifies this opportunity. The barrier only synchronizes access to the SLM src1_row variable — no global memory coherence is needed at that point.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1-2% improvement in the gather kernel. The barrier is executed once per work-group, and the fence scope change reduces the hardware synchronization overhead slightly.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change `item_ct1.barrier()` at line 2918 to `item_ct1.barrier(sycl::access::fence_space::local_space)`. Remove the DPCT1065 comment.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The barrier protects only the SLM src1_row value written by thread 0. Global memory writes (row_mapping[src1_row]) happen in thread 0 before the barrier, but other threads don't read row_mapping — they only need src1_row. The local_space fence is sufficient.

optimization_opportunities.description: Overlap expert processing by using multiple SYCL queues or out-of-order queue with event dependencies. Currently the expert loop (line 3020) processes experts sequentially: gather(expert_i) → GEMM(expert_i) → scatter(expert_i) → gather(expert_i+1) → ... With independent queues per expert, the gather for expert_i+1 could overlap with the GEMM for expert_i, hiding copy latency behind compute.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-20% latency reduction for the batched path by overlapping gather/scatter of one expert with compute of another. More impactful when many experts are active and GEMM time is comparable to copy time (small batch sizes per expert).
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Use multiple SYCL queues (one per active expert, up to a cap) with event-based dependencies: copy_event[i] = launch_gather(q[i], ...); gemm_event[i] = launch_gemm(q[i], ..., {copy_event[i]}); scatter_event[i] = launch_scatter(q[i], ..., {gemm_event[i]}). The contiguous buffers need to be per-expert (not shared). Alternatively, use a single out-of-order queue with explicit dependencies. This requires significant refactoring of the dispatcher.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Multiple concurrent queues add complexity for buffer management (each expert needs its own contiguous src1/dst buffer). SYCL event dependencies must be correct to avoid data races. The ggml_sycl_mul_mat function may have internal state/synchronization assumptions that prevent safe concurrent use from multiple queues. Also, pool_alloc may not be thread-safe across queues.

kernels.efficiency_notes: The MUL_MAT_ID implementation is critically inefficient due to architectural issues, not kernel-level compute issues. The two copy kernels (gather and scatter) are simple and reasonably well-written, but the dispatcher architecture creates severe performance bottlenecks: (1) blocking D2H copy of ids tensor creates a pipeline stall, (2) ne12==1 path (the common inference case) launches individual MUL_MAT per token-expert pair, (3) host-side row counting and sequential expert processing add latency. The CUDA backend avoids all of these issues with the mm_ids_helper GPU kernel that pre-computes indices without host synchronization. For MoE models (Mixtral, DeepSeek, etc.), MUL_MAT_ID is on the critical path for every MoE layer, making these inefficiencies particularly impactful. The estimated 10-20% efficiency accounts for the pipeline stalls and excessive kernel launch overhead — the actual GEMM compute (once dispatched) may be reasonably efficient via MMVQ or oneMKL GEMM, but the overhead per-call dominates.

launch_config.global_size_expression: 1D: num_quant_blocks * WARP_SIZE where num_quant_blocks = ky * (kx / QK8_1). WARP_SIZE=16 on Intel, QK8_1=32, so ElementsPerWI=2.
launch_config.notes: Work-group size = WARP_SIZE = 16 (single sub-group per work-group). This is below the recommended 256-512 for Intel GPUs. However, since each sub-group independently processes one quantization block, the hardware can schedule multiple work-groups per Xe-core to achieve occupancy. The sub-group size is correctly specified as WARP_SIZE (16 on Intel) and is needed because the kernel uses reduce_over_group(sub_group). Increasing WG size to pack multiple sub-groups per work-group would improve scheduling granularity but not fundamentally change occupancy since the hardware already batches independent work-groups.

memory_patterns.notes: Already uses sycl::vec<float, 2> for input loads and sycl::vec<int8_t, 2> for output stores — good vectorization. Each WI reads 8 bytes (2 floats) and writes 2 bytes (2 int8s) plus one WI per sub-group writes 4 bytes (half2 d/sum). Memory access is coalesced: WI i loads x[subgroup_id*32 + 2*i], so consecutive WIs access adjacent 8-byte blocks. Total per sub-group: 128 bytes in, 36 bytes out. With ElementsPerWI=2 on Intel, the vector width is small but the kernel is already vectorized.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM used. Each sub-group processes an independent quantization block with no data sharing between sub-groups. SLM is not needed for this embarrassingly parallel workload.

reduction_pattern.notes: Uses sycl::reduce_over_group(sub_group) for both sum (plus) and amax (maximum) reductions — this is the optimal pattern for Intel GPUs. No manual butterfly or SLM reduction.

data_types.notes: Quantization requires float32 precision for finding amax and computing scale factor d=amax/127. The output is int8 quantized values + half2 (d, sum). Joint matrix is not applicable — this is quantization, not matrix multiply.

math_functions.notes: Uses standard math (fmax, fabs, round). round() is used for rounding quantized values to nearest int8. These could potentially use native equivalents but precision is important for quantization accuracy.

hot_loops: ElementsPerWI loop (lines 41-45): 2 iterations on Intel (QK8_1/WARP_SIZE=32/16=2), UNROLLED via #pragma unroll(ElementsPerWI) — computes sum and amax
ElementsPerWI loop (lines 51-53): 2 iterations on Intel, UNROLLED via #pragma unroll(ElementsPerWI) — computes quantized values
loop_analysis.notes: Both loops are only 2 iterations with #pragma unroll — they will be fully unrolled by the compiler. The kernel body is very simple: 2 fabs+fmax+add, 2 sub-group reductions, 2 round+div. Minimal register pressure.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: Quantization is purely memory-bandwidth bound. Compute intensity: ~20 FLOPs per 128-byte input (0.16 ops/byte) — far below the 27 ops/byte compute intensity threshold. The kernel reads 128 bytes of float32 input and writes 36 bytes of quantized output per sub-group. Performance is dominated by global memory bandwidth.
anti_patterns: MINOR: __dpct_inline__ artifact on quantize_q8_1_impl (cosmetic — should be inline or let compiler decide)
MINOR: Work-group size of 16 (single sub-group) — could pack multiple sub-groups for better scheduling, though hardware can compensate with concurrent work-groups
MINOR: dpct::queue_ptr and dpct::has_capability_or_fail in launch wrapper — DPCT artifacts

optimization_opportunities.description: Increase work-group size from 16 to 256 (16 sub-groups per WG) for improved scheduling and reduced launch overhead
optimization_opportunities.notes: Pack 16 sub-groups per work-group (256 WIs) instead of 1. Each sub-group still independently processes one quant block. Benefits: (1) reduced kernel launch overhead with 16x fewer work-groups, (2) slightly better hardware scheduling with larger work-groups, (3) potential for better L1 cache utilization when processing adjacent blocks. The kernel would need to use get_sub_group().get_group_id() instead of get_group(0) for block indexing. Impact is likely small since the hardware already schedules independent WGs efficiently.

optimization_opportunities.description: Increase vector width from 2 to 4+ elements per work-item for better bandwidth utilization
optimization_opportunities.notes: With WARP_SIZE=16 and QK8_1=32, ElementsPerWI=2. Could use a work-group of 8 WIs with ElementsPerWI=4 (vec4 loads) for better memory bandwidth utilization. However, this conflicts with the sub-group reduction pattern which needs all 16 WIs participating. Alternative: use 16 WIs but have each load vec4 and process 64 elements (2 quant blocks per sub-group) — this changes the algorithm. The current vec2 is already reasonably efficient.

kernels.name: element_wise (unary ops)

launch_config.global_size_expression: 1D: ceil(k / 256) * 256, where k = total elements
launch_config.notes: All 6 kernel launch sites use nd_range<1> with work-group size 256 (SYCL_NEG_BLOCK_SIZE or SYCL_GLU_BLOCK_SIZE). Work-group size is appropriate for Intel GPUs (256 / 16 = 16 sub-groups per work-group). However, NONE of the 6 launch sites specify [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]], unlike other SYCL kernels in this codebase which consistently use it. This is a clean manual port — no DPCT artifacts.

strided_accesses: Gated kernels (GLU, SwiGLU-OAI): index j0 = (i / n) * o0 + (i % n) can be strided when o0 != n (non-contiguous row layouts)
memory_patterns.notes: All kernels process exactly 1 element per work-item. Unary kernels: thread i reads x[i], writes dst[i] — perfectly coalesced. Gated kernels read 2 inputs + write 1 output. silu_back reads 2 inputs + writes 1 output. No sycl::vec types, no multi-element processing. This is the single biggest optimization opportunity for these purely memory-bound kernels.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM used. Appropriate for embarrassingly parallel element-wise operations.

reduction_pattern.notes: No reductions. All operations are pure element-wise maps.

data_types.notes: Supports both F32 and F16 via template parameter T. F16 path reads half, converts to float for computation, converts back. All internal compute in float32 for accuracy. swiglu_oai is F32-only. Using half-precision compute would risk accuracy for operations like GELU and SILU.

math_functions.notes: All math functions use standard C library functions (IEEE compliant). No sycl::native:: usage anywhere in this file (or in any SYCL file in the project). For inference workloads, native math (1-2 ULP accuracy) is typically acceptable and faster. expf is the most impactful target (used in GELU_quick, SILU, sigmoid, exp, softplus, swiglu_oai, silu_back).

loop_analysis.notes: No loops in any kernel. Every kernel is a pure single-element map: read x[i], compute op(x[i]), write dst[i]. No #pragma unroll directives in the file.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: ALL operations are deeply memory-bound. Arithmetic intensity ranges from 0.12 FLOP/byte (trivial ops: abs, neg, relu) to 2.5 FLOP/byte (GELU with tanh). The B60's ridge point is ~27 FLOP/byte, so even the most compute-heavy op is ~10x below the threshold. Memory bandwidth optimization (vectorized loads/stores) is the primary lever.
anti_patterns: Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] on all 6 parallel_for launch sites — inconsistent with rest of codebase
No vectorized loads/stores — 1 element per work-item for purely memory-bound operations
Standard math functions where native math could improve throughput for inference
Integer division/modulo in gated kernels (i / n, i % n) — expensive on GPU, could use bitwise ops for power-of-2 n
Redundant block size macros in presets.hpp (SYCL_GELU_BLOCK_SIZE, SYCL_SILU_BLOCK_SIZE, etc.) all defined as 256 but never used

optimization_opportunities.description: Process 4-8 elements per work-item using sycl::vec<float,4> or manual multi-element processing. Currently each work-item handles exactly 1 float element (4B read + 4B write = 8 bytes traffic). For trivial ops like abs, neg, relu, sqr, floor — which are purely memory-bound at 0.12-0.25 FLOP/byte — vectorized 16-byte loads/stores would reduce work-item count by 4x and enable wider memory transactions, better amortizing launch overhead and improving effective bandwidth utilization.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.5-2.5x throughput for trivial ops (abs, neg, relu, sqr, floor, ceil, round, trunc). 1.2-1.5x for transcendental-heavy ops (GELU, SILU, sigmoid) where compute is a larger fraction. The improvement depends on how much of the kernel time is spent in memory access overhead vs compute.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Modify unary_op_kernel to process 4 elements per thread: each thread loads a sycl::vec<float,4>, applies op() to each component, and stores the result. Adjust global_size to k/4 (with a scalar cleanup loop for the tail). For the gated kernels, use sycl::vec<float,4> for both x and g inputs. The template structure makes this easy: add a vec4 variant of unary_op_kernel and dispatch based on alignment and size. For F16 path, use sycl::vec<sycl::half,8> (same 16-byte width).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Element-wise operations are embarrassingly parallel — vectorization does not change the computation, only the memory access pattern. Tail handling (k not divisible by 4) needs a scalar cleanup path. Must ensure 16-byte alignment of input/output pointers for vec4 loads.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] to all 6 kernel lambda functions (lines 93, 151, 389, 466, 510, 560). Every other kernel file in the SYCL backend consistently specifies this attribute, but element_wise.cpp omits it. Without it, the Intel compiler may select a non-optimal sub-group size (SIMD8 or SIMD32), potentially affecting register allocation, occupancy, and scheduling on Xe2.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 2-5% improvement from predictable sub-group scheduling. Ensures compiler generates SIMD16 code matching the hardware's native width. More importantly, this is a consistency fix aligning with the rest of the codebase.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] (or [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]]) to each lambda in parallel_for. Since these kernels don't use sub-group operations directly, the attribute primarily serves as a compiler hint for optimal code generation. Per the optimization guide section 1.2, only specify sub-group size when kernel logic requires it — these kernels don't strictly need it, but consistency with the codebase is valuable.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Simple attribute addition. No algorithmic change. If the compiler was already selecting SIMD16, this is a no-op. If it was selecting SIMD8 or SIMD32, this forces the native width which is generally better for element-wise ops on Xe2.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use sycl::native:: math functions for inference-time activation functions. Key targets: sycl::native::exp (used in 7+ ops: GELU_quick, SILU, sigmoid, exp, softplus, swiglu_oai, silu_back), sycl::native::log (softplus, log), sycl::native::sqrt (sqrt), sycl::native::sin/cos (sin, cos). Native math trades IEEE compliance for speed (1-2 ULP accuracy). For ML inference, this is typically acceptable.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% for transcendental-heavy ops (GELU, SILU, sigmoid, softplus). Minimal impact on trivial ops. The improvement is limited by the memory-bound nature — even with free compute, memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. Native math primarily helps by reducing instruction count and freeing execution units.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Create native math wrappers: native_expf() = sycl::native::exp(), etc. Gate behind a compile-time flag (GGML_SYCL_NATIVE_MATH) or runtime flag for accuracy-sensitive workloads. Apply to op_gelu_quick, op_silu, op_sigmoid, op_exp, op_softplus, swiglu_oai_single, silu_back_op_kernel, op_sin, op_cos, op_sqrt, op_log. Note: erff() and expm1f() have no native equivalents — keep standard versions.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Native math has lower accuracy (1-2 ULP vs 0.5 ULP). For most inference workloads this is fine, but for training or precision-sensitive applications it could cause issues. Should be gated behind a flag. GELU is the most sensitive — its tanh(x) based implementation amplifies any exp() error.

optimization_opportunities.description: For the gated kernels (GLU variants), replace integer division/modulo (i / n, i % n) with bitwise operations when n is a power of 2. In LLM architectures, the hidden dimension n is almost always a power of 2 (e.g., 4096, 11008, 14336). Integer division and modulo are expensive on GPUs (tens of cycles vs 1 cycle for bitwise ops).
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1-3% for gated kernels only. The integer div/mod is only 2 instructions per work-item, but at the GPU's clock rate of 2.4 GHz with 160 XVEs, saving 10+ cycles per work-item across millions of elements adds up. However, this is dwarfed by the memory bandwidth bottleneck.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add a power-of-2 fast path: if (n & (n-1) == 0) { j0 = (i >> log2_n) * o0 + (i & (n-1)); } else { j0 = (i / n) * o0 + (i % n); }. The log2_n can be computed once on the host and passed as a kernel argument. Alternatively, rely on the compiler to optimize when n is constexpr — but it's not constexpr in the current implementation.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Straightforward optimization. The bitwise path produces identical results for power-of-2 n. The fallback path handles non-power-of-2 cases. No accuracy impact.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add a small-tensor fast path that uses sycl::range<1>(k) (without nd_range) for tensors with fewer than 256 elements. Currently, even a 1-element tensor launches a full 256-wide work-group with 255 threads doing nothing. While this is a minor overhead for typical LLM workloads (hidden dims are thousands), it could matter for small auxiliary tensors in preprocessing or attention masking.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Negligible for typical inference (hidden dims > 1024). Could improve latency by 2-5 microseconds for small tensors (k < 256), which matters only if such kernels are on the critical path.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: In each *_sycl launch wrapper, add: if (k <= 256) { stream.parallel_for(sycl::range<1>(k), [=](sycl::id<1> idx) { ... }); } else { /* existing nd_range path */ }. This avoids the bounds check overhead for small tensors. Low priority because small tensors are rare in the hot path.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Adding a separate code path increases maintenance burden. The sycl::range path doesn't guarantee sub-group size. For small tensors the performance difference is negligible in practice.

kernels.efficiency_notes: This is a clean manual port with no DPCT artifacts, correct nd_range<1> usage, and appropriate work-group size (256). The primary efficiency loss is from scalar (1-element-per-thread) processing of purely memory-bound operations — vectorized loads/stores could nearly double throughput for trivial ops. The transcendental ops (GELU, SILU) are slightly compute-heavy but still memory-bound at the B60's ridge point. Using native math functions would help at the margins. Overall, the kernel is reasonably well-implemented but leaves bandwidth on the table due to lack of vectorization.

current_analysis.description: Gated Linear Unit (GLU) activation functions used in modern LLM architectures (SwiGLU, ReGLU, GeGLU, etc.). Covers 6 GLU ops (SWIGLU, REGLU, GEGLU, GEGLU_ERF, GEGLU_QUICK, SWIGLU_OAI) plus XIELU. GLU ops compute dst[i] = gate(x[i]) * g[i] where gate() varies by variant. Math copied from ggml-cuda/unary.cu to ensure numerical equivalence. Clean manual SYCL port — no DPCT artifacts.

launch_config.notes: All GLU ops use nd_range<1> with SYCL_GLU_BLOCK_SIZE=256 (defined in element_wise.hpp line 8). No [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size]] specified. swiglu_oai uses SYCL_NEG_BLOCK_SIZE=256 from presets.hpp. XIELU also uses 256.

memory_access.pattern: Linear coalesced reads and writes for contiguous tensors. GLU ops read 2 input arrays (x and g) and write 1 output array. XIELU reads 1 input and writes 1 output.
memory_access.notes: Each work-item processes exactly 1 element — no vectorization. Output writes are perfectly coalesced. Input reads are coalesced within rows but may stride at row boundaries when the output offset o0 != n (used for non-contiguous tensors). swiglu_oai has a different indexing pattern: reads from src0 with stride (3*n) to extract x, g, b components.

compute.dominant_operations: Transcendental math (expf, tanhf, erff, expm1f) for gate functions plus multiply with gate value. REGLU is simplest (relu + multiply = 0.17 FLOP/byte). GEGLU is most complex (tanh-based GELU approximation + multiply = 1.25 FLOP/byte).
compute.notes: All variants are deeply memory-bandwidth bound. The B60's ridge point is ~27 FLOP/byte — even GEGLU at 1.25 FLOP/byte is ~20x below threshold. Standard math functions used throughout (not native/fast-math variants).

data_types.notes: Generic GLU ops (glu_sycl template) support both F32 and F16 via src0->type dispatch. swiglu_oai is F32-only — explicitly operates on float pointers with no F16 path. XIELU supports F32 and F16.

sub_group_usage.notes: No sub-group operations. Pure element-wise map — each work-item is completely independent.

loop_structure.notes: No loops in any GLU kernel. Every kernel is a pure single-element map: read x[i] and g[i], compute gate(x[i]) * g[i], write dst[i]. swiglu_oai reads 3 components (x, g, b) from a strided layout.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: ALL GLU operations are deeply memory-bound. With 2 reads + 1 write per element (12 bytes for F32), arithmetic intensity ranges from 0.17 FLOP/byte (REGLU) to 1.25 FLOP/byte (GEGLU). Far below the B60's 27 FLOP/byte ridge point. Memory bandwidth is the sole bottleneck.
anti_patterns: No vectorized loads/stores — 1 element per work-item for purely memory-bound operations
64-bit integer division/modulo (i / n, i % n) in the hot path of every GLU kernel — expensive on GPU (tens of cycles per work-item)
Standard math functions where native math (sycl::native::exp, etc.) could improve throughput for inference
swiglu_oai is F32-only while all other GLU ops support F16 — inconsistent type coverage
Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] — same issue as sk_010

optimization_opportunities.description: Process 4 elements per work-item using sycl::vec<float,4> for both x and g inputs. Currently each work-item handles 1 element (8B read for x + 4B read for g + 4B write = 16 bytes per work-item for F32 GLU ops, or 12B for XIELU). Vectorized 16-byte loads/stores would reduce work-item count by 4x and enable wider memory transactions.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.3-1.8x throughput for GLU ops. Less impactful than sk_010 vectorization because GLU ops have slightly higher compute intensity (more transcendental math per byte transferred). Still the dominant optimization lever since all ops are memory-bound.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Modify glu_sycl kernel template to process 4 elements per thread. Load sycl::vec<float,4> for both src_x and src_g, apply gate function component-wise, store result. Adjust global_size to k/4 with scalar cleanup. For swiglu_oai, vectorization is more complex due to stride-3n indexing — may need to keep scalar path or use gather loads.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: GLU operations are embarrassingly parallel — vectorization changes only memory access pattern. Tail handling needed for k not divisible by 4. swiglu_oai's strided access pattern makes vectorization less straightforward than the generic GLU ops.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace 64-bit integer division/modulo (i / n, i % n) with cheaper alternatives. Every GLU kernel computes j0 = (i / n) * o0 + (i % n) to map global work-item index to source offsets. 64-bit integer division costs tens of cycles on GPU vs 1 cycle for bitwise ops. For power-of-2 n (common in LLMs: 4096, 8192, 14336), use bitwise AND and shift. For non-power-of-2, use Barrett reduction or compiler intrinsics.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1-3% for GLU kernels. The division is executed once per work-item, but with millions of elements the aggregate overhead is non-trivial. However, still dwarfed by memory bandwidth bottleneck.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add power-of-2 fast path: if ((n & (n-1)) == 0) { int shift = __builtin_ctz(n); j0 = (i >> shift) * o0 + (i & (n-1)); }. Alternatively, precompute the magic number for Barrett reduction on host and pass as kernel arg. Could also restructure the kernel to iterate over rows explicitly (outer loop over rows, inner range over columns) to eliminate division entirely.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Bitwise operations produce identical results for power-of-2 n. Barrett reduction needs careful implementation to avoid off-by-one. Restructuring to explicit row iteration is the safest approach but changes the kernel structure.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use sycl::native:: math functions for GLU gate computations. Key targets: sycl::native::exp (SWIGLU, GEGLU_QUICK), sycl::native::tanh via exp (GEGLU), erff (GEGLU_ERF). For inference workloads, 1-2 ULP accuracy loss is acceptable.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 3-8% for transcendental-heavy GLU variants (GEGLU, SWIGLU). Minimal for REGLU (which uses only relu — no transcendentals). Impact limited by memory-bound nature.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Same approach as opt_010_003 — use native math wrappers gated behind GGML_SYCL_NATIVE_MATH compile flag. Apply to: expf in op_swiglu/swiglu_oai, tanhf in op_geglu, erff in op_geglu_erf, expm1f in op_xielu. Note: erff has no sycl::native equivalent — keep standard version.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Same risk profile as opt_010_003. Native math has lower accuracy but is fine for inference. Should be gated behind a compile flag. GEGLU's tanh approximation is the most accuracy-sensitive.

optimization_opportunities.description: Specialize the contiguous case (o0 == n) to eliminate index computation entirely. When the output tensor is contiguous, j0 simplifies to just i — no division or modulo needed. In typical LLM inference, tensors are contiguous most of the time. Add a host-side branch to dispatch a simpler kernel for the contiguous case.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1-5% when tensors are contiguous (the common case). Eliminates both the 64-bit division and the multiply-add index computation. Combined with vectorization (opt_011_001), the contiguous path becomes a trivial load-compute-store loop.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: In glu_sycl wrapper, add: if (o0 == n) { dispatch simplified kernel where j0 = i directly; } else { dispatch current kernel with division; }. The simplified kernel can also more easily be vectorized since memory access is guaranteed sequential.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Host-side branch adds no GPU overhead. The contiguous kernel is strictly simpler than the general case. Only risk is code duplication — can be mitigated with a template parameter for contiguity.

kernels.efficiency_notes: Very similar to sk_010 (unary ops) — same code structure, same clean manual port, same WG=256 with nd_range<1>. The primary efficiency loss is from scalar processing of memory-bound operations. GLU ops have slightly higher arithmetic intensity than simple unary ops (0.17-1.25 vs 0.12-2.5 FLOP/byte) but are still deeply memory-bound. The 64-bit integer division is an additional overhead not present in sk_010's unary ops. Overall optimization potential is LOW because: (1) these are not on the critical inference path (GLU activation is a small fraction of total compute vs matmul), (2) the kernel is already correctly implemented with proper launch config, and (3) the main optimization (vectorization) provides only modest 1.3-1.8x improvement on an already-fast kernel.

kernels.name: element_wise (special unary)

launch_config.global_size_expression: 1D: ceil(k / BLOCK_SIZE) * BLOCK_SIZE where k = ggml_nelements(src0) or ggml_nelements(dst)
launch_config.notes: All 5 kernels (leaky_relu, silu_back, xielu, expm1, swiglu_oai) use nd_range<1> with work-group size 256. leaky_relu/silu_back/xielu/expm1 use SYCL_NEG_BLOCK_SIZE=256; swiglu_oai uses SYCL_GLU_BLOCK_SIZE=256. No [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size()]] specified on any kernel. Clean manual port — no DPCT artifacts, no nd_item<3>.

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: leaky_relu, silu_back, xielu, expm1: fully coalesced — each work-item reads x[i] and writes dst[i] where i = get_global_id(0). swiglu_oai: potentially strided when o0 != n due to index computation j0 = (i/n)*o0 + (i%n) — within a row, accesses are contiguous, but at row boundaries there's a stride gap when row stride differs from column count.
strided_accesses: swiglu_oai: index computation j0 = (i/n)*o0 + (i%n) introduces stride gaps at row boundaries when o0 != n
memory_patterns.notes: No sycl::vec types used in any kernel. All loads/stores are scalar (4 bytes for FP32, 2 bytes for FP16). Each work-item processes exactly 1 element.

slm_usage.notes: None of the 5 kernels use shared local memory. All are pure element-wise maps with no cross-work-item communication.

reduction_pattern.notes: Pure element-wise operations — no reductions needed.

data_types.supported_types: FP32 and FP16 for leaky_relu, silu_back, xielu, expm1; FP32-only for swiglu_oai
data_types.notes: All computation done in FP32 with casts from/to T (sycl::half or float). FP16 support via template <typename T> pattern on 4 of 5 kernels. swiglu_oai is explicitly FP32-only (matching CUDA). No opportunity for joint_matrix — these are element-wise ops.

math_functions.notes: All math functions use standard C/SYCL math (not sycl::native::). For inference-level precision (~2-3 ULP error acceptable), sycl::native::exp() could replace expf for silu_back and swiglu_oai. expm1f has no native equivalent in SYCL.

loop_analysis.notes: No inner loops in any of the 5 kernels. Each work-item processes exactly 1 element. No #pragma unroll directives needed.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: All 5 kernels are deeply memory-bound. Arithmetic intensity ranges: leaky_relu ~0.4 FLOP/byte, expm1 <0.5 FLOP/byte, silu_back ~0.7 FLOP/byte, swiglu_oai ~0.8 FLOP/byte, xielu ~1.5-2.0 FLOP/byte. All are far below the B60's compute intensity threshold of ~27 FLOP/byte. Performance is entirely determined by memory bandwidth utilization.
anti_patterns: No vectorized loads/stores — each work-item processes only 1 element for purely memory-bound operations
Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size()]] on all kernel launches — compiler free to choose sub-group size
swiglu_oai: 64-bit integer division/modulo (i/n, i%n) in hot path — expensive on GPU, no hardware support for int64 division
swiglu_oai: FP32-only while other special unary ops support FP16
Standard math functions (expf, expm1f) used where native approximations would suffice for inference precision

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized 4-wide loads/stores (sycl::vec<float,4> or sycl::vec<sycl::half,4>) so each work-item processes 4 elements instead of 1. For purely memory-bound kernels, vectorized access reduces memory transactions by 4x. Apply to all 5 kernels. leaky_relu, expm1, xielu, and silu_back have simple linear indexing that trivially supports vec4. swiglu_oai needs care due to strided index computation.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.5-2x throughput improvement from better memory bus utilization. The B60's 456 GB/s bandwidth is better utilized with 16-byte transactions (vec4 float) vs 4-byte scalar loads. Diminishing returns if the memory subsystem is already near saturation from concurrent work-groups.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change kernel to process 4 elements per work-item: load sycl::vec<float,4> v = *reinterpret_cast<const sycl::vec<float,4>*>(&x[i*4]); apply operation to each component; store similarly. Adjust grid size: num_blocks = ceil(k/4 / BLOCK_SIZE). Handle tail elements (k not divisible by 4) with a scalar fallback or by processing the last partial vec separately. For sycl::half, use sycl::vec<sycl::half,4> (8-byte loads). For swiglu_oai, vectorization is only safe when o0 == n (contiguous case).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Alignment must be ensured — ggml tensors are typically 32-byte aligned so vec4 float (16 bytes) is safe. Tail handling adds minor code complexity. No correctness risk for the math operations themselves.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace standard expf() with sycl::native::exp() in silu_back and swiglu_oai kernels. Native exp provides ~2-3 ULP error vs full precision, which is acceptable for activation function computation in neural network inference. This reduces the per-element compute latency, though the kernels are memory-bound so the impact is limited.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 2-5% throughput improvement. The expf call is the most expensive single operation in silu_back and swiglu_oai (~20+ cycles vs ~1-4 cycles for native). However, since these kernels are memory-bound, reducing compute latency only helps if it allows the memory pipeline to stay busier. More impactful for xielu's expm1f, but there is no sycl::native::expm1 equivalent.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace `expf(-x)` with `sycl::native::exp(-x)` in silu_back_op_kernel (line 502) and swiglu_oai_single (line 357). Verify inference accuracy is maintained by running the full test suite. Do NOT replace expm1f in xielu/expm1 — there is no native equivalent, and manual implementation (native::exp(x) - 1.0f) loses precision for small x.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Native math has lower precision (~2-3 ULP error). For activation functions this is generally acceptable, but edge cases near zero or very large/small inputs should be tested. The CUDA backend uses standard math for these same operations, so switching to native would make SYCL slightly less precise than CUDA.

optimization_opportunities.description: Evaluate increasing work-group size from 256 to 512 for these memory-bound kernels. Larger work-groups mean more concurrent memory requests per Xe-core, potentially improving memory-level parallelism and bandwidth utilization. However, 256 is already within the recommended range (256-512) and may be sufficient.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 0-5% throughput improvement. The benefit depends on whether the current 256-thread work-groups generate enough outstanding memory requests to saturate the memory bus. With 16 sub-groups per 256-thread work-group, occupancy may already be adequate.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change SYCL_NEG_BLOCK_SIZE from 256 to 512 for these kernels. This affects all unary/GLU/special-unary kernels that share this constant, so must verify no regressions. Alternatively, use a separate constant for the special unary kernels.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Doubling work-group size from 256 to 512 is within hardware limits (max 1024). May slightly increase register pressure per work-group but these simple kernels use very few registers. Main risk is shared constant affecting other kernels.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add FP16 support to swiglu_oai to match the other 4 special unary kernels. The current FP32-only restriction (matching CUDA) means FP16 models must dequantize to FP32 for SwiGLU-OAI, wasting bandwidth. The other GLU kernels in sk_011 already support FP16 via the generic gated template.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Up to 2x throughput for FP16 models using SwiGLU-OAI (halving memory traffic: 2 bytes per element vs 4 bytes). Only applicable when the model uses FP16 weights/activations with the SwiGLU-OAI activation pattern.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Template swiglu_oai_op_kernel and swiglu_oai_sycl on <typename T> (already done), but also need to add the FP16 dispatch in ggml_sycl_swiglu_oai. The math (fminf, fmaxf, expf) should remain in FP32 — only the load/store should use half. Update the assertion from src0->type == GGML_TYPE_F32 to allow GGML_TYPE_F16.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The CUDA backend does not support FP16 for swiglu_oai, so enabling it in SYCL would be a divergence. Must verify that the FP32 intermediate computation provides sufficient precision when inputs are FP16 (may lose information during the fminf/fmaxf clamping if half's limited range affects the limit parameter). Need to verify upstream dispatch actually sends FP16 tensors.

kernels.efficiency_notes: All 5 kernels are cleanly written native SYCL with zero DPCT artifacts. They use proper nd_range<1> with WG=256, correct bounds checking, and support FP16 (4 of 5). The primary efficiency loss is from scalar 1-element-per-work-item processing on purely memory-bound operations (0.4-2.0 FLOP/byte, all far below the 27 FLOP/byte ridge point). Vectorized vec4 loads/stores could improve bandwidth utilization by 1.5-2x. The integer division overhead in swiglu_oai adds ~5% cost. Overall optimization potential is LOW because: (1) special unary activations are not on the critical inference path (tiny fraction of total compute time vs matmul kernels), (2) the kernels are already correctly implemented with recommended launch configuration, (3) the main optimization (vectorization) provides modest improvement on already-fast kernels, and (4) native math provides marginal gains on memory-bound operations. These kernels fix 2 latent bugs from the CUDA source (xielu block count off-by-one, silu_back wrong divisor constant).

kernels.name: binbcast (binary broadcast)

launch_config.work_group_size: 3D: (bz, by, bx) where bx*by*bz <= 128. Typical: (1, 1, 128) for large ne0, (1, 4, 32) for medium ne0. 1D fallback: 128.
launch_config.global_size_expression: 3D: (gz*bz, gy*by, gx*bx) where gx=ceil(hne0/bx), gy=ceil(ne1/by), gz=ceil(ne2*ne3/bz), hne0=max(ne0/2,1). 1D fallback: ceil(ne0*ne1*ne2*ne3/128)*128.
launch_config.notes: Work-group size of 128 is below the recommended 256-512 for Intel GPUs. The grid halving (hne0 = ne0/2) means each work-item processes ~2 elements via the grid-stride loop. The 3D launch uses (z,y,x) ordering matching SYCL convention. The 1D fallback (k_bin_bcast_unravel) is used when gz > 65535 or gy > 65535. No [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size()]] specified — correct per optimization guide since no sub-group operations are used.

strided_accesses: When s00 != 1 (non-contiguous src0), src0_row[i0*s00] has strided access pattern
When s10 != 1 (non-contiguous src1), src1[i_src1 + i10*s10] has strided access
Broadcasting dimension access (i0 % ne10) can cause non-contiguous src1 reads when ne10 < ne0
memory_patterns.notes: All loads/stores are scalar. Adjacent work-items in dim-x read adjacent elements (i0, i0+1, ...), giving coalesced access when s00=1 and s10=1 (contiguous case). For the common case of contiguous ADD with no broadcasting, memory access is well-coalesced. The dimension collapsing optimization (lines 185-199) merges contiguous non-broadcast dimensions to maximize the inner dimension, which improves coalescing.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM used. The kernel is a simple element-wise operation with no data reuse. SLM would not help since each element is read once and written once.

reduction_pattern.notes: Pure element-wise operation — no reductions needed.

data_types.notes: All computation done in FP32 via casts: (float)src0_row[i0] and (float)src1[...], result cast back to dst_t. This matches CUDA behavior. The FP32 intermediate is needed for numerical correctness (especially for DIV). For F16×F16→F16 path, the FP32 intermediate adds 2 casts per element but ensures accuracy. No opportunity for joint_matrix — these are element-wise ops.

math_functions.notes: Only basic arithmetic (+, -, *, /) used. No transcendental functions. Division is the most expensive operation but is FP32 division which is hardware-supported.

hot_loops: Grid-stride loop in k_bin_bcast (line 75): for (i0 = i0s; i0 < ne0; i0 += grid_x) — processes ~2 elements per work-item due to hne0=ne0/2 grid halving. Not unrolled.
loop_analysis.notes: The grid-stride loop typically iterates 2 times (due to hne0=ne0/2). This is a reasonable approach but the loop body has integer modulo (i0 % ne10) which is expensive on GPU. The k_bin_bcast_unravel kernel has no inner loop — each work-item processes exactly 1 element.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: All 5 binary operations (ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV, REPEAT) are deeply memory-bound. Arithmetic intensity: ADD/SUB/MUL = 1 FLOP / 12 bytes (2 reads + 1 write × 4B each for F32) = 0.08 FLOP/byte. DIV = 1 FLOP / 12 bytes = 0.08 FLOP/byte. REPEAT = 0 FLOP / 8 bytes. All are far below the B60's compute intensity threshold of ~27 FLOP/byte. Performance is entirely determined by memory bandwidth utilization. The hne0=ne0/2 grid halving means each work-item processes 2 elements, giving 2x work per item, but this is partially offset by the grid-stride loop overhead.
anti_patterns: Work-group size 128 — below recommended 256-512 for Intel GPUs. Reduces occupancy and memory-level parallelism for memory-bound kernels.
No vectorized loads/stores — each work-item processes elements one-at-a-time via scalar loads. For contiguous tensors, vec4 loads could reduce memory transactions by 4x.

Expensive integer modulo operations: i2=i23/ne3, i3=i23%ne3, i0%ne10, i1%ne11, i2%ne12, i3%ne13 — all use plain % operator. CUDA uses fastdiv/fastmodulo (multiplication-based). On Intel GPUs, 32-bit integer division is ~20-30 cycles vs ~4 cycles for the multiply-shift trick.

Missing fused-add support — CUDA has ggml_cuda_op_fused_add supporting up to 8 additions in a single kernel launch (reduces kernel launch overhead and increases data reuse). SYCL version only supports 1 src1 operand.

3D nd_range with small per-dimension sizes — when ne1 is small (e.g., 1 for vector operations), the by dimension collapses to 1, wasting 2 of 3 nd_range dimensions. A 1D kernel with vectorized loads would be simpler and potentially faster.
Grid halving hne0=ne0/2 with grid-stride loop — an indirect way to get 2 elements per work-item. Direct vec2/vec4 processing with adjusted grid would be cleaner and more efficient.

optimization_opportunities.description: Increase work-group size from 128 to 256 for better occupancy and memory-level parallelism. For purely memory-bound kernels, larger work-groups generate more concurrent memory requests per Xe-core, improving bandwidth utilization. The current 128 gives 8 sub-groups per work-group (at SIMD16); 256 would give 16 sub-groups, doubling the memory-level parallelism per work-group.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% throughput improvement from better memory bandwidth utilization. The B60 has 20 Xe-cores each running multiple work-groups concurrently. With WG=128, fewer memory requests are in-flight per Xe-core. The improvement is larger for small tensors where fewer work-groups are launched.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change const int block_size = 128 to const int block_size = 256 on line 252. This affects both the 3D and 1D kernel paths. The bx/by/bz factorization (lines 257-259) will automatically adapt: for large ne0, bx=256 with by=bz=1. For moderate ne0, bx might be smaller with by>1. Verify that gz and gy don't exceed 65535 more often with the larger work-group (should be fine since gz/gy decrease with larger bz/by).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: 256 is within hardware limits (max 1024) and is the standard recommended size. The bx/by/bz factorization logic handles arbitrary block_size correctly. Main risk is edge cases where larger WG creates fewer total work-groups, reducing GPU utilization for small tensors.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized 4-wide loads/stores (sycl::vec<float,4>) for contiguous tensors where s00=1 and s10=1 (no striding). Each work-item would process 4 elements instead of the current ~2 (from hne0 grid halving). For F16, use sycl::vec<sycl::half,4> for 8-byte loads. This directly reduces memory transactions by 2-4x for the common contiguous case.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.5-3x throughput improvement for contiguous tensors (the dominant case in LLM inference: residual ADD, bias ADD, attention scaling MUL). The B60's 456 GB/s bandwidth is better utilized with 16-byte transactions (vec4 float) vs 4-byte scalar loads. For broadcasting cases (ne10 < ne0), vectorization is only safe when ne0 is a multiple of vec_width AND ne10 is a multiple of vec_width.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add a fast-path check in launch_bin_bcast: if s00==1 && s10==1 && s01==ne0 && s11==ne10 (both src0 and src1 are row-contiguous), launch a vectorized kernel variant. The vectorized kernel processes 4 elements per iteration: load vec4 from src0 and src1 (handling broadcasting by loading vec4 from src1 with appropriate index mapping), apply op, store vec4 to dst. The grid-stride loop iterates ceil(ne0/4/WG_SIZE) times. Keep the scalar kernel as fallback for strided/non-contiguous cases. Remove the hne0=ne0/2 halving for the vectorized path — process exactly ceil(ne0/4) work-items instead.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Alignment: ggml tensors are typically 32-byte aligned, so vec4 float (16 bytes) is safe. Tail handling needed when ne0 is not a multiple of 4. Broadcasting complicates vectorization — when ne10 < ne0, the src1 access pattern (i0 % ne10) means src1 elements repeat, preventing simple vec4 loads. The safe approach is to only vectorize when ne10 == ne0 (no broadcasting on dim 0) or ne10 == 1 (scalar broadcast, can use sycl::vec splat).

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace expensive integer division/modulo (%) operations with multiplication-based fast division. The kernel has 6 modulo operations per work-item (i23/ne3, i23%ne3, i0%ne10, i1%ne11, i2%ne12, i3%ne13). On Intel GPUs, 32-bit integer division takes ~20-30 cycles vs ~4 cycles for the multiply-shift trick. The CUDA version uses fastdiv/fastmodulo for all of these. Implement the standard Barrett reduction or magic number division technique.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-10% throughput improvement. With 6 division/modulo operations per work-item and ~2 elements per work-item, the integer math overhead is ~120-180 cycles vs ~24 cycles with fast division. For small tensors where the kernel is less memory-bound (compute becomes a larger fraction), the improvement is more significant. For large tensors that are deeply memory-bound, the improvement is smaller since the memory latency dominates.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Pre-compute magic numbers on host: for each divisor d, compute magic multiplier m and shift s such that (x * m) >> s == x / d. Pass m and s as kernel arguments alongside the original ne values. In the kernel, replace i23 / ne3 with fast_div(i23, ne3_magic, ne3_shift) and i23 % ne3 with i23 - fast_div(i23, ne3_magic, ne3_shift) * ne3. The CUDA reference uses uint3 to pack {divisor, magic, shift} into a single struct — a similar approach works for SYCL. Apply to both k_bin_bcast and k_bin_bcast_unravel kernels.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The multiply-shift fast division technique is well-established and exact for all 32-bit dividends when the magic numbers are computed correctly. No precision risk. The main complexity is computing the magic numbers on the host side and passing them as additional kernel arguments (6 extra uint32_t pairs). For power-of-2 divisors, can use simple bit shift instead.

optimization_opportunities.description: Implement fused multi-source ADD kernel to match CUDA's ggml_cuda_op_fused_add supporting up to 8 additions in a single kernel launch. In transformer inference, multiple residual additions are often chained (e.g., x + attn_out + ffn_out). Fusing these into a single kernel reduces kernel launch overhead (significant for small tensors) and improves data locality (the base tensor is loaded once instead of N times).
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Up to Nx bandwidth reduction for N-way fused add (since the destination tensor is only read/written once instead of N times). For 2-way fused add: ~33% fewer memory transactions (1 read base + 2 read addends + 1 write vs 2×(1 read + 1 read + 1 write)). Kernel launch overhead reduction: ~2-5 µs per fused kernel on Intel GPUs. Most impactful for small-to-medium tensors in batch-1 inference where launch overhead is a larger fraction of total time.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add variadic template parameter pack for additional src1 pointers, matching CUDA's approach: template <bin_op_type op, typename src0_t, typename src1_t, typename dst_t, typename... src1_ptrs>. The kernel accumulates: result = apply_bin_op<op>(result, src1[...]); result = apply_bin_op<op>(result, src1s[0][...]); ...; for each additional source. Host-side dispatch: ggml_sycl_op_fused_add(ctx, dst, n_fuse) with switch on n_fuse (2-8) to instantiate the correct template. Requires graph-level support to identify fusible sequences.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Requires upstream graph-level changes to identify and schedule fused operations. The kernel itself is straightforward (variadic template expansion), but the dispatch logic and tensor validation add complexity. Each n_fuse instantiation (2-8) generates a separate kernel binary, increasing compile time. Risk of template bloat with 7 fuse levels × 4 type combos × 5 ops = 140 kernel variants (though only ADD fusion is practically needed).

optimization_opportunities.description: Add a 1D fast-path for the common case of contiguous element-wise operations (no broadcasting, all strides=1). When src0, src1, and dst are all contiguous with no broadcasting (nr0=nr1=nr2=nr3=1 after collapsing), the entire operation is a simple 1D element-wise: dst[i] = op(src0[i], src1[i]). A 1D nd_range kernel avoids the overhead of 3D indexing, dimension collapsing logic, and the multiple modulo operations for broadcast index mapping.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 2-5% throughput improvement from eliminating 3D indexing overhead and modulo operations. The dimension collapsing already partially achieves this, but a dedicated 1D kernel avoids all the stride/broadcast machinery. More impactful combined with vectorization (opt_013_002).
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: In launch_bin_bcast, after dimension collapsing, check if ne1==1 && ne2==1 && ne3==1 && s00==1 && s10==1 (fully collapsed 1D contiguous). If so, launch a simple 1D kernel: q.parallel_for(nd_range<1>({N_rounded}, {256}), [=](nd_item<1> item) { int i = item.get_global_id(0); if (i < ne0) dst[i] = (dst_t)apply_bin_op<op>((float)src0[i], (float)src1[i]); }). This combines well with vectorization for maximum throughput on the common case.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The fast-path condition check adds trivial host-side overhead. The 1D kernel is simpler than the 3D kernel, so less risk of bugs. Must ensure the dimension collapsing has correctly reduced the problem to 1D before using this path.

kernels.efficiency_notes: The binbcast kernel is a clean native SYCL implementation with zero DPCT artifacts. It correctly handles 4D broadcasting, dimension collapsing for contiguous tensors, type dispatch for F32/F16 mixed types, and has a 1D fallback for large grids. However, it has several performance gaps: (1) WG=128 is below the recommended 256 for memory-bound kernels, reducing occupancy, (2) no vectorized loads despite being purely memory-bound (0.08 FLOP/byte for ADD — deeply below the 27 FLOP/byte ridge point), (3) 6 expensive integer modulo operations per work-item where CUDA uses fast division, (4) missing fused-add support that CUDA provides for up to 8-way addition fusion. The overall potential is MEDIUM because: (a) ADD is the most frequently called operation in transformer inference (residual connections, every layer), so even modest per-call improvement accumulates across the model, (b) the vectorization + fast-div + WG size improvements are complementary and can compound to 1.5-3x improvement for contiguous ADD, (c) the fused-add feature provides an additional bandwidth reduction path for chained additions.

kernels.name: repeat_back

launch_config.global_size_expression: 3D: (ne2*ne3, ne1, ceil(ne0/WARP_SIZE)*WARP_SIZE). block_dims=(1,1,WARP_SIZE=16). Each work-item handles one output element in dim0, with nested loops summing over repeat factors in all 4 dimensions.
launch_config.notes: Work-group size of 16 (just WARP_SIZE) is extremely small — well below the recommended 256-512 for Intel GPUs. Only 1 sub-group per work-group, providing minimal memory-level parallelism. The 3D nd_range uses dimensions (ne2*ne3, ne1, gx*WARP_SIZE) but only dim2 (x) has multiple work-items per work-group — dims 0 and 1 have work-group extent of 1, making them single-thread dimensions within each work-group. Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] attribute.

strided_accesses: When s00 != 1 (non-contiguous src0), reads become strided with stride s00 elements between consecutive thread accesses in dim0
Higher-dimensional loop iterations (i1, i2, i3 loops) access non-adjacent memory locations separated by s01, s02, s03 strides
memory_patterns.notes: Source reads: src[i3*s03 + i2*s02 + i1*s01 + i0*s00]. When s00==1 (contiguous, the common case), consecutive work-items in dim0 read consecutive elements — coalesced. The innermost loop (over i0) strides by ne0 elements, which may not be cache-friendly for large ne0. Output writes: dst[tid3*ne2*ne1*ne0 + tid2*ne1*ne0 + tid1*ne0 + tid0] — fully coalesced since consecutive work-items write to consecutive dst positions. All loads and stores are scalar (4-byte float), no vectorization.

slm_usage.notes: No shared local memory used. Each work-item independently accumulates its own sum in a private register. No cross-thread communication or reduction is needed because each output element maps to exactly one work-item.

reduction_pattern.notes: Each work-item accumulates sum in a private T register across a 4-deep nested loop: for i3 (stride ne3), for i2 (stride ne2), for i1 (stride ne1), for i0 (stride ne0). The total iterations per work-item = (ne03/ne3) * (ne02/ne2) * (ne01/ne1) * (ne00/ne0) — which is the product of repeat factors across all dimensions. No cross-thread reduction is needed.

data_types.notes: Template parameter T but only instantiated for float (GGML_TYPE_F32) in the switch statement (line 84-93). The default case asserts false. No FP16 support — this limits usage to F32-only backward pass operations.

math_operations.notes: No special math functions used. The kernel performs only: (1) integer index arithmetic (multiplication and addition for linear index computation), (2) integer modulo/division (tid23 % ne2, tid23 / ne2), (3) floating-point addition (sum += ...). Purely arithmetic with no transcendental or special functions.

synchronization.notes: No barriers, no atomics, no synchronization of any kind. Each work-item is fully independent — reads from src, accumulates in private register, writes to unique dst location. Clean async submission via queue.parallel_for with no explicit wait.

loop_structure.notes: 4-deep nested loop (lines 32-40): for i3 (tid3 to ne03, step ne3), for i2 (tid2 to ne02, step ne2), for i1 (tid1 to ne01, step ne1), for i0 (tid0 to ne00, step ne0). Trip counts equal the repeat factors: typically 1 in most dimensions (no repeat), occasionally 2-4 for models that use repeat on specific dimensions. When all repeat factors are 1, each loop body executes exactly once (degenerate case — simple copy with reduction). No #pragma unroll annotations despite typically short trip counts.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: Arithmetic intensity is extremely low: for the common case of repeat factor 1 in all dimensions, the kernel performs 0 FLOPs per element (just a copy: sum = src[...], dst[...] = sum). For repeat factor R (total across all dims), it performs R-1 additions per output element with R reads × 4 bytes + 1 write × 4 bytes = (R+1)*4 bytes, giving (R-1)/((R+1)*4) FLOP/byte. Even with R=8, that's 7/36 = 0.19 FLOP/byte — far below the B60's 27 FLOP/byte ridge point. Performance is entirely determined by memory bandwidth utilization, which is poor due to the tiny work-group size (16) and lack of vectorization.
anti_patterns: Work-group size of 16 (WARP_SIZE only) — far below recommended 256-512. Only 1 sub-group per work-group, severely limiting memory-level parallelism and occupancy per Xe-core. Should increase to at least 256.

3D nd_range with work-group dims (1,1,16) — dims 0 and 1 have extent 1, providing no parallelism within the work-group for those dimensions. The 3D structure adds overhead for what is essentially a 1D parallel-for over output elements.
No vectorized loads or stores — all memory accesses are scalar 4-byte float. For the contiguous case (s00==1), vec4 loads could reduce memory transactions by 4x.
Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] attribute — compiler may choose suboptimal sub-group size.
Integer division and modulo in hot path: tid23 % ne2 and tid23 / ne2 (lines 24-25) use expensive 64-bit integer division since tid23 is int64_t. Could use 32-bit or fast-division trick.
No #pragma unroll on the 4-deep nested loop — for the common case of repeat factor 1, the compiler may not optimize away the loop overhead without the hint.
FP32 only — no F16 support despite F16 being common in inference. The CUDA version (k_repeat_back in binbcast.cu) is also F32-only, so this is inherited.
Direct CUDA port structure — the kernel retains CUDA's thread/block mapping pattern (WARP_SIZE as work-group width) without adapting to Intel GPU's preferred larger work-groups.

optimization_opportunities.description: Increase work-group size from 16 to 256 for better occupancy and memory-level parallelism. The current WG=16 means only 1 sub-group per work-group, severely underutilizing the Xe-core's ability to interleave memory requests across multiple sub-groups. With WG=256, 16 sub-groups can be active per work-group, providing much better memory latency hiding.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-30% throughput improvement from better memory bandwidth utilization, especially for larger output tensors. The improvement is most significant when there are few output elements (ne0*ne1*ne2*ne3 is small), where the GPU cannot fill enough work-groups to saturate the memory subsystem with the current tiny WG size.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change block_dims from (1,1,WARP_SIZE) to (1,1,256). Update gx calculation: gx = (ne0 + 255) / 256. Alternatively, use a 1D nd_range since dims 0 and 1 have work-group extent of 1 anyway — flatten the 3D grid into 1D with total_work_items = ne0 * ne1 * ne2 * ne3, then recover (tid0, tid1, tid2, tid3) via division/modulo inside the kernel. This is cleaner and avoids the 3D overhead.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: 256 is within hardware limits. The kernel has no inter-thread communication, so changing WG size has no correctness impact. The only risk is if ne0 is very small (< 256), in which case some work-items will exit early via the tid0 >= ne0 guard — but this already happens with WG=16 when ne0 < 16.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add vectorized vec4 loads/stores for the contiguous case (s00==1, all repeat factors are 1). When repeat_back is a simple copy (all repeat factors = 1), vec4 float loads would reduce memory transactions by 4x. When s00==1 and repeat factors > 1 in dim0 only, the innermost loop reads can be vectorized.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.5-2x throughput for the contiguous copy case. For the more common case with small repeat factors, the improvement is smaller since the inner loop has few iterations and vectorization of the accumulation loop is less straightforward.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add a fast-path: if s00==1 and ne00/ne0 is the only non-trivial repeat factor, process 4 elements per work-item using sycl::vec<float,4>. For the general case, keep the scalar kernel. Check ne0 % 4 == 0 for the vectorized path. The output write is always contiguous (dst is asserted contiguous on line 69), so vec4 stores are always safe when ne0 % 4 == 0.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Vectorized path is only used for the contiguous case with aligned dimensions, so no correctness risk. The scalar fallback handles all edge cases. Main complexity is determining when vectorization is safe across the nested loop structure.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] attribute to ensure the compiler uses the native SIMD16 width. Without this, the compiler may choose SIMD8 or SIMD32, potentially causing incorrect behavior if any sub-group operations are added in the future, and suboptimal register allocation.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 0-5% improvement — primarily ensures predictable behavior rather than direct speedup. The compiler likely already chooses SIMD16 for this simple kernel, but the attribute makes this explicit and prevents regressions.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add the attribute to the lambda in the parallel_for call: [=](sycl::nd_item<3> item) [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] { ... }. This is a one-line change.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: No risk — this is a best-practice annotation that the current code already implicitly relies on (WARP_SIZE=16 is the work-group x-dimension).

kernels.efficiency_notes: The repeat_back kernel is a direct CUDA port that correctly implements backward-pass summation over repeated dimensions. It has zero DPCT artifacts and clean SYCL code. However, it has several performance gaps: (1) WG=16 is far below recommended 256, providing only 1 sub-group per work-group and severely limiting memory-level parallelism, (2) no vectorized loads/stores for the memory-bound operation, (3) 64-bit integer division in the hot path (tid23 % ne2, tid23 / ne2), (4) no sub-group size attribute. The overall potential is LOW because: (a) repeat_back is a backward-pass kernel rarely called during inference (the primary use case), (b) it typically processes small tensors with small repeat factors (often all 1s), (c) the optimization opportunities (larger WG, vectorization) would provide meaningful improvement but the kernel's total contribution to end-to-end latency is negligible, (d) only F32 is supported, matching the CUDA reference. The 35-50% efficiency estimate reflects the poor WG utilization and scalar memory access pattern, but the absolute time spent in this kernel is tiny.

kernels.name: softmax

launch_config.global_size_expression: Forward: nrows * 256 (1D). Backward: nrows * WARP_SIZE (1D)
launch_config.notes: Forward kernel uses proper nd_range<1> with WG=256 — good for Intel GPUs. Backward kernel uses only WG=WARP_SIZE=16 (1 sub-group per work-group) — far below recommended 256-512. Both correctly specify [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]]. 1D nd_range is cleaner than the 3D CUDA grid but requires manual decomposition of rowx into (i01, i02, i03) with expensive 64-bit integer division.

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: Both kernels use row-parallel processing where adjacent threads access adjacent columns: x_row[col0 + tid]. Since columns are contiguous in memory, this yields perfectly coalesced accesses within each sub-group.
strided_accesses: Mask addressing uses byte-offset computation (nb11/nb12/nb13) which may produce non-unit stride for non-contiguous mask tensors
In use_shared=false mode, Pass 2 reads from dst_row (written in Pass 1) which may have been evicted from L1 cache for large rows
memory_patterns.notes: All loads/stores are scalar 4-byte (float) via direct array indexing. No sycl::vec types used. For the common case of ncols=4096 (LLaMA head dim), each thread processes 4096/256=16 elements across 16 loop iterations — each iteration loads 1 float. Using vec4 loads could reduce memory transactions by 4x and process 4 elements per iteration.

slm_usage.slm_bytes_forward_with_cache: variable: (WARP_SIZE + padded_ncols) * 4 bytes. For ncols=4096: (16+4096)*4 = 16448 bytes
slm_usage.slm_threshold: 49152 bytes (48KB hardcoded) — rows with padded_ncols > ~12272 fall back to use_shared=false
slm_usage.notes: Forward kernel has two SLM modes: use_shared=true caches all intermediate vals in SLM (good for locality but limited by 48KB hardcoded threshold), use_shared=false writes to dst (global memory) as scratch. The 48KB limit is conservative — Intel Xe2 has 64KB SLM per Xe-core, but multiple work-groups may share an Xe-core. Backward kernel uses zero SLM — relies only on sub-group shuffles via warp_reduce_sum(). The WARP_SIZE floats for inter-warp reduction in block_reduce is minimal (64 bytes).

reduction_pattern.reduction_details: Forward: uses block_reduce<MAX> and block_reduce<SUM> which internally call warp_reduce_max/warp_reduce_sum (sub-group butterfly via dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor) followed by SLM-based inter-warp reduction (lane 0 of each warp writes to shared_vals[], first warp reads and reduces again). The broadcast after block_reduce uses an explicit SLM write-barrier-read pattern (lines 80-84, 106-110). Backward: uses warp_reduce_sum() — pure sub-group butterfly reduction, no SLM needed since WG=WARP_SIZE.

data_types.notes: Softmax requires float32 precision for numerical stability (log-sum-exp can overflow in FP16). The mask input supports FP16 (converted to float via t2f32), which is correct. No matrix operations, so joint_matrix is not applicable.

math_functions.notes: sycl::exp is called once per element per row (Pass 2). For ncols=4096, WG=256: each thread calls exp 16 times. Using sycl::native::exp could save 2-4 cycles per call with sufficient precision for softmax (the normalization step corrects small errors). sycl::fmax is a built-in that should already compile to native hardware min/max. dpct::pow in get_alibi_slope is called once per row — negligible.

hot_loops: Forward Pass 1 (line 67): iterates ceil(ncols/256) times per thread, NOT unrolled (dynamic trip count)
Forward Pass 2 (line 88): iterates ceil(ncols/256) times per thread, NOT unrolled
Forward Pass 3 (line 115): iterates ceil(ncols/256) times per thread, NOT unrolled
Backward dot product loop (line 238): iterates ceil(ncols/WARP_SIZE) times per thread, NOT unrolled
Backward output loop (line 244): iterates ceil(ncols/WARP_SIZE) times per thread, NOT unrolled
loop_analysis.notes: None of the loops are unrolled. The CUDA version has compile-time specializations for ncols_template={32,64,128,256,512,1024,2048,4096} which enable #pragma unroll and eliminate bounds checks. The SYCL version lacks this entirely — always uses runtime ncols with 'if (col >= ncols) break' bounds checks in every iteration. For the common case ncols=128 (head_dim in attention), the loop body executes only once but still pays the bounds-check overhead.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: Softmax is a 3-pass algorithm over the row data (load+max, exp+sum, normalize), giving arithmetic intensity of ~3 FLOPs per byte read (3 passes * 1 FLOP / 4 bytes). This is far below the 27 ops/byte compute intensity threshold, making it firmly memory-bandwidth bound. The key to performance is minimizing memory traffic (use SLM caching to avoid 3 global memory passes) and maximizing bandwidth utilization (coalesced vectorized loads). For small rows (ncols <= 256), the overhead of block_reduce and barrier operations can dominate.
anti_patterns: Missing column-parallel cooperative variant (ck_100) — CUDA has soft_max_f32_parallelize_cols for the large-ncols few-rows case, SYCL has no equivalent
No compile-time specialization for common ncols values — CUDA specializes for {32,64,128,256,512,1024,2048,4096} with unrolled loops, SYCL always uses runtime ncols with bounds checks
Hardcoded 48KB SLM threshold (line 171) instead of querying device's actual local memory size — Intel Xe2 has 64KB per Xe-core
Backward kernel work-group size = WARP_SIZE (16) — only 1 sub-group, far below recommended 256-512 for Intel GPUs
No vectorized loads/stores — all scalar float loads for a purely memory-bound kernel
64-bit integer division in rowx decomposition (lines 44-46) — i03 = rowx / (ne01*ne02), i02 = (rowx - ...) / ne01 — could use the 3D grid from CUDA to avoid this
dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor in warp_reduce_sum/warp_reduce_max (called from block_reduce) — DPCT artifact, should use sycl::reduce_over_group
dpct::pow in get_alibi_slope — DPCT artifact, should use sycl::pow or std::pow
Three separate passes over global memory when use_shared=false (vals written to dst as scratch) — could be fused into fewer passes with register tiling

optimization_opportunities.description: Add compile-time specialization for common ncols values to match CUDA's approach. The CUDA kernel specializes for ncols_template={32,64,128,256,512,1024,2048,4096} with matched block sizes, enabling #pragma unroll and eliminating bounds checks. The SYCL kernel always uses runtime ncols with 'if (col >= ncols) break' in every loop iteration. For softmax in attention (ncols=head_dim, typically 64/80/96/128), this overhead is proportionally significant since each thread only processes 1-2 elements per loop body.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-25% throughput improvement for common ncols values. Largest impact for small ncols (64-256) where the loop body is very short and bounds-check overhead is proportionally high. Compile-time ncols also allows the compiler to constant-fold the number of iterations and optimize register allocation.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Create a launch_soft_max_kernels_sycl template dispatcher similar to CUDA's variadic fold expression (softmax.cu lines 272-300). Use constexpr ncols_template and block_size_template parameters on the kernel. Specialize for ncols_template in {32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096}. For ncols matching a template value, the loops become compile-time fixed trip counts enabling #pragma unroll. The block_size should also be specialized: min(ncols, 1024) as in CUDA. Fall through to the dynamic variant for non-matching ncols.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: No algorithmic change — just wrapping existing kernel in templates. Increases binary size (8 specializations * 4 variants = 32 kernel instances) but this is acceptable. Well-proven approach (CUDA uses the same technique).

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized vec4 loads/stores (sycl::vec<float,4>) for all three passes of the forward kernel and both passes of the backward kernel. Currently all loads are scalar (1 float = 4 bytes per transaction). For the memory-bound softmax kernel, wider loads directly improve bandwidth utilization. Each thread would process 4 elements per loop iteration instead of 1, reducing the loop trip count by 4x and the number of memory transactions proportionally.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 30-50% throughput improvement. Softmax is purely memory-bandwidth bound (~3 FLOPs/byte vs 27 threshold). Wider loads improve memory bus utilization from ~40% (scalar) to ~80% (vec4) by better matching the 64-byte cache line granularity. The forward kernel performs 3 passes, so the savings compound.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: In each loop, replace `float val = x_row[col]` with `sycl::vec<float,4> v = *reinterpret_cast<const sycl::vec<float,4>*>(&x_row[col])` for the 4-element load. Process all 4 elements, then store 4-wide. Requires ncols alignment to 4 (common in practice). The loop step changes from block_size to block_size*4. Need a scalar tail loop for ncols not divisible by 4. For the use_shared path, vals in SLM should also be accessed as vec4. For the mask, if T=sycl::half, use sycl::vec<sycl::half,4> loads.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Requires alignment checking — ncols must be divisible by 4 for the fast path (fall back to scalar for unaligned). Some mask tensors may have non-standard strides that prevent vectorized access. The use_shared=true path needs careful SLM alignment for vec4 access.
