optimization_opportunities.description: Increase backward kernel (soft_max_back) work-group size from WARP_SIZE (16) to 256 by grouping 16 sub-groups per work-group, each computing a different row. Current single-sub-group work-groups severely underutilize Intel GPU occupancy. The backward kernel uses only sub-group reduction (no SLM), so grouping independent sub-groups is straightforward.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 20-40% throughput improvement for the backward kernel from better occupancy and memory-level parallelism. The B60 has 64 hardware threads per Xe-core; with 16-thread work-groups, utilization is poor. With 256-thread work-groups (16 sub-groups), 16 rows are processed concurrently per work-group.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change from `global(nrows * WARP_SIZE), local(WARP_SIZE)` to `global(ceil(nrows/16) * 256), local(256)`. Each sub-group computes a different row: `rowx = item.get_group(0) * num_subgroups + sub_group_id`. Add bounds check `if (rowx >= nrows) return`. No SLM needed — each sub-group is fully independent. The warp_reduce_sum call already operates on the sub-group level.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Sub-groups are independent (each computes a different row's dot product). Pattern proven in MMVQ reordered kernels. Only edge case: nrows < 16 → some sub-groups idle, but bounds check handles this.

optimization_opportunities.description: Increase the SLM threshold from the hardcoded 48KB (49152 bytes) to the device's actual local memory limit. Intel Xe2 has 64KB SLM per Xe-core. The current conservative 48KB limit causes rows with ncols > ~12272 to fall back to use_shared=false (writing intermediate values to global memory as scratch), when they could fit in the actual 64KB SLM budget. For ncols=16384 (needed for some long-context models), this would keep the kernel in the fast SLM-cached path.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-20% improvement for ncols in the range 12272-16000 that currently fall back to the slow use_shared=false path. The fast path avoids writing intermediate exp() values to global memory and re-reading them, saving 2 global memory round-trips per row.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Query the device's local memory size at dispatch time: `stream.get_device().get_info<sycl::info::device::local_mem_size>()`. Store this in the backend context for reuse. Compare against `shared_bytes_needed` dynamically. For 64KB devices, the threshold becomes ~15872 columns (vs 12272 currently). Alternatively, use a conservative 56KB threshold (64KB minus overhead for inter-warp reduction buffers and runtime alignment).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Straightforward parameter change. Only risk is if multiple work-groups share the same Xe-core and both allocate SLM — but the runtime handles this by scheduling fewer work-groups per Xe-core. Query-based approach is safe and portable.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace dpct::permute_sub_group_by_xor butterfly reductions in warp_reduce_sum/warp_reduce_max (called by block_reduce) with sycl::reduce_over_group(sub_group, val, op). The current implementation uses a manual XOR butterfly pattern (DPCT artifact of CUDA __shfl_xor_sync). While functionally correct, the sycl::reduce_over_group API allows the compiler to generate optimal reduction code for the target hardware and eliminates the DPCT dependency.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 3-8% improvement from potentially better compiler code generation. The reduce_over_group API is the idiomatic SYCL approach and maps directly to Intel GPU sub-group reduction instructions. Note: this optimization is in common.hpp and affects ALL kernels using block_reduce/warp_reduce_sum/warp_reduce_max.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: In common.hpp, replace the float warp_reduce_sum() overloads (lines 444-452, 417-424) with `return sycl::reduce_over_group(sg, val, sycl::plus<float>())`. Replace warp_reduce_max() (lines 484-503) with `return sycl::reduce_over_group(sg, val, sycl::maximum<float>())`. The int warp_reduce_sum (lines 438-442) already uses reduce_over_group — extend this pattern to all types. Keep backward compatibility by maintaining the function signatures.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Standard SYCL API replacement. The int overload already uses reduce_over_group successfully. Affects all kernels using these helpers, so broad testing needed, but the replacement is semantically identical.

optimization_opportunities.description: Implement dynamic block_size scaling for the forward kernel matching CUDA's approach. Currently SYCL always uses block_size=256 regardless of ncols. CUDA dynamically selects block_size as the next power of 2 >= ncols, from WARP_SIZE up to 1024. For ncols <= 32 (e.g., head_dim=32 in some models), CUDA uses only 32 threads per work-group, minimizing thread divergence and wasted work. For ncols=8192+, CUDA uses 1024 threads to maximize parallelism within a row.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% improvement for extreme ncols values. For ncols=32, reducing from 256 to 32 threads eliminates 224 idle threads. For ncols=8192, increasing from 256 to 512 or 1024 threads reduces the loop trip count from 32 to 8-16, improving throughput. For the common ncols=128 case, 256 is already near-optimal.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Compute `nth = WARP_SIZE; while (nth < ncols && nth < 1024) nth *= 2;` then pass as template parameter if using compile-time specialization (opt_015_001), or as a runtime parameter. The block_reduce function already handles dynamic block sizes via its template parameter. Must adjust SLM allocation for the WARP_SIZE inter-warp buffer size.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: CUDA already uses this exact approach. block_reduce supports dynamic block sizes. Only risk is if some ncols values cause degenerate performance at certain block sizes — profile to verify.

optimization_opportunities.description: For the use_shared=false path (large rows that don't fit in SLM), implement a 2-pass fused approach instead of the current 3-pass approach. Pass 1: load x, compute scaled+masked values, find max, store to dst. Pass 2: load from dst, compute exp(val-max), accumulate sum, write exp/sum to dst. This saves one full global memory round-trip compared to the current 3-pass approach (load-max, load-exp-sum, load-normalize).
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-15% improvement for the use_shared=false path (ncols > ~12K). Saving one global memory pass for a memory-bound kernel is significant. However, this path is only triggered for very wide rows, which are less common in typical transformer inference.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Fuse Pass 2 and Pass 3: after computing exp(vals[col] - max_val), immediately multiply by inv_sum and write to dst. This requires computing inv_sum first, which means Pass 2 must do the exp and sum reduction, then a third mini-pass (using only registers for the most recent block of values) writes the normalized result. Alternatively, use online softmax (compute running max and running sum in a single pass, then normalize in a second pass) for a true 2-pass implementation.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Online softmax (running max+sum in single pass) changes the numerical computation order, which may produce slightly different results. The fused approach requires register spilling for the overlap block. Need to validate numerical accuracy against the 3-pass reference.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace 64-bit integer division in rowx decomposition (lines 44-46) with either a 3D nd_range grid (like CUDA's dim3(ne01, ne02, ne03)) or precomputed reciprocals. The current code performs i03 = rowx / (ne01*ne02) and i02 = (...) / ne01 — expensive 64-bit integer divisions executed once per row per work-item. For the forward kernel this is minor (once per row), but for the backward kernel with WARP_SIZE threads processing one row each, it adds latency.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1-3% improvement. The division is executed once per work-group (forward) or once per row (backward), so the absolute time is small. However, 64-bit integer division on Intel GPUs is emulated (tens of cycles), so it's pure overhead.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Option A: Use nd_range<3>(sycl::range<3>(ne03, ne02, ne01) * sycl::range<3>(1, 1, block_size), sycl::range<3>(1, 1, block_size)) to get i01/i02/i03 directly from work-group IDs. Option B: Pass precomputed reciprocals (1.0/ne01, 1.0/(ne01*ne02)) and use float multiply + truncate for the division. CUDA uses Option A via its 3D grid.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Using nd_range<3> is straightforward and matches CUDA's approach. The block_size only applies to dimension 0. No algorithmic change.

kernels.efficiency_notes: The forward softmax kernel is reasonably well-implemented for Intel GPUs: proper WG=256, correct reqd_sub_group_size, SLM caching of intermediate values, and efficient block_reduce for inter-warp communication. The main gaps are: (1) no vectorized loads for a purely memory-bound kernel, (2) no compile-time specialization for common ncols values (CUDA has 8 specializations), (3) hardcoded 48KB SLM threshold missing 16KB of available space on Xe2, (4) missing cooperative column-parallel variant for extreme ncols cases. The backward kernel is weaker: only 16 threads per work-group, pure scalar loads, no vectorization. Overall, the forward kernel is the most important variant (used in every attention layer), and it's at roughly 40-55% of achievable bandwidth for common sequence lengths.

kernels.name: rope

launch_config.global_size_expression: nd_range<2>(range<2>(nr, n_blocks_x * 256), range<2>(1, 256)) where n_blocks_x = ceil(ne00 / (2*256))
launch_config.notes: All 4 kernel variants (rope_norm, rope_neox, rope_multi, rope_vision) use the same launch configuration: nd_range<2> with WG=(1, 256). Grid dim 0 dispatches one work-item per row (nr = total rows across all batches/heads/seq), dim 1 tiles over element pairs within a row. Each work-item processes exactly 2 elements (one rotation pair). WG=256 is correct for Intel GPUs. All have [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]]. Matches CUDA's dim3(1, CUDA_ROPE_BLOCK_SIZE, 1) = dim3(1, 256, 1) grid layout. The backward pass (rope_back) reuses the same kernels with forward=false template parameter — no separate backward kernel.

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: For rope_norm: adjacent work-items in dim 1 process adjacent element pairs (i0=2*global_id(1)), so x[ix+0] and x[ix+1] are strided by 2 elements across work-items — partially coalesced. For rope_neox/multi/vision: the two elements of each pair are at offset n_dims/2 apart (x[ix+0] and x[ix+n_dims/2]), causing two separate cache line accesses per work-item, but within each access, adjacent work-items touch adjacent addresses — coalesced within each half.
strided_accesses: rope_neox/multi/vision read split-half pairs: x[ix+0] and x[ix+n_dims/2] are n_dims/2 elements apart (typically 32-64 elements = 128-256 bytes), causing dual cache line access per work-item
pos[i2] read is broadcast-like — all work-items in same row read same pos value, but different rows read different pos values. L1 cache handles this well.
memory_patterns.notes: All loads and stores are scalar 4-byte (float) or 2-byte (half). CUDA's rope_norm uses ggml_cuda_memcpy_1<8> (float2) / ggml_cuda_memcpy_1<4> (half2) for coalesced paired writes via store_coaelsced lambda. SYCL uses two separate scalar stores: dst[idst+0] and dst[idst+1]. For rope_norm where the pair is adjacent, this could be a single float2/sycl::vec<float,2> store. For neox/multi/vision, the pair is at n_dims/2 offset so paired stores don't help.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM is used. RoPE is an embarrassingly parallel element-wise operation — each work-item independently rotates one pair of elements. No inter-work-item communication needed. pos[] and freq_factors[] are read-only and small enough to fit in L1/L2 cache. SLM would not help here.

reduction_pattern.notes: No reduction. Each work-item independently reads 2 elements, computes sin/cos rotation, writes 2 elements. No cross-work-item communication.

data_types.notes: Rotation is always computed in FP32 (input cast to float via static_cast, result cast back to T). This is correct — sin/cos need FP32 precision. SYCL version enforces src0->type == dst->type, so only F32→F32 and F16→F16 are supported. CUDA additionally supports F32→F16 conversion for the fused ROPE+VIEW+SET_ROWS path. No matrix operations, so joint_matrix is not applicable.

functions: sycl::pow(theta_scale, i0/2.0f) — called once per work-item in all 4 variants to compute theta_base
sycl::cos(theta) — called once per work-item via rope_yarn
sycl::sin(theta) — called once per work-item via rope_yarn
sycl::fmax — called once per work-item in rope_yarn_ramp (only when ext_factor != 0)
sycl::fmin — called once per work-item in rope_yarn_ramp (only when ext_factor != 0)
sycl::log — called once per work-item in rope_yarn (only when ext_factor != 0)
math_functions.notes: The dominant transcendentals are sycl::pow, sycl::sin, and sycl::cos, each called once per work-item. sycl::pow(theta_scale, i0/2.0f) computes theta_scale^(i0/2) — this is equivalent to exp(i0/2 * log(theta_scale)) which could use a precomputed log(theta_scale) value and native::exp for significant speedup. sycl::sin and sycl::cos could be replaced with sycl::native::sin/cos or combined via sincos-style computation. For RoPE in inference, ~1-2 ULP error from native math is acceptable since position encodings are approximate by nature. CUDA uses powf/cosf/sinf which are fast-math-compatible device functions.

loop_analysis.notes: No loops in the kernel bodies — each work-item processes exactly one pair of elements. The work is fully distributed across the grid. This is optimal for an element-wise kernel. The rope_multi and rope_vision variants have branching (section selection) but no loops.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: RoPE is a 1-pass element-wise kernel: read 2 floats (8 bytes), compute rotation (2 FMA + sin/cos), write 2 floats (8 bytes). Arithmetic intensity for the rotation itself: ~4 FLOPs / 16 bytes = 0.25 FLOP/byte — deeply memory-bandwidth bound (threshold is 27 FLOP/byte). However, the sin/cos and pow transcendentals add significant compute cost per work-item (~100-200 cycles each on Intel GPUs). For small head dimensions (ne00=64-128 with typical n_dims=64-128), the ratio of transcendental compute to memory traffic is higher, potentially making the kernel compute-limited on the transcendentals. For large ne00, the out-of-n_dims passthrough branch (i0 >= n_dims: just copy) dilutes the transcendental overhead. Overall: memory-bound for the data movement, but transcendental-latency-sensitive per work-item.
anti_patterns: Missing ROPE+VIEW+SET_ROWS fusion — CUDA supports row_indices and set_rows_stride parameters for a fused kernel that combines RoPE rotation with indirect scatter writes, eliminating an intermediate buffer and a separate SET_ROWS kernel launch. SYCL lacks this entirely, requiring 2 kernel launches instead of 1.
Missing F32→F16 mixed-precision dispatch — CUDA supports src0=F32, dst=F16 for the fused path. SYCL enforces src0->type == dst->type via GGML_ASSERT. This blocks fusion with F16 KV-cache writes.

Scalar paired stores in rope_norm — CUDA uses float2/half2 wide stores via ggml_cuda_memcpy_1 for the adjacent-pair norm variant. SYCL uses two separate scalar stores (dst[idst+0], dst[idst+1]), wasting a store instruction and potentially a write-combining opportunity.

Expensive transcendentals: sycl::pow/sin/cos are full-precision IEEE-compliant. For RoPE, native::sin/cos (~1-2 ULP error) and exp2-based pow replacement would be 3-5x faster per work-item with acceptable accuracy loss.

Redundant sycl::pow per work-item in rope_multi/vision — the theta_base computation calls sycl::pow(theta_scale, i0/2.0f) in every branch of the sector selection, even though the power base and the relationship between i0 and theta_scale are the same. The pow call could be hoisted before the branch.

optimization_opportunities.description: Implement ROPE+VIEW+SET_ROWS fusion to match CUDA parity. CUDA's rope kernels accept row_indices and set_rows_stride parameters that enable fused ROPE→SET_ROWS operation: the rotated output is written directly to the KV-cache at an indirect offset (row_indices[i2] * set_rows_stride), eliminating an intermediate buffer and a separate SET_ROWS kernel launch. The SYCL version lacks this fusion entirely, requiring 2 separate kernels and an intermediate tensor allocation.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 15-30% latency reduction for the combined ROPE+SET_ROWS operation. Eliminates one full read+write pass over the tensor (16 bytes/element saved) and one kernel launch overhead (~5-10us). For a typical LLaMA-7B attention layer with 32 heads, ne00=128, seq_len=1: saves ~32*128*16 = 64KB memory traffic and 1 kernel launch. The benefit scales with batch size and sequence length.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add row_indices (const int64_t*) and set_rows_stride (int) parameters to all 4 rope kernel variants. In the kernel body, after computing the rotated pair, use the indirect addressing: if (set_rows_stride != 0) { idst = i1*s1 + i0; idst += row_indices[i2] * set_rows_stride; }. Also add a ggml_sycl_rope_fused() entry point that accepts the set_rows tensor. Requires plumbing through the SYCL backend's fused op detection. Reference: CUDA rope.cu lines 80-84 (rope_norm), 152-157 (rope_neox).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Requires adding fused op detection in the SYCL backend dispatch layer. The kernel-level change is straightforward (add conditional offset computation). The main risk is ensuring row_indices tensor data is on-device and properly synchronized. CUDA implementation provides a working reference.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace sycl::pow/sin/cos with native-precision alternatives for 3-5x transcendental throughput improvement. (1) Replace sycl::pow(theta_scale, i0/2.0f) with sycl::native::exp2(i0/2.0f * log2_theta_scale) where log2_theta_scale = sycl::native::log2(theta_scale) is precomputed once on the host. (2) Replace sycl::sin/cos pair with sycl::native::sin and sycl::native::cos (or use a sincos-style combined computation). Native math has ~1-2 ULP error which is acceptable for position encodings.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-25% end-to-end RoPE kernel speedup. The transcendentals (pow, sin, cos) are each ~50-100 cycles on Intel GPUs at full precision vs ~10-20 cycles at native precision. For ne00=128 (64 rotation pairs per row), the transcendental compute is 64 * (pow+sin+cos) per row. With 256 threads/WG, each thread handles 1 pair, so the transcendental latency directly gates the kernel execution time for small head dimensions where memory accesses are fast (data fits in L1).
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Precompute on the host: float log2_theta_scale = log2f(powf(freq_base, -2.0f / n_dims)). Pass to kernel. In kernel: float theta_base = pos[i2] * sycl::native::exp2(i0 / 2.0f * log2_theta_scale). In rope_yarn: cos_theta = sycl::native::cos(theta) * mscale; sin_theta = sycl::native::sin(theta) * mscale. Alternatively, compute sin and cos together using the identity sin(x) = cos(pi/2 - x) to save one transcendental call, but this is less portable.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Native math is well-supported on Intel GPUs and produces acceptable results for position encodings. The pow→exp2 transformation is mathematically exact (just different base). Sin/cos native precision (~1-2 ULP) is well within the noise floor of RoPE. CUDA's cosf/sinf already use reduced precision device intrinsics.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use float2/sycl::vec<float,2> paired stores (and loads) for the rope_norm variant where the element pair (x[i], x[i+1]) is adjacent in memory. CUDA uses ggml_cuda_memcpy_1<8> (float2 = 8 bytes) for float and ggml_cuda_memcpy_1<4> (half2 = 4 bytes) for half, combining two scalar stores into one wider store. This doubles the store throughput for the norm variant. For neox/multi/vision, the pairs are at n_dims/2 offset, so paired stores don't apply.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% throughput improvement for rope_norm variant. The norm variant processes adjacent pairs, so float2 stores write 8 bytes in one transaction instead of two 4-byte transactions. This improves write-combining and reduces store port pressure. The improvement is modest because RoPE is already launching enough work-items to saturate memory bandwidth for typical head dimensions. Larger impact for F16 where half2 (4 bytes) aligns to a single 4-byte store slot.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: In rope_norm_sycl kernel body, replace the two scalar stores with: sycl::vec<float,2> result(x0*cos_theta - x1*sin_theta, x0*sin_theta + x1*cos_theta); *reinterpret_cast<sycl::vec<float,2>*>(&dst[idst]) = result; For half: sycl::vec<sycl::half,2> result(...); Similarly, loads of adjacent pairs can use float2: sycl::vec<float,2> xpair = *reinterpret_cast<const sycl::vec<float,2>*>(&x[ix]). Requires idst and ix to be 8-byte aligned (true when ne00 is even, which is asserted).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Alignment is guaranteed by GGML_ASSERT(ne00 % 2 == 0) and contiguous row layout. reinterpret_cast to vec<float,2> is a standard SYCL pattern. Only applies to rope_norm — the other variants have split-half addressing where paired loads/stores don't help.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add F32→F16 mixed-precision dispatch to match CUDA parity. CUDA supports src0=F32, dst=F16 for the fused ROPE+VIEW+SET_ROWS path, where the rotation is computed in FP32 and the result is downcast to FP16 for the KV-cache. SYCL enforces src0->type == dst->type, blocking this optimization. The kernel already computes in FP32 and casts back to T, so the change is to allow separate input and output types.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Functional parity — enables the ROPE+SET_ROWS fusion (opt_016_001) to write directly to F16 KV-cache without a separate type conversion kernel. Saves one full-tensor read+write pass for type conversion. For a LLaMA-7B KV-cache update: 32 heads * 128 dims * 4 bytes = 16KB saved per token per layer.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add a second template parameter D (destination type) to rope_norm_sycl and rope_neox_sycl (the two variants that support fusion in CUDA). Change dst pointer type from T* to D*. The final cast becomes static_cast<D>(...) instead of static_cast<T>(...). Update dispatch macros DISPATCH_ROPE_FF to handle src0_type != dst_type combinations. Update the GGML_ASSERT to allow F32→F16. Reference: CUDA rope.cu lines 43-44 (template<...typename T, typename D>), 596-600 (F32→F16 dispatch).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The kernel already works in FP32 internally and casts on output. Changing the output cast from T to D is a minimal change. The main work is in the dispatch layer. CUDA provides a working reference for all the type combinations.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace per-work-item integer division for row decomposition (i3 = row_dst / (ne01*ne02), i2 = (...) / ne01) with a 3D nd_range or precomputed reciprocals. Currently each work-item performs 2 integer divisions to decompose the flat row index into (i1, i2, i3). On Intel GPUs, 32-bit integer division is emulated in ~20-30 cycles. CUDA has the same pattern — neither uses a 3D grid for this.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1-3% improvement. The divisions execute once per work-item and are 32-bit (not 64-bit), so the absolute cost is small. For ne01*ne02 that are powers of 2 (common for batch_size * n_heads), the compiler may already optimize to shifts. The benefit is primarily for non-power-of-2 cases.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Option A: Use nd_range<3>(range<3>(ne03, ne02, ne01 * n_blocks_x * block_size), range<3>(1, 1, block_size)) and extract i1, i2, i3 from work-group IDs directly. This requires restructuring the grid to separate the 3 batch/head/seq dimensions. Option B: Pass precomputed magic-number reciprocals for ne01 and ne01*ne02, use multiply-shift for fast division. Option A is cleaner and matches what the CUDA code's dim3 grid naturally provides (though CUDA also uses flat row indexing).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: A 3D grid restructuring changes how work is distributed but not the computation. Each work-item still processes the same elements. Only edge case: very large ne03*ne02*ne01 exceeding max grid dimensions (unlikely for typical transformer shapes).

kernels.efficiency_notes: The RoPE kernel is a clean, well-structured SYCL port with no DPCT artifacts. All 4 variants correctly use WG=256, [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]], and nd_range<2>. The kernel is embarrassingly parallel with no reductions or inter-work-item communication. The main optimization gaps are: (1) missing ROPE+SET_ROWS fusion that CUDA has — this is the highest-impact opportunity as it eliminates an entire kernel launch and buffer, (2) full-precision transcendentals where native math would be 3-5x faster, (3) scalar stores where CUDA uses float2/half2 paired stores for the norm variant, (4) missing F32→F16 mixed-precision support needed for fusion. RoPE is called once per attention layer per token — for a 32-layer model it's 32 kernel launches per token. It's not typically the bottleneck (matmul and softmax dominate), but the fusion opportunity makes the absolute improvement significant. The kernel is purely memory-bandwidth bound for the rotation math but transcendental-latency-sensitive for the per-element sin/cos computation.

kernels.name: norm (normalization kernels)

launch_config.global_size_expression: nd_range<1>(num_groups * block_size, block_size) where num_groups = nrows * nchannels * nsamples (NORM/RMS_NORM/L2_NORM) or total_groups = num_groups * ne[3] (GROUP_NORM) or nrows (RMS_NORM_BACK)
launch_config.notes: All 5 kernel variants (NORM, GROUP_NORM, RMS_NORM, RMS_NORM_BACK, L2_NORM) use identical launch configuration: nd_range<1> with WG=256, [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]]. This is correct and matches the block_reduce limit of WARP_SIZE^2=256 on Intel. However, CUDA's norm.cu uses adaptive block_size: WARP_SIZE (32) for small ncols, up to 1024 for large ncols. SYCL always uses 256 regardless of ncols. For very small ncols (e.g., 64), 256 threads means most are idle (only 4 columns per thread with 64/256 < 1). For large ncols (e.g., 8192), 512 would give better occupancy. The block_reduce implementation in common.hpp limits max WG to WARP_SIZE^2=256, so using 512 would require a 3-level reduction or different approach.

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: Adjacent work-items access adjacent columns: x_row[tid], x_row[tid+block_size], etc. This is perfectly coalesced for contiguous rows. For NORM/RMS_NORM/L2_NORM with non-contiguous src (nb01 != ne00*sizeof(float)), the source stride s01 may cause non-unit-stride access, but the column-within-row access pattern is still coalesced since nb00 == sizeof(float) is asserted.
strided_accesses: Source tensor may have non-contiguous row strides (s01, s02, s03 computed from byte strides). The column-within-row access is contiguous, but the base pointer computation uses potentially non-unit strides for the higher dimensions.
GROUP_NORM accesses src0_d[gid * group_size + tid + j*block_size] which is contiguous within the group, but group boundaries may not align to cache lines.
memory_patterns.notes: All loads and stores are scalar 4-byte (float). No sycl::vec or multi-element loads. This is a purely memory-bandwidth-bound kernel family (arithmetic intensity: NORM ~3 FLOP/8 bytes ≈ 0.375 FLOP/byte, RMS_NORM ~2 FLOP/8 bytes ≈ 0.25 FLOP/byte). Vectorized vec4 loads (sycl::vec<float,4>) could improve effective bandwidth utilization by 1.5-2x. CUDA also uses scalar loads, so this is a SYCL-specific opportunity since Intel GPUs benefit more from wider loads due to the instruction issue model.

slm_usage.slm_bytes_expression: num_warps * sizeof(float) = 16 * 4 = 64 bytes (RMS_NORM/L2_NORM) or num_warps * sizeof(sycl::float2) = 16 * 8 = 128 bytes (NORM/RMS_NORM_BACK) or num_warps * sizeof(float) = 64 bytes (GROUP_NORM)
slm_usage.notes: SLM usage is minimal — only for the inter-warp reduction in block_reduce (one float or float2 per warp). 64-128 bytes out of 64KB available (0.1% utilization). No bank conflicts since each warp writes to its own index. The SLM is efficiently used for its purpose. No opportunity to cache input data in SLM since each element is read only 1-2 times per pass (no reuse across work-items within a row).

reduction_pattern.reduction_type: block_reduce (2-level: sub-group shuffle + SLM + sub-group shuffle)
reduction_pattern.notes: Each work-item accumulates a partial sum over its strided columns, then block_reduce performs a hierarchical reduction: (1) sub-group shuffle reduction within each of the 16 sub-groups, (2) write per-sub-group results to SLM, barrier, (3) sub-group 0 reads from SLM and does a final shuffle reduction. The result is broadcast via SLM write + barrier + SLM read. This is a correct and efficient 2-level reduction for WG=256 with WARP_SIZE=16. NORM and RMS_NORM_BACK use float2 reductions (sum and sum-of-squares or sum-of-squares and sum-of-x*grad simultaneously), which is efficient — avoids two separate reductions.

data_types.notes: All normalization kernels are FP32-only, matching CUDA. GGML_ASSERT enforces src0->type == GGML_TYPE_F32 and dst->type == GGML_TYPE_F32. The reduction accumulator and intermediate values are all float. Half-precision normalization is not supported (nor is it in CUDA's norm.cu). Joint matrix is not applicable — these are reduction + element-wise operations, not matrix multiplications.

functions: sycl::rsqrt(var + eps) — called once per work-group in NORM (inverse standard deviation)
sycl::rsqrt(mean + eps) — called once per work-group in RMS_NORM and L2_NORM (inverse RMS)
sycl::rsqrt(variance + eps) — called once per work-group in GROUP_NORM
sycl::rsqrt(mean_eps) — called once per work-group in RMS_NORM_BACK
sycl::fmax(tmp, eps*eps) — called once per work-group in L2_NORM
sycl::min(end, ne_elements) — called once per work-group in GROUP_NORM
math_functions.notes: Math function usage is minimal — only sycl::rsqrt called once per work-group (after the reduction). This is the correct function for normalization (1/sqrt(x)). No per-element transcendentals. The rsqrt call is not a bottleneck since it's called once per row, not per element. Using sycl::native::rsqrt would save a few cycles per work-group but is negligible in the overall kernel time.

barriers: item.barrier(sycl::access::fence_space::local_space) — called once after block_reduce broadcast (tid==0 writes result to SLM, all threads read it)
GROUP_NORM has 2 additional barriers (one after mean reduction broadcast, one after variance reduction broadcast)
synchronization.notes: Barrier usage is minimal and correct. NORM/RMS_NORM/L2_NORM/RMS_NORM_BACK each have 1 barrier (plus the internal barrier in block_reduce). GROUP_NORM has 3 barriers total (2 for the two separate reductions plus their broadcasts, and the internal block_reduce barriers). No unnecessary barriers.

hot_loops: NORM: 2 loops over ncols (Pass 1: accumulate sum and sum-of-squares; Pass 2: normalize output)
GROUP_NORM: 3 loops over group_size (Pass 1: accumulate mean; Pass 2: subtract mean + accumulate variance; Pass 3: scale by inv_std)
RMS_NORM: 2 loops over ncols (Pass 1: accumulate sum of squares; Pass 2: scale output)
RMS_NORM_BACK: 2 loops over ncols (Pass 1: accumulate sum_xx and sum_xg; Pass 2: compute gradient)
L2_NORM: 2 loops over ncols (Pass 1: accumulate sum of squares; Pass 2: scale output)
loop_analysis.notes: No #pragma unroll on any loop. All loops are col-strided (col += block_size) which is a standard parallel reduction pattern. For typical ncols values (4096-8192), each work-item processes 16-32 iterations. Unrolling could reduce loop overhead and enable instruction-level parallelism. GROUP_NORM makes 3 passes over data while NORM/RMS_NORM only make 2 — GROUP_NORM could potentially merge pass 2 and pass 3 into a single pass (compute mean, then in pass 2: subtract mean, accumulate variance, AND scale in one pass by deferring writes to a register). However, this would require knowing the scale before the pass completes, which creates a dependency. The current 3-pass approach is correct but makes 50% more memory traffic than necessary.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: All normalization kernels are deeply memory-bandwidth bound. Arithmetic intensity: NORM reads N floats and writes N floats in 2 passes = 4N reads + N writes = 20N bytes for ~3N FLOPs = 0.15 FLOP/byte. RMS_NORM: 2 passes = 3N reads + N writes = 16N bytes for ~2N FLOPs = 0.125 FLOP/byte. GROUP_NORM: 3 passes = 4N reads + 2N writes = 24N bytes for ~3N FLOPs = 0.125 FLOP/byte. All far below the 27 FLOP/byte ridge point. Memory bandwidth is the sole bottleneck. For ncols=4096 (typical hidden dim), each row is 16KB — fits in L1 cache (48KB per EU) for the second pass, so the effective bandwidth is likely limited by L1 rather than DRAM.
anti_patterns: MISSING kernel fusion: CUDA has fused rms_norm_f32<block_size, do_multiply, do_add> variants that combine RMS_NORM with element-wise MUL (weight scaling) and ADD (bias) in a single kernel. In transformer models, RMS_NORM is always followed by element-wise MUL (weight * normalized_x). The SYCL version lacks this fusion entirely, requiring 2 separate kernel launches and an extra read+write pass over the tensor. This is the highest-impact optimization opportunity.

MISSING adaptive block_size: CUDA's norm.cu selects block_size based on ncols: WARP_SIZE for ncols <= WARP_SIZE, 128 for ncols <= 128*WARP_SIZE, otherwise 1024. SYCL always uses 256 regardless of ncols. For small ncols (e.g., 64), 256 threads means each thread processes < 1 element on average, wasting sub-group slots. For large ncols (e.g., 8192+), 512 threads would process fewer elements per thread with better pipelining.

No vectorized loads/stores: All memory accesses are scalar float (4 bytes). For a memory-bandwidth-bound kernel, using sycl::vec<float,4> loads could improve effective bandwidth by 1.5-2x on Intel GPUs. The column loop is strided by block_size, so vec4 loads would require restructuring to process 4 consecutive columns per iteration.

GROUP_NORM makes 3 passes over data: Pass 1 (mean), Pass 2 (variance + mean subtraction), Pass 3 (scale). NORM uses a clever float2 accumulator to compute mean and variance in a single pass, then writes in pass 2. GROUP_NORM could use the same float2 trick to merge mean and sum-of-squares into pass 1, then merge mean-subtraction and scaling into pass 2, reducing from 3 passes to 2 passes (33% less memory traffic).

Integer division/modulo in group_id decomposition: group_id % nrows, (group_id / nrows) % nchannels, group_id / (nrows * nchannels) — 3 integer divisions per work-group (executed by all work-items). On Intel GPUs, 32-bit integer division is ~20-30 cycles. Could use fast-division multiply-shift trick or 3D nd_range. However, this is per-work-group, not per-element, so the impact is negligible.

block_reduce limits WG to 256 on Intel: The 2-level hierarchical reduction (sub-group shuffle → SLM → sub-group shuffle) supports at most WARP_SIZE^2 = 16^2 = 256 work-items. To use WG=512, a 3-level reduction would be needed. This is a systemic limitation affecting all reduction kernels, not specific to norm.

optimization_opportunities.description: Implement fused RMS_NORM+MUL kernel to match CUDA's rms_norm_f32<block_size, true, false> variant. In transformer models, RMS_NORM is always followed by element-wise multiplication with a weight vector (x_normalized * weight). The fused kernel reads src0 (input), reads src1 (weight vector), computes RMS normalization, and writes dst = scale * src0[col] * src1[col] in a single pass — eliminating one full read+write pass over the tensor and one kernel launch. CUDA also has a do_add variant for RMS_NORM+MUL+ADD (with bias), though bias is less common in modern transformers.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 20-40% latency reduction for the RMS_NORM+MUL operation pair. Eliminates one full tensor read+write (8 bytes/element) and one kernel launch (~5-10us). For typical hidden_dim=4096: saves 4096*4*2 = 32KB memory traffic per row. With 32 layers and batch_size=1, that's 32*32KB = 1MB saved per token. The fusion also improves cache utilization since the normalized values are consumed immediately rather than written to DRAM and re-read.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add template parameters do_multiply and do_add to the RMS_NORM kernel. When do_multiply=true, accept an additional src1_d pointer (the weight vector) and multiply: dst_row[col] = scale * x_row[col] * weight[col]. The weight vector is shared across all rows, so it could be cached in SLM (4096*4 = 16KB fits in 64KB SLM). Add ggml_sycl_op_rms_norm_fused() that detects when the next op is MUL with a 1D weight tensor and fuses them. Reference: CUDA norm.cu rms_norm_f32<block_size, true, false> (line ~180-220).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Requires fused op detection in the SYCL backend dispatch layer, similar to what CUDA does. The kernel-level change is straightforward (add conditional multiply). The risk is in correctly detecting the fusion opportunity in the graph and ensuring the weight tensor is available. CUDA implementation provides a working reference.

optimization_opportunities.description: Implement adaptive block_size selection based on ncols, matching CUDA's approach. CUDA selects: WARP_SIZE (32) for ncols <= WARP_SIZE, 128 for ncols <= 128*WARP_SIZE, otherwise 1024. For SYCL with WARP_SIZE=16: use 16 for ncols <= 16 (rare), 128 for ncols <= 2048, 256 for ncols <= 4096, and 256 (current max due to block_reduce limit) for larger. The current fixed 256 is suboptimal for small ncols where fewer threads are needed and for the block_reduce overhead.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% improvement for small ncols (64-256) where the current 256-thread WG has many idle threads. For typical transformer ncols (4096-8192), the current 256 is close to optimal given the block_reduce limit. The primary benefit is for models with small hidden dimensions (e.g., 256-512) or for GROUP_NORM where group_size may be small.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add a host-side block_size selection: if (ncols <= WARP_SIZE) block_size = WARP_SIZE; else if (ncols <= 128*WARP_SIZE) block_size = 128; else block_size = 256. Each block_size variant needs a separate kernel instantiation (due to the SLM allocation size depending on num_warps). Use template instantiation or if-else dispatch. To go beyond 256, would need to upgrade block_reduce to support 3-level reduction (sub-group → SLM → sub-group → SLM → sub-group) for WG=512.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Block size selection is a host-side change with no impact on correctness. Each variant is independently testable. The block_reduce function already works correctly for any power-of-2 block_size up to 256.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized vec4 loads and stores (sycl::vec<float,4>) for the data-pass loops. Currently all loads/stores are scalar 4-byte. For a memory-bandwidth-bound kernel, wider loads improve effective bandwidth utilization by reducing instruction count and enabling better memory coalescing on Intel GPUs. Restructure the column loop from 'for (col = tid; col < ncols; col += block_size)' to 'for (col = tid*4; col < ncols; col += block_size*4)' with vec4 load/accumulate.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-25% throughput improvement for large ncols (4096+). The improvement comes from reduced load/store instruction count (4x fewer) and better utilization of the memory subsystem. For small ncols where data fits in L1 cache, the improvement is smaller since L1 latency is already low. The vec4 approach also enables better instruction-level parallelism in the accumulation loop.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: For the accumulation loop: sycl::vec<float,4> xv = *reinterpret_cast<const sycl::vec<float,4>*>(&x_row[col]); tmp += xv[0]*xv[0] + xv[1]*xv[1] + xv[2]*xv[2] + xv[3]*xv[3]; For the output loop: similar vec4 store. Requires ncols to be a multiple of 4 (add scalar tail handling for non-multiple cases). Most transformer hidden dims (4096, 5120, 8192) are multiples of 4. Alignment should be checked (GGML tensors are typically 32-byte aligned).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Vec4 loads are a standard SYCL optimization pattern. The only risk is for ncols not divisible by 4 (requires scalar tail loop). GGML tensor alignment guarantees make this safe for the common case.

optimization_opportunities.description: Reduce GROUP_NORM from 3 passes to 2 passes using the float2 accumulator technique already used in NORM. Currently GROUP_NORM makes: Pass 1 (sum for mean), Pass 2 (subtract mean + sum squares for variance), Pass 3 (scale by inv_std). Using a float2 accumulator in Pass 1 to compute both sum and sum-of-squares simultaneously (like NORM does), then in Pass 2: subtract mean AND scale by inv_std in one pass. This eliminates Pass 3 entirely, reducing memory traffic by 33%.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 25-33% latency reduction for GROUP_NORM specifically. Eliminates one full read+write pass over group_size elements. For typical diffusion model GROUP_NORM with group_size = H*W*C/num_groups (e.g., 64*64*256/32 = 32768 elements), saves 32768*4*2 = 256KB memory traffic per group. GROUP_NORM is critical for diffusion models (Stable Diffusion) but less common in LLM inference.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace Pass 1 accumulator with sycl::float2 mean_var(0.0f, 0.0f); accumulating sum and sum-of-squares simultaneously. After reduction: mean = mean_var.x() / group_size; variance = mean_var.y() / group_size - mean*mean; scale = rsqrt(variance + eps). Then single Pass 2: dst_d[j] = (src0_d[j] - mean) * scale. This matches the pattern already used in the NORM kernel (lines 58-63). SLM allocation changes from float to sycl::float2 (128 bytes instead of 64 bytes — negligible).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The float2 accumulation pattern is already proven in the NORM kernel in the same file. The numerical result is identical (Welford's online algorithm is not needed here since sum-of-squares is numerically stable for the typical value ranges in normalization). The only consideration is that the current 3-pass approach writes intermediate (x-mean) values to dst in pass 2 and reads them back in pass 3, while the 2-pass approach would compute (src0_d[j] - mean) * scale directly from src0 — this requires re-reading src0 in pass 2 instead of reading dst, which has identical cost.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add #pragma unroll directives to the column-stride loops in all 5 kernel variants. The inner loops iterate ncols/block_size times (typically 16-32 iterations for ncols=4096-8192, block_size=256). Partial unrolling (#pragma unroll 4) would reduce loop overhead and enable instruction-level parallelism for the accumulation operations.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 3-8% throughput improvement. Loop unrolling reduces branch overhead and enables the compiler to interleave independent load-accumulate operations. The improvement is modest because the loops are already simple (1-2 operations per iteration) and the bottleneck is memory bandwidth, not instruction throughput.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add '#pragma unroll 4' before each 'for (int col = tid; col < ncols; col += block_size)' loop. The unroll factor of 4 matches the vec4 optimization (opt_017_003) — combining both gives 4x fewer loop iterations with vec4 loads in each iteration. Without vec4, unrolling still helps by allowing the compiler to pipeline multiple scalar loads.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Pragma unroll is a compiler hint with no correctness impact. The DPC++ compiler may already unroll these simple loops, in which case the pragma has no effect. If ncols is not a compile-time constant, partial unrolling with a scalar tail is safe.

kernels.efficiency_notes: The normalization kernels are a clean, well-structured native SYCL port with zero DPCT artifacts. All 5 variants correctly use nd_range<1>, WG=256, [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]], sycl::local_accessor for SLM, and proper barrier synchronization. The block_reduce pattern is correct and efficient for the 2-level hierarchical reduction. The NORM kernel cleverly uses float2 to compute mean and sum-of-squares in a single reduction. The primary optimization gaps are: (1) CRITICAL: missing RMS_NORM+MUL fusion — in transformer inference, RMS_NORM is always followed by weight multiplication, and CUDA has fused variants that eliminate an entire kernel launch and memory pass. This is the single highest-impact optimization. (2) No vectorized loads on a purely memory-bandwidth-bound kernel family. (3) GROUP_NORM makes 3 passes where 2 would suffice (the float2 technique from NORM is not applied). (4) Fixed block_size=256 instead of adaptive selection. RMS_NORM is called twice per transformer layer (once for attention, once for FFN), making it a high-frequency kernel. The fusion opportunity alone justifies medium-high priority.

kernels.name: getrows (row gathering)

launch_config.sub_group_size_attribute: none — missing on all 3 kernel functions
launch_config.global_size_expression: k_get_rows_quant/float: nd_range<3>((ne10, gridDim_y, gridDim_z * 256), (1, 1, 256)) where gridDim_y = min((ne00+2*256-1)/(2*256), 65535) for quant or min((ne00+256-1)/256, 65535) for float, gridDim_z = min(ne11*ne12, 65535). k_get_rows_back: nd_range<3>((1, ne1, block_num_x * 256), (1, 1, 256)) where block_num_x = ceil(ne00/256).
launch_config.notes: All 3 kernels use nd_range<3> with only dim2 threaded (local_range = (1,1,256)). This is a direct CUDA→SYCL port preserving the dim3 grid structure. The nd_range<3> with unused dimensions (local=1) is a DPCT-style artifact — should be simplified to nd_range<1> with grid loops. WG=256 matches CUDA's CUDA_GET_ROWS_BLOCK_SIZE=256 and is correct for Intel GPUs. CRITICAL: Missing [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]] on all kernel functions. The quant kernel processes 2 elements per work-item (dfloat2), the float kernel processes 1 element per work-item. The backward kernel has 1 work-item per column with a serial loop over all gradient rows.

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: k_get_rows_float: Adjacent work-items access adjacent columns src0_row[i00] and dst_row[i00] — perfectly coalesced within each gathered row. However, src0 access is inherently random (indirect through src1 row indices), so different work-groups access non-contiguous src0 rows. k_get_rows_quant: Output writes are strided — dst_row[iybs + iqs + 0] and dst_row[iybs + iqs + y_offset] where y_offset = qk/2 for qr>1, causing non-coalesced writes for some formats. k_get_rows_back: grad[i*ncols + col] reads are strided by ncols across the serial loop iterations.
strided_accesses: Quantized kernel output: writes to dst_row[iybs + iqs + 0] and dst_row[iybs + iqs + y_offset] with y_offset = qk/2 — creates stride-16/32 access pattern for non-trivial qr values
Backward kernel: serial loop reads grad[i*ncols + col] for i=0..nrows_grad — stride = ncols elements between iterations, causing poor spatial locality
All kernels: src0 rows accessed via indirect index src1[...] — gather pattern, inherently non-coalesced across work-groups
memory_patterns.notes: All loads and stores are scalar. For the float kernel, each work-item copies a single element (4 bytes for F32, 2 bytes for F16/BF16). This is a pure memory copy with type conversion, so vectorized loads (vec4/vec8) would directly improve throughput. For the quantized kernel, the dequantization produces 2 elements per call, but writes them to non-adjacent locations. The SYCL version is functionally identical to CUDA — neither uses vectorized loads.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM used. This is correct — get_rows is an embarrassingly parallel gather operation with no inter-work-item communication. Each work-item independently looks up and copies one or two elements. SLM would not help since there's no data reuse within a work-group (each row index leads to a different src0 row).

reduction_pattern.notes: No reduction in the forward kernels. The backward kernel (k_get_rows_back_float) has a pseudo-reduction: it serially sums gradient values from matching row indices. However, this is not a parallel reduction — it's a serial accumulation in a single work-item, iterating over all nrows_grad to find matches. This is O(nrows_grad) per output element and extremely inefficient for large index sets.

data_types.notes: Supports 9 quantized source types (Q4_0, Q4_1, Q5_0, Q5_1, Q8_0 via traits, plus F16, F32, I32, BF16 via float path) with 4 destination types (F32, F16, BF16, I32). The SYCL version uses compile-time dequant_traits template dispatch instead of CUDA's function pointer approach — this is actually superior since it enables inlining and avoids function pointer overhead on GPUs. All intermediate computation is in FP32. Joint matrix is not applicable — this is a gather/copy operation, not a matrix multiply.

math_functions.notes: No math functions used. The kernel is purely memory operations: index lookup, byte offset computation, optional dequantization (bit manipulation only, no transcendentals), and type casting. The sycl_cast helper uses static_cast with float intermediary for type conversion.

synchronization.notes: No barriers or synchronization. Each work-item operates independently on different elements. This is correct for a gather/copy operation.

hot_loops: Forward quant: outer loop 'for z = group(2); z < ne11*ne12; z += gridDim_z' — iterates over batch*sequence dimensions beyond grid capacity
Forward quant: inner loop 'for i00 = 2*(group(1)*block_sz+thread); i00 < ne00; i00 += 2*gridDim_y*block_sz' — iterates over columns beyond grid capacity
Forward float: same dual-loop structure as quant but processing 1 element per iteration instead of 2
Backward: 'for i = 0; i < nrows_grad; ++i' with 'if (rows[i] != dst_row) continue' — serial scan of ALL gradient rows per output element
loop_analysis.notes: The forward kernel loops handle grid dimension overflow (gridDim_y and gridDim_z are capped at 65535). For typical shapes, these loops execute 1 iteration (the grid is large enough). The backward kernel's serial loop is the main performance concern — it's O(nrows_grad) with branch-heavy execution (if/continue). No #pragma unroll on any loop.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: The forward kernels are purely memory-bandwidth bound — they perform gather (indirect load) + optional dequantization + scatter (indexed store). Arithmetic intensity: float kernel = 0 FLOP/8 bytes (pure copy), quant kernel = ~2-4 FLOPs/byte (bit extraction + scale/offset). The gather access pattern means L2/L3 cache hit rate depends on the distribution of row indices — for embedding lookups with large vocabulary, cache misses are common. The backward kernel is compute-bound on the serial row-matching loop for large nrows_grad, but memory-bound for the actual gradient accumulation.
anti_patterns: nd_range<3> with local_range=(1,1,256) — only dim2 is threaded, dims 0 and 1 are used as grid-level iteration indices. This is a direct CUDA dim3 port. Should be simplified to nd_range<1> with explicit grid-overflow loops, reducing kernel argument overhead and enabling the SYCL runtime to optimize dispatch.

Missing [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]] on all 3 kernel functions — the compiler may select a non-optimal sub-group size, and the code implicitly assumes certain work-item ordering that may not hold without this attribute.

No vectorized loads/stores for the float copy path — k_get_rows_float copies one element per work-item. For F32→F32 (the common case), vec4 loads/stores would process 16 bytes per work-item, reducing instruction count 4x.

k_get_rows_back_float uses brute-force O(nrows_grad) serial scan per output element — for large index sets (e.g., vocabulary embedding backward), this is extremely slow. Both CUDA and SYCL use this same naive approach (CUDA comments 'TODO: atomicAdd'). An atomic scatter-add approach would be O(nrows_grad) total instead of O(nrows_grad * ne1) total.

Integer division z / ne12 and z % ne12 in hot path of forward kernels — computed per work-item in every loop iteration. Could use fast-division trick or precompute on host when ne11*ne12 fits in grid.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized vec4 loads and stores for k_get_rows_float when src0 and dst types are the same (F32→F32, which is the common case for embedding lookups). Each work-item would process 4 consecutive elements using sycl::vec<float,4>, reducing instruction count 4x and improving memory subsystem utilization for this purely memory-copy kernel.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.5-2.5x throughput for F32→F32 path. The kernel is a pure memory copy with gather, so wider loads directly translate to higher effective bandwidth. For F16→F32 or quant→F32 paths, vec4 stores on the output side still help.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: For the F32→F32 same-type path: change the inner loop to process 4 columns per iteration. sycl::vec<float,4> src = *reinterpret_cast<const sycl::vec<float,4>*>(&src0_row[i00]); *reinterpret_cast<sycl::vec<float,4>*>(&dst_row[i00]) = src; Adjust loop stride to block_sz*4. Add scalar tail for ne00 not divisible by 4. For F16→F32 conversion: load vec4<half> and convert to vec4<float>. Requires GGML tensor alignment (typically 32-byte aligned).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Standard vectorization pattern. Requires ne00 >= 4 (always true for practical shapes). Alignment is guaranteed by GGML tensor allocation.

optimization_opportunities.description: Simplify nd_range<3> with local=(1,1,256) to nd_range<1> with local=256. The current 3D range has dimensions 0 and 1 serving as grid-level indices (local_range=1), while only dimension 2 is actually threaded (local_range=256). This is a CUDA dim3 port artifact. Converting to nd_range<1> with explicit grid loops (already present in the kernel code) simplifies the launch configuration and potentially reduces kernel dispatch overhead.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1-3% from reduced kernel dispatch overhead and cleaner code. The nd_range<3> with mostly-1 local ranges creates unnecessary complexity in the SYCL runtime's work-group scheduling. The primary benefit is code maintainability.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace nd_range<3>(global, local) with nd_range<1>(total_work_items, 256). In the kernel, replace item.get_group(0) with a computed index from the 1D work-group ID: group_id = item.get_group(0); i10 = group_id / (gridDim_y * gridDim_z); remainder = group_id % (gridDim_y * gridDim_z); ... Or keep the existing loop structure and just use the 1D grid to cover all rows.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Purely structural change — same computation, different launch configuration. The kernel already has grid-overflow loops that handle arbitrary grid sizes.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]] attribute to all 3 kernel functions. Currently none of the kernel functions specify the sub-group size, allowing the compiler to select any supported width. On Intel GPUs, this could result in SIMD32 selection which changes the sub-group behavior and may not match the intended work distribution.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Correctness safeguard + 0-5% performance from guaranteed SIMD16 execution enabling better compiler optimization. The compiler can make stronger assumptions about memory coalescing and register allocation when the sub-group size is known at compile time.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]] to the parallel_for lambda in all 3 launch sites (get_rows_sycl_q, get_rows_sycl_float, ggml_sycl_op_get_rows_back). The kernel functions themselves are called from within the lambda, so the attribute goes on the lambda.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Adding a sub-group size attribute is a correctness improvement with no functional change when the current execution already uses SIMD16. If the current execution silently uses SIMD32, this change makes the kernel explicitly use SIMD16 which is the intended behavior.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace k_get_rows_back_float's brute-force O(nrows_grad) serial scan with an atomic scatter-add approach. Currently each output element serially scans ALL gradient rows to find matching indices, making the total work O(ne1 * nrows_grad * ncols). An atomic scatter-add kernel would iterate over gradient rows (nrows_grad) and atomically add each gradient value to dst[rows[i] * ncols + col], making total work O(nrows_grad * ncols) — a ne1 factor reduction.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-50x speedup for large nrows_grad (e.g., vocabulary size 32000 with batch*seq_len gradient rows). For small nrows_grad (< 32), the current approach may actually be faster due to atomic overhead. The backward pass is only used during training, not inference.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: New kernel: each work-item processes one (gradient_row, col) pair. For each gradient_row i: atomically add grad[i*ncols + col] to dst[rows[i]*ncols + col]. Use sycl::atomic_ref<float, sycl::memory_order::relaxed, sycl::memory_scope::device, sycl::access::address_space::global_space> for the atomic add. Grid: nd_range<1>(nrows_grad * ceil(ncols/256) * 256, 256). Requires zeroing dst first (memset to 0). CUDA's getrows.cu has the same TODO comment suggesting this approach.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Atomic FP32 adds may have limited hardware support on some Intel GPUs. The relaxed memory ordering is sufficient for commutative addition but needs verification. Numerical results may differ slightly from the serial version due to floating-point non-associativity. This is a training-only kernel, so the risk-reward tradeoff may not justify the effort for inference-focused optimization.

kernels.efficiency_notes: The getrows kernel is a clean native SYCL port with minimal DPCT artifacts (only the nd_range<3> layout). The template-based dequant_traits dispatch is actually superior to CUDA's function pointer approach. The forward kernels are simple gather operations with WG=256, which is correct for Intel GPUs. The main optimization gaps are: (1) no vectorized loads/stores for the float copy path — this is the highest-impact opportunity since F32→F32 embedding lookup is a pure memory copy. (2) Missing reqd_sub_group_size attribute. (3) nd_range<3> cleanup. (4) The backward kernel uses brute-force serial scan, but this is training-only and both CUDA and SYCL share the same limitation. Overall low optimization potential because: get_rows is called infrequently during inference (only for initial token embedding lookup), the gather pattern means performance is dominated by cache behavior rather than kernel efficiency, and the kernel is already well-structured with correct work-group size.

kernels.name: cpy (tensor copy with type conversion)

launch_config.sub_group_size_attribute: none — missing on both kernel functions
launch_config.global_size_expression: nd_range<1>(num_blocks * 256, 256) where num_blocks = ceil(ne / 256), ne = total elements
launch_config.notes: Both k_cpy_scalar and k_cpy_scalar_contiguous use identical nd_range<1> with WG=256 (SYCL_CPY_BLOCK_SIZE). This is clean native SYCL with no DPCT artifacts. WG=256 is appropriate for Intel GPUs. Missing [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]] on both kernels. The same-type contiguous case bypasses the kernel entirely with stream.memcpy() — optimal fast path. Each work-item processes exactly 1 element.

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: k_cpy_scalar_contiguous: perfectly coalesced — adjacent work-items access adjacent elements in both src and dst. k_cpy_scalar (non-contiguous): depends on the actual strides. For row-contiguous tensors (nb00 == sizeof(src_t)), the innermost dimension access is coalesced. For transposed or arbitrary-stride tensors, access can be completely non-coalesced since the 4D offset computation allows arbitrary byte strides.
strided_accesses: k_cpy_scalar: arbitrary strides via nb00/nb01/nb02/nb03 and nb10/nb11/nb12/nb13 — the src and dst offset computations allow fully non-contiguous access patterns. For a transposed tensor (swapped nb01/nb00), adjacent work-items may access elements separated by full row strides.
k_cpy_scalar_contiguous: no strided accesses — purely sequential element access
memory_patterns.notes: All loads and stores are scalar — one element per work-item. For the contiguous same-type case (F32→F32), this is a pure memcpy done with 4-byte scalar operations. sycl::vec<float,4> loads/stores would process 16 bytes per work-item. For F16→F32 conversion, vec4 loads of half4 with conversion to float4 would improve throughput. CUDA also uses scalar operations for cpy_scalar but has an optimized cpy_scalar_transpose with shared-memory tiling that SYCL lacks entirely.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM used. CUDA has a cpy_scalar_transpose kernel that uses __shared__ float tile[32][33] (32x33 = 4224 bytes) for coalesced transpose via tiled shared memory — this entire kernel is missing from the SYCL port. For non-transpose copy, SLM is not beneficial since there's no data reuse.

reduction_pattern.notes: No reduction. Pure element-wise copy/conversion.

data_types.notes: Supports 12 type combinations via template instantiation: F32↔F16, F32↔I32, F32↔BF16, F16↔BF16, and same-type (F32, F16, I32, BF16). Type conversion is done via C-style cast (dst_t)(src_t) which goes through float intermediary for half/bf16 conversions. CUDA additionally supports float→quantized (cpy_f32_q) and quantized→float (cpy_q_f32) copy paths that the SYCL version lacks — these require F32→Q4_0/Q4_1/Q5_0/Q5_1/Q8_0/IQ4_NL quantization kernels.

math_functions.notes: No math functions. Pure memory copy with optional type casting.

synchronization.notes: No synchronization. Each work-item operates independently.

loop_analysis.notes: No loops in either kernel — each work-item processes exactly 1 element via a flat global index. The work distribution is fully grid-based. The CUDA cpy_scalar_transpose kernel has loops with #pragma unroll for tiled processing — this entire kernel is missing from SYCL.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: Pure memory-bandwidth-bound operation. Arithmetic intensity: 0 FLOP/byte for same-type copy, negligible for type conversion (F32→F16 is just a truncation, ~1 FLOP/4 bytes). The non-contiguous kernel has significant integer arithmetic overhead: 12+ 64-bit integer divisions and multiplications per work-item for the 4D index decomposition. On Intel GPUs, 64-bit integer division is extremely expensive (~80-160 cycles vs ~4 cycles for a float multiply). For tensors with small inner dimensions, the index computation may actually dominate the kernel time, making it compute-bound on integer arithmetic rather than memory-bound.
anti_patterns: Missing cpy_scalar_transpose: CUDA has an optimized 2D tiled transpose kernel using __shared__[32][33] that enables coalesced reads AND writes during transpose operations. The SYCL version handles transpose via the generic k_cpy_scalar which computes arbitrary 4D byte offsets per element, resulting in completely non-coalesced access patterns for transposed tensors. Transpose is a common operation in attention mechanisms (e.g., view permutations).

Missing cpy_f32_q and cpy_q_f32: CUDA supports direct float→quantized and quantized→float copy (e.g., F32→Q8_0 for KV-cache quantization). The SYCL version only supports float/half/bf16/i32 type combinations, requiring separate dequantize+copy for quantized types.

Heavy 64-bit integer arithmetic in k_cpy_scalar: 12+ 64-bit integer divisions and multiplications per work-item for 4D index decomposition (i03 = i/(ne00*ne01*ne02), etc.). On Intel GPUs, 64-bit division is emulated in ~80-160 cycles. For small tensors where the copy time is short, this integer overhead can dominate. CUDA has the same pattern but NVIDIA GPUs have faster 64-bit integer division hardware.

No vectorized loads/stores in k_cpy_scalar_contiguous: The contiguous kernel copies 1 element per work-item with scalar loads/stores. For F32→F32 (4 bytes), vec4 would process 16 bytes per work-item. For F16→F16 (2 bytes), vec8 would process 16 bytes per work-item. The same-type contiguous case is already handled by memcpy, but different-type contiguous (e.g., F32→F16) still uses scalar operations.
Missing [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]] on both kernels.

optimization_opportunities.description: Implement cpy_scalar_transpose using SLM-tiled 2D transpose to match CUDA parity. CUDA's cpy_scalar_transpose uses __shared__ float tile[32][33] with 2D thread blocks (32x8) to read a 32x32 tile with coalesced reads, store to shared memory, then write the transposed tile with coalesced writes. The +1 padding avoids bank conflicts. The SYCL version handles transpose via the generic k_cpy_scalar with per-element 4D offset computation, resulting in non-coalesced accesses for transposed tensors.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 2-5x throughput for transpose operations. The current generic path has non-coalesced reads OR writes (depending on which dimension is transposed), wasting memory bandwidth. The tiled approach ensures both reads and writes are coalesced, achieving near-peak memory bandwidth. Transpose is used in attention view permutations.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Detect transpose pattern at dispatch time: src0 is contiguous with swapped ne[0]/ne[1] relative to dst. Use nd_range<2>((ceil(ne01/32)*32, ceil(ne00/32)*8), (32, 8)) with SLM tile[32][33]. Each 32x8 thread block: (1) coalesced read 32x32 tile from src, (2) barrier, (3) coalesced write transposed 32x32 tile to dst. Handle boundary tiles with bounds checks. The +1 SLM padding (33 instead of 32) avoids bank conflicts. Support F32, F16, BF16 via template. Reference: CUDA cpy.cu cpy_scalar_transpose (lines 42-92).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: SLM-tiled transpose is a well-understood pattern. The main risk is detecting the transpose case correctly at the dispatch level (must identify when src0 strides represent a simple 2D transpose). The kernel itself is straightforward.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized vec4/vec8 loads and stores in k_cpy_scalar_contiguous for different-type contiguous copies. Currently each work-item copies 1 element with scalar operations. For F32→F16 (the most common different-type contiguous copy), each work-item would load 4 F32 values, convert to 4 F16 values, and write 4 F16 values, reducing instruction count 4x.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.5-2.5x throughput for contiguous different-type copies (F32→F16, F16→F32, F32→BF16, BF16→F32). The same-type contiguous case already uses memcpy (no improvement possible). The improvement comes from reduced instruction count and better memory subsystem utilization.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add a k_cpy_vec4_contiguous template: each work-item processes 4 elements. sycl::vec<src_t,4> src = *reinterpret_cast<const sycl::vec<src_t,4>*>(&x[i*4]); sycl::vec<dst_t,4> dst_v; for each component: dst_v[k] = (dst_t)(src[k]); Write dst_v. Requires ne to be a multiple of 4 (add scalar tail). Use for contiguous different-type paths only.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Standard vectorization pattern. Requires ne >= 4 (always true in practice). Half→float conversion in vec4 is well-supported by SYCL.

optimization_opportunities.description: Reduce 64-bit integer arithmetic overhead in k_cpy_scalar by precomputing reciprocals or using 32-bit arithmetic where possible. The current kernel performs 12+ 64-bit integer divisions per work-item for the 4D index decomposition. For tensors where all dimensions fit in 32 bits (ne00*ne01*ne02 < 2^31, which is true for all practical transformer shapes), 32-bit arithmetic would be ~4x faster for the division operations.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% for non-contiguous copy of small tensors where integer arithmetic overhead is significant relative to memory access time. For large tensors, memory bandwidth dominates and the integer arithmetic is hidden by memory latency. The improvement is primarily for the non-contiguous path (contiguous uses memcpy or k_cpy_scalar_contiguous which has no index decomposition).
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Option A: Add a 32-bit fast path when ne00*ne01*ne02*ne03 < INT32_MAX (cast all dimensions to int32_t before the division chain). Option B: Precompute magic-number reciprocals on the host for ne00, ne00*ne01, ne00*ne01*ne02 and pass them to the kernel. Option C: Use nd_range<3> or nd_range<2> to let the runtime handle some of the index decomposition. Option A is simplest and covers 99% of cases.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: 32-bit arithmetic is always safe when dimensions are checked to fit. The host-side check is trivial. CUDA has the same 64-bit arithmetic pattern.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]] attribute to both kernel launch lambdas for consistent sub-group behavior and compiler optimization.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 0-3% from compiler optimization hints. Primarily a correctness safeguard.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add the attribute to the parallel_for lambdas in launch_cpy_scalar and launch_cpy_scalar_contiguous.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: No functional change for kernels that don't use sub-group operations.

kernels.efficiency_notes: The cpy kernel is a clean native SYCL implementation with zero DPCT artifacts, proper nd_range<1>, and an intelligent memcpy fast path for same-type contiguous tensors. The code supports 12 type combinations with clean template dispatch. However, the SYCL version is missing 3 of 5 CUDA kernel variants: (1) cpy_scalar_transpose (SLM-tiled coalesced transpose) — this is the most impactful missing feature since transpose operations in attention use the slow generic path. (2) cpy_f32_q (float→quantized for KV-cache quantization). (3) cpy_q_f32 (quantized→float). The generic non-contiguous kernel has heavy 64-bit integer arithmetic (12+ divisions per work-item) that dominates for small tensors. The contiguous different-type path uses scalar 1-element-per-work-item processing. The cpy kernel is called frequently — every tensor reshape, view, transpose, and type conversion goes through it. The missing transpose optimization particularly impacts attention mechanisms which perform frequent view permutations. Medium potential overall because the missing transpose kernel and the frequency of copy operations make the aggregate impact significant.

kernels.name: concat (tensor concatenation along dims 0-3)

launch_config.sub_group_size_attribute: none — not specified on any kernel lambda
launch_config.global_size_expression: Contiguous dim0/1/2: nd_range<3>((ne2, ne1, ceil(ne0/256)*256), (1,1,256)). Non-contiguous: nd_range<3>((d_ne3, d_ne2, d_ne1*256), (1,1,256)). Contiguous dim3: no kernel, uses memcpy.
launch_config.notes: Uses nd_range<3> for all kernels with local size (1,1,256). Only dimension 2 of the local range has real work-group parallelism — dimensions 0 and 1 are both 1, using grid dimensions for ne2/ne1 (contiguous) or ne3/ne2 (non-contiguous). WG=256 (SYCL_CONCAT_BLOCK_SIZE) matches the CUDA CUDA_CONCAT_BLOCK_SIZE=256 and is appropriate for Intel Xe2. No DPCT artifacts — this is clean native SYCL. The contiguous dispatch has a host-side loop over i3 (for (int i3 = 0; i3 < dst->ne[3]; i3++)) that launches a separate kernel per i3 slice, while the CUDA version does the same. The dim3 contiguous case uses two stream.memcpy() calls with .wait() after each.

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: Contiguous dim0/1/2: perfectly coalesced. Adjacent work-items in the innermost dimension (dim2 of nd_range) access adjacent float elements via nidx = item.get_global_id(2). Each work-item reads 1 float from src0 or src1 and writes 1 float to dst. The branch on nidx < ne00 (dim0) or row < ne01 (dim1) or slice < ne02 (dim2) determines which source to read from — within each branch, access is sequential. Non-contiguous: coalescing depends on the actual byte strides (nb00, nb10, nb0). When nb00 = nb10 = nb0 = sizeof(float), the inner loop over i0 is coalesced within a work-group. For arbitrary strides, access can be non-coalesced.
strided_accesses: Non-contiguous kernel: byte-offset addressing via arbitrary strides (nb00-nb03, nb10-nb13, nb0-nb3) allows non-coalesced access patterns for tensors with non-standard strides.

Contiguous dim0: the branch nidx < ne00 splits the work-group into two halves reading from different source pointers with different strides (ne00 vs ne0-ne00) — this causes warp divergence within sub-groups straddling the ne00 boundary.
memory_patterns.notes: All loads and stores are scalar 4-byte (float) operations. Each work-item processes exactly 1 float element (contiguous) or 1 float per loop iteration (non-contiguous). No sycl::vec usage. For contiguous kernels, vec4 (16 bytes per work-item, 4 floats) would reduce instruction count 4x and improve memory subsystem utilization. The concat operation is purely memory-bound (0 FLOPs, just copy with address computation), so maximizing memory throughput via vectorization is the primary optimization lever.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM used. SLM is not beneficial for concat — there is no data reuse within a work-group. Each element is read once and written once.

reduction_pattern.notes: No reduction. Pure element-wise copy with address remapping.

data_types.notes: F32 only — both SYCL and CUDA versions only support GGML_TYPE_F32 for concat (enforced by GGML_ASSERT at line 222-224). No type conversion or computation. The CUDA version has the same F32-only limitation.

math_functions.notes: No math functions. Pure memory copy with offset computation.

barriers: stream.memcpy(...).wait() called twice in the dim3 contiguous path (lines 245-246) — each .wait() is a full host-device synchronization that blocks the host thread until the copy completes. These two copies are independent and could be overlapped.
synchronization.notes: The two memcpy calls in the dim3 contiguous path (lines 245-246) each call .wait(), creating unnecessary host-device synchronization. The second memcpy does not depend on the first completing. These should use events or be submitted without .wait() and synchronized once at the end. The CUDA version uses cudaMemcpyAsync which does not block — it just queues to the stream.

hot_loops: Non-contiguous kernel inner loop (line 190): for (int64_t i0 = item.get_local_id(2); i0 < ne0; i0 += item.get_local_range(2)) — iterates ceil(ne0/256) times per work-item. This is the hot loop for the non-contiguous path.
loop_analysis.notes: The non-contiguous kernel's inner loop iterates ne0/256 times, with each iteration doing 64-bit address arithmetic (multiply + add per stride dimension) plus a branch (if i0 < ne00) and a scalar float copy. No #pragma unroll. The contiguous kernels have no loops — each work-item processes exactly 1 element. The host-side loop over i3 (line 233) launches ne3 separate kernel invocations, each with its own dispatch overhead.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: Purely memory-bandwidth-bound operation. Arithmetic intensity: 0 FLOPs/byte — the kernel does zero floating-point computation, only integer address arithmetic and float load/store. For contiguous tensors, the operation reads N floats and writes N floats (8 bytes/element). At 456 GB/s peak B60 bandwidth, a 64MB concat (16M floats) should take ~0.14ms. The actual time will be limited by: (1) scalar 4-byte loads vs potential 16-byte vectorized loads, (2) kernel launch overhead (especially with ne3 > 1 launching multiple kernels), (3) the dim3 path's unnecessary .wait() synchronization. For non-contiguous tensors, the bottleneck may shift toward the 64-bit integer address arithmetic if strides are irregular and the L1 cache is ineffective.
anti_patterns: Unnecessary host-device synchronization in dim3 contiguous path: stream.memcpy(dst_d, src0_d, size0).wait() followed by stream.memcpy(dst_d + size0/4, src1_d, size1).wait() — the two memcpy operations write to non-overlapping regions and do not depend on each other. The .wait() blocks the host thread, preventing overlap. CUDA uses cudaMemcpyAsync without blocking. Fix: submit both without .wait(), or use events.

Host-side loop over i3 (ne[3]) launches multiple kernel invocations for contiguous dim0/1/2: for (int i3 = 0; i3 < dst->ne[3]; i3++) { concat_f32_sycl(...); } — each iteration submits a separate nd_range kernel. For ne3 > 1, this incurs per-kernel dispatch overhead. The CUDA version has the same pattern, but SYCL kernel dispatch overhead is typically higher than CUDA. Could fold i3 into the grid (nd_range<3> already has 3 dimensions, but the i3 loop could be incorporated by launching a 4D-equivalent grid).

No vectorized loads/stores: scalar 4-byte float reads/writes waste potential memory bandwidth. For contiguous dim1/dim2 kernels where the entire row is from a single source (no mid-row branch), vec4 loads/stores would process 16 bytes per work-item.

nd_range<3> used where nd_range<1> would suffice for contiguous kernels: the contiguous dim0/1/2 kernels use nd_range<3>((ne2, ne1, num_blocks*256), (1,1,256)). The dimensions 0 and 1 of the local range are both 1, meaning only dimension 2 has real work-group parallelism. While not incorrect, this is a CUDA-ism (mapping to dim3 grid) that adds minor overhead for the 3D dispatch. However, this is cosmetic — the compiler should optimize it away.

optimization_opportunities.description: Remove unnecessary .wait() calls on the two memcpy operations in the dim3 contiguous path. The current code calls stream.memcpy(...).wait() twice in sequence (lines 245-246), blocking the host thread after each copy. The two copies write to non-overlapping destination regions and are independent. Replace with two non-blocking submits followed by a single stream.wait() or event dependency.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-50% latency reduction for dim3 contiguous concat specifically, depending on tensor sizes. For small tensors, the .wait() latency (host-device round-trip ~5-20us) dominates the actual copy time. For large tensors, the improvement comes from overlapping the two DMA transfers. This only affects the dim3 path, which is less common than dim0/1/2.
