optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace: stream.memcpy(dst_d, src0_d, size0).wait(); stream.memcpy(dst_d+size0/4, src1_d, size1).wait(); With: auto e1 = stream.memcpy(dst_d, src0_d, size0); auto e2 = stream.memcpy(dst_d+size0/4, src1_d, size1); e1.wait(); e2.wait(); Or simply: stream.memcpy(dst_d, src0_d, size0); stream.memcpy(dst_d+size0/4, src1_d, size1); stream.wait(); — the second approach is simpler and matches the CUDA behavior of sequential async copies on the same stream.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The two memcpy targets are non-overlapping (dst_d vs dst_d+size0/4). Removing .wait() is safe. This matches the CUDA behavior (cudaMemcpyAsync).

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized sycl::vec<float,4> loads and stores for contiguous dim1 and dim2 kernels. In these kernels, each work-item reads from a single source (either x or y) — the source selection is based on row (dim1) or slice (dim2), not on the column index nidx. This means the entire row/slice is from one contiguous source, enabling vec4 loads/stores without branch complications. Dim0 has a mid-row branch (nidx < ne00) that complicates vectorization but can be handled with a vec4 fast path for work-items entirely within one source.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.5-2.5x throughput for contiguous dim1/dim2 concat. The current kernel does scalar 4-byte reads and writes (8 bytes/element). Vec4 does 16-byte reads and writes (still 8 bytes/element but with 4x fewer instructions and better memory subsystem utilization). The improvement is most significant for large ne0 where the kernel is clearly memory-bandwidth-bound. Dim0 improvement is smaller due to the mid-row branch requiring boundary handling.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: For dim1/dim2: add vec4 kernel variants that process 4 floats per work-item. Each work-item: nidx4 = get_global_id(2) * 4; if (nidx4 + 3 < ne0) { vec4 load/store } else { scalar tail }. Launch with global size ceil(ne0/4)/256 * 256 instead of ceil(ne0)/256 * 256. For dim0: split into 3 regions — (a) nidx < ne00-3: vec4 from x, (b) nidx >= ne00+0: vec4 from y (adjusted offset), (c) boundary: scalar. Or: launch separate kernels for the x and y portions of dim0 (since they're just two memcpys from different sources into adjacent dst regions).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Standard vec4 pattern. Requires ne0 >= 4 (always true in practice for F32 concat). The dim0 boundary case needs careful handling but can fall back to scalar.

optimization_opportunities.description: Eliminate the host-side loop over i3 for contiguous dim0/1/2 by folding the ne3 dimension into the kernel grid. Currently, the host code loops for (int i3 = 0; i3 < dst->ne[3]; i3++) and launches a separate kernel per i3 slice. Each kernel launch incurs SYCL dispatch overhead (~5-15us). For ne3 > 1 (e.g., batch dimension > 1), this launches ne3 separate kernels. Folding i3 into the grid would use a single kernel launch for all i3 slices.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: For ne3 == 1 (most common case in inference): zero improvement — only one kernel is launched anyway. For ne3 > 1 (batched operations): eliminates (ne3-1) * kernel_dispatch_overhead. If dispatch overhead is ~10us, ne3=4 saves ~30us. This is only significant for small tensors where the kernel execution time is comparable to dispatch overhead.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Use a 4D mapping: add i3 to the grid. Since nd_range only supports up to 3 dimensions, encode i3 into dimension 0: global = (ne3 * ne2, ne1, num_blocks * 256), local = (1, 1, 256). Inside the kernel: i3 = get_group(0) / ne2; i2 = get_group(0) % ne2. Alternatively, switch to a fully flattened 1D dispatch with total_elements = ne0 * ne1 * ne2 * ne3 and decompose indices inside the kernel (but this adds integer division overhead). The first approach (packing ne3*ne2 into dim0) is cleaner. Pass src0_d, src1_d, dst_d base pointers plus nb3 offsets as kernel parameters.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Well-understood grid dimension packing. The integer division i3 = group(0)/ne2 adds trivial overhead (one division per work-group, not per work-item). Only affects ne3 > 1 cases which are less common in inference.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add #pragma unroll to the non-contiguous kernel's inner loop (line 190) for compiler optimization hint. The loop iterates ceil(ne0/256) times per work-item with 64-bit address arithmetic per iteration. Unrolling by 2 or 4 can reduce loop overhead and enable the compiler to interleave memory operations.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-10% for non-contiguous path only. The non-contiguous path is the slow fallback for non-contiguous tensors. The improvement comes from reduced loop overhead (branch prediction, increment) and potential instruction-level parallelism from interleaved loads/stores. Minimal impact since this path is already marked 'slow' and non-contiguous concat is uncommon in typical inference.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add #pragma unroll 2 or #pragma unroll 4 before the for loop at line 190. Ensure the compiler can handle the unroll with the 64-bit arithmetic. No functional change.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Standard loop unrolling hint. If ne0 is not a multiple of the unroll factor, the compiler generates a tail loop automatically.

kernels.efficiency_notes: The concat kernel is a clean, well-structured native SYCL implementation with zero DPCT artifacts, proper nd_range<3> dispatch, correct 3D grid mapping, and an intelligent memcpy fast path for dim3 contiguous tensors. The code achieves near-perfect CUDA feature parity — all 4 CUDA kernel variants (dim0/1/2 contiguous, non-contiguous template) are present with equivalent functionality. The template dispatch for the non-contiguous kernel using std::integral_constant is particularly clean. WG=256 is appropriate for Intel Xe2. The main issues are: (1) unnecessary .wait() synchronization on dim3 memcpy (easy fix), (2) scalar loads/stores where vec4 could improve throughput (medium effort), (3) host-side loop over ne3 for contiguous kernels (low priority since ne3=1 in inference). The concat operation itself is not on the critical path — it's called infrequently compared to matmul, softmax, or normalization kernels, and the total time spent in concat is typically < 1% of inference time. The non-contiguous path is correctly marked 'slow' and is a faithful translation of the CUDA fallback. Overall low optimization potential due to the operation's inherent simplicity (pure copy, no compute), already-reasonable implementation quality, and low frequency of invocation.

kernels.name: im2col (2D and 3D image-to-column transformation)

im2col_2d.notes: local_range(1, 1, local_size) — only dimension 2 has actual work-group parallelism; dimensions 0 and 1 are trivially 1 in the local range, using grid dims for output spatial dims. Grid z = min(N_OH, 65535) maps to batch*output_height with MAX_GRIDDIM_Z clamping and a loop inside the kernel for overflow. Grid y = OW maps 1 work-group per output width column. Grid x = ceil(IC_KH_KW / 256) * local_size maps to the flattened input_channels * kernel_height * kernel_width dimension. Work-group size is well-chosen at up to 256 (matches SYCL_IM2COL_BLOCK_SIZE and CUDA's CUDA_IM2COL_BLOCK_SIZE=256).

im2col_3d.notes: Same structure as 2D but with an additional depth dimension. Grid z = min(N_OD_OH, 65535) maps to batch*output_depth*output_height. The kernel iterates via iz loop when N_OD_OH > MAX_GRIDDIM_Z.

launch_config.sub_group_size_attribute: none — not specified on any kernel lambda
launch_config.notes: Both 2D and 3D kernels use the same launch pattern. WG=256 is appropriate for Intel Xe2. The local_range(1,1,N) pattern with only dim-2 active is a CUDA grid/block mapping artifact. Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] on both kernel lambdas.

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: Output writes (dst[offset_dst]): Adjacent work-items in the innermost local dimension have sequential global_id(2) values, mapping to sequential i values (i = iic*KH_KW + ikh*KW + ikw). The output offset formula ((in*OH+ioh)*OW+iow)*IC_KH_KW + i means adjacent threads write to adjacent output elements within the same (in, ioh, iow) slice — COALESCED for the output. Input reads (x[offset_src + iih*IW + iiw]): The input read depends on iih and iiw which are computed from kernel position (ikh, ikw), stride (s0, s1), dilation (d0, d1), and padding (p0, p1). Adjacent threads map to different (iic, ikh, ikw) triples, and the resulting (iih, iiw) values are NOT sequential — input reads are SCATTERED, especially with non-unit dilation or when IC > 1.
strided_accesses: Input reads: adjacent work-items compute different (iic, ikh, ikw) triples, leading to strided/scattered source addresses. With dilation > 1, strides increase further.
When IC > 1: adjacent threads with different iic values access completely different input channel planes (offset by IC_IH_IW), causing large strides in source memory.
memory_patterns.notes: All loads and stores are scalar 4-byte (float) operations. Each work-item reads 1 float from source and writes 1 float (or half) to destination per iz iteration. No sycl::vec usage. Output writes are coalesced (adjacent threads write adjacent dst elements). Input reads are inherently scattered due to the im2col transformation mapping — this is fundamental to the algorithm, not a code deficiency. The CUDA version has identical access patterns.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM used. SLM could potentially cache input tiles to reduce scattered global reads, but the access pattern depends on stride/dilation/padding parameters, making SLM tiling complex. The CUDA version also uses no shared memory. For common CNN parameters (stride=1, dilation=1), input reads have moderate spatial locality that benefits from L1 cache.

reduction_pattern.notes: No reduction. Pure element-wise transformation — each work-item independently computes one output element's source address and copies (with potential zero-padding).

data_types.notes: Input is always F32. Output is F16 or F32 depending on dst type. The type conversion from float to sycl::half is via static_cast<T>(). No compute on the float values — just load, optionally cast, and store. The address computation uses int64_t throughout (many divisions and multiplications). No opportunity for reduced-precision compute since there is no actual floating-point arithmetic.

math_functions.notes: No math functions. The kernel performs only integer address arithmetic (division, multiplication, subtraction for index decomposition) and a float load + optional type cast + store. Zero floating-point arithmetic.

hot_loops: 2D iz loop (line 35): for (iz = item.get_group(0); iz < N_OH; iz += MAX_GRIDDIM_Z) — iterates ceil(N_OH / grid_z) times. For typical CNN inference with small batch (N=1) and moderate OH (e.g., 28), this is 1 iteration. For large N*OH > 65535, iterates multiple times. NOT unrolled.
3D iz loop (line 136): for (iz = item.get_group(0); iz < N_OD_OH; iz += MAX_GRIDDIM_Z) — same pattern as 2D but over N*OD*OH. NOT unrolled.
loop_analysis.notes: The iz loops have dynamic trip count depending on N*OH (2D) or N*OD*OH (3D) vs the grid z dimension (clamped to 65535). For typical inference (N=1, OH<=256), the loop executes exactly once. The index decomposition inside the loop (iz / OH, iz % OH for 2D; iz / OD_OH, (iz-n*OD_OH)/OH, iz%OH for 3D) uses expensive 64-bit integer divisions that could be replaced with multiplications/shifts for power-of-2 dimensions or strength-reduced.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: Purely memory-bandwidth bound operation. Arithmetic intensity: 0 FLOPs/byte — zero floating-point computation. Each output element requires: reading 1 float (4 bytes) from scattered source location + writing 1 float or half (4 or 2 bytes) to coalesced destination = 6-8 bytes of memory traffic. The kernel is dominated by address computation (integer arithmetic) and memory access latency. For padding regions (iih < 0 || iih >= IH || iiw < 0 || iiw >= IW), no read is needed — just a zero write. The scattered input reads are the primary bottleneck because they defeat cache line prefetching and waste bandwidth when adjacent threads access different cache lines. At 456 GB/s peak B60 bandwidth, a typical im2col for a 224x224 image with 3x3 kernel and 64 channels processes ~2.3M output elements (~9.2 MB output) in ~0.02 ms. The kernel is not on the critical path for LLM inference but is important for CNN-based vision models.
anti_patterns: nd_range<3> with local_range(1, 1, local_size) — only dimension 2 has real parallelism in the work-group; dimensions 0 and 1 are trivially 1. This is a CUDA grid/block mapping artifact. Could use nd_range<1> with the batch/spatial dimensions encoded in the global range and decoded inside the kernel.

Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] on both kernel lambdas — compiler may select a suboptimal sub-group size. While correctness is not at risk (no sub-group operations used), specifying the native SIMD16 width helps the compiler generate optimal code.

Scalar 4-byte loads/stores — no vectorization of output writes. Since adjacent threads write to adjacent output elements, vectorized stores (sycl::vec<float,4> or sycl::vec<sycl::half,8>) could reduce store transactions.

Heavy 64-bit integer division in hot path: i / KH_KW, rem / KW (2D) and i / KD_KH_KW, (i - iic*KD_KH_KW) / KH_KW, ... / KW (3D) — four 64-bit divisions per work-item in the 3D kernel. Also iz / OH (2D) or iz / OD_OH, (iz-n*OD_OH)/OH (3D) per loop iteration. 64-bit integer division is ~30-50 cycles on Xe2 vs ~4 cycles for multiply. These could be strength-reduced to 32-bit divisions (dimensions fit in int32) or multiply-shift for known values.
No #pragma unroll on the iz loop — for the common case of 1 iteration, the compiler can typically optimize this, but for multi-iteration cases, unrolling by 2 could help overlap memory operations.

The 3D kernel recomputes compound products (OD_OH_OW_IC_KD_KH_KW, OH_OW_IC_KD_KH_KW, OW_IC_KD_KH_KW) inside the kernel from captured values, while the CUDA version passes all pre-computed products as kernel parameters. The SYCL approach avoids parameter bloat but the on-device computation is redundant (computed identically by all work-items). However, with lambda capture, the compiler should hoist these to registers automatically.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace 64-bit integer divisions with 32-bit or multiply-shift alternatives. The 2D kernel performs 2 int64 divisions per work-item (i/KH_KW, rem/KW) plus 1-2 per iz iteration (iz/OH, iz-in*OH). The 3D kernel performs 4 int64 divisions per work-item and 2-3 per iz iteration. All dimension values (IC, KH, KW, OH, OW, OD, etc.) fit comfortably in int32, so 64-bit division is unnecessary. Additionally, for power-of-2 dimensions (common in CNNs), divisions can be replaced with right-shifts. For non-power-of-2, use the multiply-and-shift magic number trick (precompute on host, pass as kernel parameter).
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-20% throughput improvement. On Xe2, 64-bit integer division takes ~30-50 cycles vs ~4 cycles for 32-bit multiply. With 4-6 divisions per work-item in the 3D kernel, this is significant instruction overhead for a kernel with zero floating-point compute. The improvement is most pronounced when the iz loop iterates multiple times.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Option A (simple): Cast all dimension variables to int32_t at the top of the kernel lambda — iic = (int32_t)i / (int32_t)KH_KW, etc. This works because typical CNN dimensions (IC*KH*KW, N*OH*OW) are well within int32 range. Only the output offset computation needs 64-bit for large tensors. Option B (optimal): Precompute magic numbers on host for each divisor (KH_KW, KW, OH, OD_OH) using the standard fast-division algorithm, pass as kernel parameters, and use multiply-shift in the kernel. The CUDA version also uses 64-bit divisions but NVIDIA hardware has faster int64 division than Intel Xe2. Priority: the 3D kernel benefits more due to more divisions.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Narrowing to int32 is safe as long as individual dimensions fit in int32 (they always do for practical CNN parameters). The multiply-shift approach is mathematically exact for all inputs within the divisor's range. Must ensure the output offset computation remains 64-bit for large total element counts.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized output stores for the common non-padding case. Adjacent work-items write to adjacent output elements (dst[offset_dst] with sequential offset_dst values for adjacent i). For the non-padding case (iih and iiw in bounds), a group of 4 adjacent work-items could cooperatively write a sycl::vec<float,4> or sycl::vec<sycl::half,8>. For the F16 output path, 8 half values = 16 bytes per store (matching a single 128-bit memory transaction). The padding case (writing zero) is even more amenable to vectorized stores since no input reads are needed.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 10-25% throughput improvement for output writes. The kernel is memory-bound with coalesced output writes, so reducing store transactions directly improves effective bandwidth. For F16 output (2 bytes/element), the improvement is larger because scalar stores waste more of the cache line. Improvement is lower for scattered input reads which remain the primary bottleneck.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Restructure the kernel so each work-item processes 4 consecutive output elements (for F32) or 8 (for F16) instead of 1. Change the global range from num_blocks * local_size to ceil(IC_KH_KW/4) * local_size, with each work-item computing i_base = get_global_id(2) * 4 and processing elements i_base through i_base+3. Store results as sycl::vec<T,4>. Input reads remain scalar (different source addresses per element due to different iic/ikh/ikw). Must handle the tail case where IC_KH_KW is not divisible by 4. For the padding check, use sycl::select or conditional store per element.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The vectorized store requires 4 (or 8) adjacent output elements to be in the same padding/non-padding state. If they straddle a padding boundary, mixed scalar/vector stores are needed, complicating the code. The input reads remain scattered regardless, limiting the overall bandwidth improvement. For small IC_KH_KW values (< 4), must fall back to scalar.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] to both kernel lambdas. While the kernel does not use sub-group operations, specifying the native SIMD16 width prevents the compiler from choosing a suboptimal sub-group size (e.g., SIMD8 which would halve vectorization or SIMD32 which would require emulation). This is a standard best practice for all SYCL kernels on Intel GPUs.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 0-5% improvement. Ensures the compiler generates SIMD16 code without wasting instruction slots. May enable better auto-vectorization of the scalar load/store pattern by the compiler.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] to the lambda in both parallel_for calls (line 23 for 2D, line 124 for 3D). This is a one-line addition per kernel. Example: stream->parallel_for(sycl::nd_range<3>(global_range, local_range), [=](sycl::nd_item<3> item) [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] { ... });
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Standard attribute that matches the hardware's native SIMD width. No correctness risk since the kernel does not depend on sub-group size.

optimization_opportunities.description: Convert from nd_range<3> with local_range(1,1,N) to nd_range<1> with a flattened 1D dispatch. The current 3D dispatch uses dimensions 0 and 1 of the local range as trivially 1, wasting the 3D dispatch overhead. A 1D dispatch would flatten the (iz, iow, i) triple into a single global index, decoded inside the kernel. However, this would replace the implicit grid mapping (get_group(0)=iz, get_group(1)=iow) with explicit integer arithmetic, adding division overhead. Alternative: keep nd_range<3> but note it as a cosmetic issue.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 0-2% improvement. Primarily a code quality fix. The 3D dispatch overhead is trivial on Intel GPUs. The compiler likely optimizes away the unused dimensions.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Option A: Convert to nd_range<1> with total_work_items = grid_z * OW * num_blocks * local_size. Inside kernel: decode item.get_global_id(0) back to (iz, iow, i). This adds 2 divisions per work-item which partly negates any benefit. Option B: Keep nd_range<3> but document it as a CUDA mapping artifact. Option B is recommended — the 3D dispatch is not a real performance issue and the explicit grid mapping is clearer. Not recommended for implementation.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: No correctness risk. The 3D dispatch pattern works correctly. Converting to 1D would add integer divisions that could slightly hurt performance.

kernels.efficiency_notes: The im2col kernel is a clean, direct port from CUDA with near-perfect feature parity — both 2D and 3D variants are present with identical algorithmic structure. The code is well-organized with templated type support (F16/F32 output), proper MAX_GRIDDIM_Z overflow handling, and appropriate work-group size (up to 256 via SYCL_IM2COL_BLOCK_SIZE). Zero DPCT artifacts — this appears to be a manual port, not DPCT-migrated. The kernel's efficiency is primarily limited by the inherent nature of im2col: scattered input reads (each work-item reads from a different location in the input tensor based on kernel position, stride, and dilation), heavy 64-bit integer address arithmetic (4-6 divisions per work-item), and scalar memory operations. These are fundamental algorithmic characteristics shared with the CUDA version. The main Intel-specific optimization is reducing 64-bit integer divisions to 32-bit or multiply-shift equivalents (medium impact, ~10-20%). Vectorized output stores offer moderate improvement (~10-25%). Adding reqd_sub_group_size is a best-practice fix with minimal impact. Overall low optimization potential because: (a) im2col is called infrequently in LLM inference — it's primarily used by CNN-based vision models (Whisper audio, image encoders) and contributes <1% of typical LLM inference time, (b) the implementation quality is already good with no DPCT artifacts and correct CUDA parity, (c) the scattered input access pattern is fundamental to the im2col algorithm and cannot be meaningfully improved without changing the algorithmic approach (e.g., implicit GEMM which eliminates im2col entirely).

kernels.name: pad

launch_config.global_size_expression: 3D: (ne2*ne3, ne1, num_blocks_x*256) where num_blocks_x = ceil(ne0/256)
launch_config.notes: WG=256 in dim2 only; dims 0 and 1 are degenerate (size 1). This is the standard CUDA grid translation pattern. 256 work-items matches Intel's preferred range. No sub-group size specified — acceptable since no sub-group ops used.

strided_accesses: Source reads when s00 != 1 (non-contiguous dim-0 stride) — inherent to data layout, matches CUDA behavior
memory_patterns.notes: Destination writes are perfectly coalesced (adjacent work-items write adjacent float elements). Source reads are coalesced when s00==1 (standard contiguous tensor). Each work-item processes exactly 1 float — no vectorization.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM used. Correct for a pure element-wise copy/fill operation with no data reuse between work-items.

reduction_pattern.notes: No reduction — each work-item independently computes one output element.

data_types.notes: FP32 only — hardcoded with GGML_ASSERT(type == GGML_TYPE_F32). Pad is a pure data-movement op (copy or zero-fill) with no arithmetic. Templating on element type to support FP16/BF16 would avoid unnecessary type conversion round-trips in half-precision pipelines.

math_functions.notes: No math functions. Only integer arithmetic for index computation (add, subtract, multiply, divide, modulus). The circular case uses int64 modulus for wrap-around.

loop_analysis.notes: No loops inside the kernel. Each work-item executes a single branch (circular vs non-circular) and processes exactly one element. Performance is purely determined by launch overhead and memory bandwidth.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: Pad is a pure memory-movement operation: one float read (or zero-fill) + one float write per work-item. Zero compute intensity (0 FLOP/byte). Performance is entirely memory-bandwidth limited. For the zero-padding path, no read is needed — just a store of 0.0f.
anti_patterns: 3D nd_range with degenerate dimensions (dims 0 and 1 have WG=1) — CUDA grid translation artifact, functionally correct
No vectorized loads/stores — each work-item processes only 1 float (4 bytes) where 16-byte vec4 loads/stores would improve bandwidth utilization
FP32-only — no FP16/BF16 support, forces type conversion in mixed-precision pipelines
Circular case uses 4x int64 modulus operations — could use conditional subtraction for faster wrap-around when padding is small relative to tensor size
Dead declaration: ggml_sycl_pad() declared in pad.hpp but never defined

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized vec4 loads/stores (sycl::vec<float,4>) for the non-circular contiguous case (s00==1). Process 4 elements per work-item, reducing memory transactions by 4x. For the non-padded interior region, this is a straightforward 128-bit load + 128-bit store. For the zero-fill boundary, use a vec4 of zeros. Handle the tail (ne0 not divisible by 4) with scalar fallback.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.5-2x throughput improvement for the memory-bound pad kernel by utilizing wider memory transactions. Impact scales with tensor size — more significant for large tensors.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Specialize the kernel launch: when s00==1 and !circular, use a vec4 kernel where each work-item processes 4 consecutive elements. Adjust num_blocks_x = ceil(ne0/4/256). Each work-item computes i0_base = (local_id + group_id * 256) * 4, then loads/stores sycl::vec<float,4>. For boundary work-items, fall back to scalar processing. This pattern is already used in other SYCL kernels in this codebase (e.g., element_wise).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The vec4 optimization only applies to the contiguous non-circular fast path. The scalar fallback handles all edge cases. No correctness risk since the underlying memory layout is unchanged.

optimization_opportunities.description: Template the pad kernel on element type to support FP16 and BF16 natively, avoiding unnecessary FP32 type conversion round-trips in mixed-precision pipelines. Pad is a pure data-movement op — it doesn't care about the element type, it just copies bytes or writes zeros.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 2x throughput for FP16 tensors (half the bytes to move). Eliminates two type conversion passes (FP16→FP32 before pad, FP32→FP16 after pad) if the pipeline uses half precision.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Template the lambda on typename T. Remove the GGML_ASSERT(type == GGML_TYPE_F32) guards. Dispatch based on dst->type: GGML_TYPE_F32 → float, GGML_TYPE_F16 → sycl::half, GGML_TYPE_BF16 → sycl::ext::oneapi::bfloat16. Use static_cast<T>(0) instead of 0.0f for zero-fill. The kernel logic is type-agnostic — only the pointer types and zero literal need parameterization.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Pad performs no arithmetic, so data type doesn't affect numerical accuracy. The only risk is ensuring the type dispatch is correct and that the caller provides matching src/dst types.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace 3D nd_range with 1D nd_range and manual index decomposition. The current 3D layout has degenerate dimensions 0 and 1 (WG=1), making it effectively 1D. A 1D nd_range simplifies the code and may reduce kernel argument overhead slightly. This is primarily a code quality improvement.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Negligible performance impact (<1%). Primarily improves code clarity and reduces kernel argument size. The 3D nd_range overhead is minimal on Intel GPUs.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace nd_range<3>(...) with nd_range<1>(total_elements_rounded, 256). Compute i0/i1/i2/i3 from the global linear index using division and modulus: i0 = gid % ne0, i1 = (gid / ne0) % ne1, etc. This matches the pattern used in element_wise.cpp and other newer SYCL kernels in this codebase.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Pure refactoring — same algorithm, different indexing. The 1D decomposition introduces integer divisions, but these are the same divisions the hardware does internally for 3D dispatch.

optimization_opportunities.description: Optimize the circular padding wrap-around: replace 4 int64 modulus operations with conditional subtraction. For the common case where padding is small relative to tensor size, most elements map to non-wrapped indices. A branch-free conditional subtraction (coord = coord >= size ? coord - size : coord) avoids expensive integer division. If coord can be negative (from the lp subtraction), use a two-step: if (coord < 0) coord += size; if (coord >= size) coord -= size;
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-10% throughput improvement for the circular padding case only. Integer division is ~30 cycles on Intel GPUs. Most pads use zero-padding (non-circular), so this only benefits circular pad use cases.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace `((i0 - lp0) + ne00) % ne00` with: `int64_t c = i0 - lp0; if (c < 0) c += ne00; else if (c >= ne00) c -= ne00;`. This works when padding is < tensor_size (which is always true for valid circular padding). Same for i1/i2/i3 coordinates.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The conditional subtraction is valid when padding amount < tensor dimension, which is guaranteed by the semantics of circular padding. For paranoid safety, can add GGML_ASSERT(lp0 < ne00) in the host wrapper.

kernels.efficiency_notes: Clean native SYCL port with zero DPCT artifacts, proper WG=256, and correct coalesced access patterns. The kernel is a faithful 1:1 translation of the CUDA original. It is purely memory-bandwidth bound with zero compute. The main inefficiency is scalar 4-byte loads/stores where vec4 could improve bandwidth utilization. Pad is called infrequently during typical LLM inference (mainly for vision encoders and diffusion models), contributing <1% of end-to-end latency. The circular padding path has expensive int64 modulus operations but is rarely used. Overall, the implementation quality is good and the optimization ROI is low.

kernels.name: pad_reflect_1d (1D reflection padding)

launch_config.global_size_expression: nd_range<3>((ne03, ne02, ne01*tiles0*bx), (1,1,bx)) where bx=256 (SYCL_PAD_REFLECT_1D_BLOCK_SIZE) and tiles0=ceil(ne0/bx)
launch_config.notes: WG=256 in dim2 only; dims 0 and 1 are degenerate (local_range=1). Grid dims 0 and 1 cover ne03 (batch) and ne02 (channels). Grid dim2 packs ne01*tiles0 work-groups — the i1 and i0-tile indices are recovered via integer division/modulus: i1 = group_x / tiles0, tile0 = group_x % tiles0. This closely mirrors the CUDA version's dim3(ne01*tiles0, ne02, ne03) layout but with axes reordered. No sub-group size specified — acceptable since no sub-group operations are used. The __launch_bounds__(256, 1) from CUDA has no direct SYCL equivalent.

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: Destination writes are perfectly coalesced — adjacent work-items in the local dimension write adjacent float elements via i0 = local_id(2) + tile0*bx. Source reads are conditionally coalesced: for the middle region (rel_i0 >= 0 && rel_i0 < ne00), reads are sequential when nb00 == sizeof(float). For left-reflection (rel_i0 < 0), src_idx = -rel_i0 reverses the access direction — adjacent work-items read in reverse order, which is still coalesced (just reversed). For right-reflection, src_idx = 2*ne00 - 2 - rel_i0 is also reversed-coalesced. The potential non-coalesced case is when nb00 != sizeof(float) (non-contiguous dim0 stride), but this is the byte-offset addressing path and matches CUDA behavior.
strided_accesses: Source reads when nb00 != sizeof(float) (non-contiguous innermost dimension) — inherent to data layout
memory_patterns.notes: All loads and stores are scalar 4-byte (float) operations. Each work-item processes exactly 1 float element. No sycl::vec usage. For the middle region (the majority of elements when padding is small), vec4 loads/stores would process 16 bytes per work-item. The reflection boundary complicates vectorization but only affects a small number of work-items near the padding edges.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM used. Correct — this is a pure element-wise copy/reflect operation with no data reuse between work-items.

reduction_pattern.notes: No reduction — each work-item independently computes one output element via a source index lookup (conditional reflection) and copies one float.

data_types.notes: FP32 only — hardcoded with GGML_ASSERT(src0->type == GGML_TYPE_F32 && dst->type == GGML_TYPE_F32). Pad_reflect_1d is a pure data-movement op (copy with index remapping) with zero floating-point arithmetic. Templating on element type to support FP16/BF16 would avoid unnecessary type conversion in mixed-precision pipelines (e.g., audio processing with Whisper). CUDA has the same F32-only limitation.

math_functions.notes: No math functions. Only integer arithmetic for index computation (subtract, compare, multiply). The reflection formula uses simple arithmetic: left = -rel_i0, right = 2*ne00 - 2 - rel_i0. No divisions or modulus in the hot path — the only division is for the work-group index decomposition (group_x / tiles0, group_x % tiles0).

loop_analysis.notes: No loops inside the kernel. Each work-item executes a single 3-way branch (left-reflect, middle-copy, right-reflect) and processes exactly one element. The code is entirely branch-based with no loops. Performance is determined by memory bandwidth and kernel launch overhead.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: Pure memory-movement operation: one float read + one float write per work-item, zero floating-point compute. Arithmetic intensity is 0 FLOP/byte. Performance is entirely memory-bandwidth limited at 456 GB/s peak. For the common case of small padding (p0, p1 << ne00), ~95%+ of work-items take the middle path (direct copy) with perfect coalescing. The reflected boundary elements are a small fraction and have reversed-but-still-coalesced access patterns.
anti_patterns: 3D nd_range with degenerate dimensions (dims 0 and 1 have local_range=1) — CUDA grid translation artifact, functionally correct but cosmetically different from the 1D nd_range pattern used in newer SYCL kernels

No vectorized loads/stores — each work-item processes only 1 float (4 bytes) where vec4 loads/stores processing 16 bytes per work-item would improve bandwidth utilization for the middle (non-reflected) region
FP32-only — no FP16/BF16 support, forces type conversion in mixed-precision pipelines (same limitation as CUDA)

Missing CUDA's fast_div_modulo optimization: CUDA uses init_fastdiv_values(ne01) to precompute magic-number reciprocal on host and avoid expensive integer division in the kernel (blockIdx.x / ne01). SYCL uses plain int64 division (group_x / tiles0, group_x % tiles0) which is ~30-80 cycles per work-item on Intel GPUs. The CUDA version's uint3 packing with fast division saves ~20-60 cycles per work-item.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized vec4 loads/stores (sycl::vec<float,4>) for the middle (non-reflected) region where nb00 == sizeof(float). The middle region (rel_i0 in [0, ne00)) is a straight copy — adjacent work-items read and write adjacent elements. For padding amounts << tensor size (typical case), 95%+ of elements are in the middle region. Process 4 elements per work-item with vec4, reducing memory transactions by 4x. Handle the left and right reflection boundaries with scalar fallback.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.5-2x throughput improvement for the memory-bound kernel. Most effective for large ne0 with small padding where the middle region dominates. Minimal improvement for large padding ratios where boundary handling is frequent.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Split the kernel into two paths based on i0 position: (1) if i0 is well within the middle region (i0 >= p0+3 && i0+3 < p0+ne00), use vec4 load from src + vec4 store to dst, processing 4 consecutive elements per work-item. (2) Otherwise, use the existing scalar path with reflection logic. Adjust launch grid to ceil(ne0/4/256) for the vec4 path. Add scalar tail handling for ne0 not divisible by 4. The vec4 path requires nb00 == sizeof(float) (contiguous source).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Standard vectorization pattern for the non-reflected interior. The reflection boundaries are handled by scalar fallback, so correctness is preserved. Requires ne00 >= 4 (always true for practical shapes).

optimization_opportunities.description: Implement fast integer division for the group_x / tiles0 and group_x % tiles0 decomposition, matching CUDA's fast_div_modulo optimization. CUDA precomputes magic-number reciprocals on the host (init_fastdiv_values) and uses multiply-shift in the kernel to avoid expensive int64 division. The SYCL version uses plain int64_t division and modulus which cost ~30-80 cycles each on Intel GPUs. Every work-item pays this cost.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% throughput improvement. The division cost is per-work-item and cannot be amortized. For small tensors where the kernel is short, this overhead is a larger fraction of total time. For large tensors, the improvement is smaller but still meaningful since the kernel is memory-bound and any compute overhead reduces the ability to saturate memory bandwidth.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Option A: Precompute magic number and shift on host: uint32_t magic = ((1ULL << 32) + tiles0 - 1) / tiles0; uint32_t shift = 32; Pass magic/shift as kernel args. In kernel: i1 = (uint32_t)((uint64_t)group_x * magic >> shift); tile0 = group_x - i1 * tiles0; This matches CUDA's fast_div_modulo pattern. Option B: Use 32-bit arithmetic if ne01*tiles0 < INT32_MAX (almost always true). Option C: Restructure the grid to use nd_range dimensions directly for i1 and tile0 instead of packing them into one dimension.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Fast integer division is a well-understood optimization. Option B (32-bit cast) is the simplest and sufficient for all practical tensor sizes. Option C (restructuring to avoid division entirely) would be even better but changes the launch config.

optimization_opportunities.description: Template the pad_reflect_1d kernel on element type to support FP16 and BF16 natively, avoiding unnecessary type conversion in mixed-precision pipelines. The kernel is a pure data-movement op — it copies floats with index remapping and performs no arithmetic. Templating on element type is trivial since only the pointer type and sizeof change.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 2x throughput for FP16 tensors (half the bytes to move per element). Eliminates two type conversion kernel launches (FP16→FP32 before pad, FP32→FP16 after pad) if the pipeline uses half precision. Relevant for audio processing (Whisper) and vision models that use FP16 throughout.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Template the lambda on typename T. Remove GGML_ASSERT(src0->type == GGML_TYPE_F32) and GGML_ASSERT(dst->type == GGML_TYPE_F32). Dispatch based on dst->type: F32 → float, F16 → sycl::half, BF16 → sycl::ext::oneapi::bfloat16. The kernel body is type-agnostic — only pointer casts change: const T value = *(const T*)(src0_ptr + src_idx * nb00); *(T*)(dst_ptr + i0 * nb0) = value;
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: No arithmetic is performed, so data type doesn't affect numerical accuracy. The only risk is ensuring nb00/nb0 are correct for the element size (nb00 = sizeof(T) for contiguous tensors). CUDA has the same F32-only limitation, so this would be a SYCL improvement over CUDA.

optimization_opportunities.description: Restructure the nd_range to avoid the packed group_x dimension. Currently ne01 and tiles0 are packed into grid dimension 2 as ne01*tiles0*bx, requiring integer division to recover i1 and tile0. An alternative is to use a 3D grid where dim0 = ne03*ne02 (batch*channel packed), dim1 = ne01, dim2 = tiles0*bx, so that i1 = get_group(1) directly without division. Or convert to nd_range<1> with total_elements and decompose all indices from a flat global ID.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-10% from eliminating the int64 division in the kernel (overlaps with opt_023_002). Primarily a code clarity improvement. The nd_range restructuring approach is architecturally cleaner than the fast-division workaround.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Option A: nd_range<3>((ne03*ne02, ne01, tiles0*bx), (1, 1, bx)) — dim0 packs batch and channel (recovered via group(0)/ne02 and group(0)%ne02), dim1 maps directly to i1, dim2 maps to tile0 and i0. This eliminates the division for i1 at the cost of one division for i3/i2 (which can use 32-bit arithmetic since ne02 is small). Option B: If ne03 and ne02 are always small (typical for 1D padding on audio), use nd_range<3>((ne03, ne02*ne01, tiles0*bx), (1,1,bx)) and recover i2/i1 from group(1).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Pure refactoring — same algorithm, different grid layout. The restructured grid must ensure all dimensions fit within the hardware grid dimension limits (65535 per dim for most Intel GPUs). For typical 1D padding shapes, this is not a concern.

kernels.efficiency_notes: Clean native SYCL port with zero DPCT artifacts, proper WG=256, and correct coalesced access patterns. The kernel is a faithful translation of the CUDA original with identical reflection logic and branching structure. It is purely memory-bandwidth bound with zero floating-point compute. The main differences from CUDA are: (1) missing fast_div_modulo optimization for the group index decomposition — SYCL uses expensive int64 division where CUDA uses a multiply-shift trick, costing ~30-80 cycles per work-item. (2) Scalar 4-byte loads/stores where vec4 could improve bandwidth for the non-reflected middle region. (3) FP32-only (same as CUDA). Pad_reflect_1d is used primarily for 1D convolution preprocessing in audio models (e.g., Whisper) and is called infrequently — typically once per audio chunk, contributing <0.1% of end-to-end latency. The implementation quality is good and optimization ROI is low.

launch_config.global_size_expression: ((total_output_elements + 255) / 256) * 256 for all 5 kernels

strided_accesses: conv2d input reads strided by stride_x/stride_y — adjacent work-items access addresses separated by stride (lines 151, 271, 332)
conv_transpose_1d input reads are broadcast (same address for work-items with same channel) (line 63)
conv2d_transpose input reads are scattered/unpredictable with conditional skips (line 458)
Output writes are coalesced in all 5 kernels (adjacent work-items write adjacent addresses)

functions: custom sycl_max64/sycl_min64 (lines 90-96) instead of sycl::max/min in conv2d; sycl::max/min correctly used in depthwise variants

hot_loops: conv_transpose_1d: 2-deep loop (for c, for i) at lines 50-67 — iterates IC * KW times per work-item
conv2d: 3-deep loop (for c_in, for ky, for kx) at lines 132-156 — iterates IC * KH * KW times
conv2d_dw_whcn: 2-deep loop (for ky, for kx) at lines 264-277 — iterates KH * KW times
conv2d_dw_cwhn: 2-deep loop (for ky, for kx) at lines 325-337 — iterates KH * KW times
conv2d_transpose: 3-deep loop (for c_in, for kh, for kw) at lines 442-463 — iterates IC * KH * KW times with heavy branching

anti_patterns: Manual global index computation (blockIdx*blockDim+threadIdx pattern) in 4 of 5 kernels — should use item.get_global_id(0) (lines 118, 244, 305, 429)
1D dispatch for 2D/4D spatial problems — flattened index space with expensive division/modulo to recover spatial coordinates (lines 125-128, 251-254, 312-315, 435-438)
No SLM tiling — direct convolution without shared memory for kernel weight or input tile reuse; each work-item independently loads all needed data
Hardcoded WG=256 without device-specific tuning (defined in presets.hpp:51-54)
Custom sycl_max64/sycl_min64 helper functions (lines 90-96) instead of sycl::max/min built-ins in conv2d kernel (depthwise variants correctly use sycl::max/min)
No sub-group size specification — compiler cannot optimize SIMD packing for Xe2 SIMD16
Heavy branching in conv_transpose_1d (line 57-59 continue) and conv2d_transpose (lines 445-453 three continue statements) causes sub-group divergence

optimization_opportunities.description: Add SLM tiling for conv2d kernel weights — kernel weight tensor K_D[c_out][c_in][KH][KW] is read by all work-items with the same c_out within a work-group. Loading the kernel tile into SLM once per work-group and reusing it across work-items eliminates redundant global memory reads proportional to work-group size.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.3-2x throughput for conv2d with large IC (input channels) — reduces global memory traffic by ~WG_SIZE/1 factor for kernel weight reads
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Allocate sycl::local_accessor<float, 1> of size IC*KH*KW (or tile thereof if it exceeds SLM budget). Cooperatively load via work-items in the WG, barrier, then each work-item reads from SLM in the accumulation loop. For 3x3 conv with 64 channels: 64*3*3*4 = 2304 bytes SLM — well within 64KB limit.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: SLM tiling is a well-understood optimization. Risk is limited to ensuring proper barrier placement and SLM budget management.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add #pragma unroll to hot inner loops in all 5 convolution kernels — the innermost loops (kx iteration in conv2d, conv2d_dw) iterate over small, frequently-constant kernel dimensions (typically 1, 3, 5, 7). Unrolling reduces loop overhead, enables better instruction scheduling, and allows the compiler to optimize register usage.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.1-1.3x throughput — primarily reduces loop control overhead and enables instruction-level parallelism in the accumulation loop
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add #pragma unroll before the innermost for-loops at lines 140 (kx in conv2d), 264 (ky in conv2d_dw), 268 (kx in conv2d_dw), 449 (kw in conv2d_transpose). For conv_transpose_1d (line 56) where loop count is dynamic, use #pragma unroll 4 for partial unroll.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Loop unrolling is safe — no functional change. Only risk is register pressure increase if loop count is large, but typical kernel sizes (3x3, 5x5) are small.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized vec4 stores for output writes — all 5 kernels write one float per work-item to coalesced output addresses. Processing 4 output elements per work-item with sycl::vec<float,4> stores would reduce memory transactions and better utilize the 456 GB/s memory bandwidth.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.2-1.5x throughput for memory-bound convolutions (small kernel sizes where accumulation loop is short)
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Each work-item computes 4 adjacent output elements (out_x, out_x+1, out_x+2, out_x+3) and writes them as a vec4 store. Requires adjusting global_size to total_elements/4 and handling tail elements. Most beneficial for depthwise conv where the accumulation loop is short (KH*KW only).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Increases register pressure (4 accumulators instead of 1). Requires careful handling of non-vec4-aligned output sizes. May not help compute-bound conv2d where accumulation loop dominates.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace custom sycl_max64/sycl_min64 with sycl::max/min built-ins and clean up CUDA anti-patterns — use item.get_global_id(0) instead of manual blockIdx*blockDim+threadIdx computation in 4 kernels. Replace custom min/max helpers (lines 90-96) with sycl::max/sycl::min which are already correctly used by the depthwise variants.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Negligible performance impact — primarily code quality and maintainability improvement
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace lines 118, 244, 305, 429 (manual global_idx computation) with item.get_global_id(0). Replace sycl_max64/sycl_min64 calls in conv2d (lines 134-137) with sycl::max/sycl::min. Remove the helper function definitions at lines 90-96.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Functionally equivalent transformation. No algorithmic change.

optimization_opportunities.description: Explore im2col+XMX path for conv2d — instead of direct convolution, rearrange patches into a matrix (im2col, already implemented as sk_021) and use joint_matrix/XMX for the GEMM. This leverages Intel XMX engines for matrix multiply at hardware peak throughput.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 2-5x throughput for conv2d with large IC*KH*KW (e.g., 64*3*3=576 FLOPs per output element) — transforms a memory-bound direct convolution into a compute-efficient matmul
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: The im2col kernel (sk_021) already exists. This optimization would add an alternative code path that calls im2col followed by oneMKL GEMM (or a custom joint_matrix kernel) for conv2d when the problem size is large enough. Requires a heuristic to choose between direct conv and im2col+GEMM based on IC, KH, KW, and batch size.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Significant architectural change. Requires careful correctness validation for all padding/stride/dilation combinations. Memory overhead of im2col buffer. May not help for small kernel sizes (1x1 conv) or depthwise conv. The im2col+GEMM path already exists at a higher level in ggml-sycl.cpp but may not be used for all conv2d cases.

kernels.name: set

launch_config.global_size_expression: ceil(ne / SYCL_CPY_BLOCK_SIZE) * SYCL_CPY_BLOCK_SIZE, where ne = total elements in src1
launch_config.notes: The set operation has NO dedicated kernel. It is a pure orchestration function (42 lines) that delegates ALL GPU work to ggml_sycl_cpy() from cpy.cpp. Step 1 (if !inplace): copies src0 → dst via stream.memcpy() (contiguous same-type fast path). Step 2 (always): copies src1 → dst_view via k_cpy_scalar kernel with strided 4D addressing. The k_cpy_scalar kernel uses nd_range<1> with SYCL_CPY_BLOCK_SIZE=256 work-group size. This is an appropriate work-group size for Intel GPUs.

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: Two distinct memory patterns: (1) The inplace=false copy (src0→dst) uses stream.memcpy() — optimal, hardware DMA. (2) The src1→dst_view copy via k_cpy_scalar uses 4D index decomposition with arbitrary strides (nb1, nb2, nb3 from op_params). When dst_view strides match src1 strides (contiguous-to-contiguous), access is coalesced. When strides differ (the common case for set — writing a small tensor into a larger one at an offset), the destination writes can be strided.
strided_accesses: k_cpy_scalar: 8 int64 divisions per work-item for 4D index decomposition (4 for src, 4 for dst) — extremely expensive on GPU
Destination writes via computed byte offsets (i10*nb10 + i11*nb11 + i12*nb12 + i13*nb13) — stride pattern depends on op_params
memory_patterns.notes: All loads/stores in k_cpy_scalar are scalar 4-byte (float or int32_t). No sycl::vec types. The 4D index decomposition performs 8 int64 divisions per work-item — extremely expensive relative to the actual data movement (1 load + 1 store per work-item).

slm_usage.notes: No SLM used. Each work-item independently computes its own source and destination addresses and copies one element.

reduction_pattern.notes: No reduction needed — set is a pure data movement operation.

data_types.notes: Set only supports F32 and I32 types (same as CUDA). The type combination is homogeneous: src0, src1, and dst must all be the same type. No type conversion occurs.

math_functions.notes: No math functions. Set is pure data movement.

loop_analysis.notes: No loops in the kernel itself. Each work-item processes exactly one element. The 4D index decomposition is straight-line code with 8 int64 divisions.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: The set operation launches UP TO 2 kernel/DMA operations: (1) stream.memcpy for inplace=false case, (2) k_cpy_scalar for the src1→dst_view copy. For small tensors (common in LLM inference — e.g., updating a single KV cache row), the kernel launch overhead and 8 int64 divisions per work-item dominate over actual data movement. For larger tensors, the operation is purely memory-bound with arithmetic intensity of 0 FLOP/byte. The lack of vectorized loads means the memory bus is underutilized.
anti_patterns: Delegates to k_cpy_scalar which performs 8 int64 divisions per work-item for 4D index decomposition — extremely expensive for a zero-compute data movement kernel
No vectorized loads/stores — scalar 4-byte per work-item
No specialized contiguous-to-strided path — even when src1 is contiguous and only the dst_view has custom strides, the kernel computes both source and destination 4D indices
Two separate GPU operations (memcpy + kernel) for non-inplace set — could potentially be fused into a single kernel
Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] on k_cpy_scalar kernel
SYCL implementation is near-identical to CUDA (1:1 port) — all optimizations in the cpy infrastructure apply here

optimization_opportunities.description: Optimize k_cpy_scalar's 4D index decomposition to use int32 arithmetic instead of int64 where possible. The current implementation performs 8 int64 divisions per work-item. For tensors where all dimension products fit in int32 (ne00*ne01*ne02 < 2^31, which is true for virtually all practical LLM tensor shapes), downcast to int32 divisions which are 2-4x faster on Intel GPUs. Alternatively, precompute divisors on the host and pass as kernel arguments to use multiply-shift fast division.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% throughput improvement for the k_cpy_scalar kernel path. The improvement is higher for small tensors where the division overhead is a larger fraction of total work.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: This optimization applies to the shared cpy.cpp kernel infrastructure, not set.cpp itself. In k_cpy_scalar, add a template parameter or runtime check: if ne00*ne01*ne02 < INT32_MAX, use int32 arithmetic for all index decomposition. Alternatively, precompute fast-division magic numbers on the host (multiply-shift trick) and pass them as kernel arguments. The latter approach benefits all cpy users (set, cpy, dup, cont).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Int32 overflow is the only risk — must verify all dimension products fit. For LLM tensors with typical shapes (ne[0] < 32768, ne[1] < 65536, etc.), int32 is sufficient. The fast-division approach has zero correctness risk since it produces identical results.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add vectorized load/store path for the common case where src1 is contiguous and the dst_view has nb0 = sizeof(float) (i.e., innermost dimension is contiguous in both). In this case, adjacent work-items access adjacent elements in both source and destination, and vec4 loads/stores (16 bytes per work-item) would reduce memory transactions by 4x. This is the dominant case for GGML_OP_SET when setting a contiguous slice into a larger tensor.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.5-3x throughput improvement for the src1→dst_view copy when the contiguous condition is met. Impact is higher for larger src1 tensors.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: In cpy.cpp, add a specialized launch path: if nb00==sizeof(src_t) && nb10==sizeof(dst_t) && src0->type==src1->type, launch a kernel that processes 4 elements per work-item using sycl::vec<float,4>. The kernel would compute 4D offsets for element i*4 and then load/store 4 consecutive elements. Only the outer 3 dimensions need 4D decomposition; the innermost dimension is handled by the vectorized access. Alternatively, add a 'k_cpy_scalar_contiguous_strided' kernel variant for when src is contiguous and dst has only non-unit stride in dimensions > 0.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Must handle tail elements when ne is not a multiple of 4. Must verify alignment of source and destination pointers. The common F32 case (4-byte aligned) naturally supports vec4 loads.

optimization_opportunities.description: For the non-inplace case, fuse the stream.memcpy (src0→dst) and k_cpy_scalar (src1→dst_view) into a single kernel that copies src0 to dst while simultaneously writing src1 into the view region. This eliminates one kernel/DMA launch and one full read+write pass over the dst buffer (since the memcpy writes all of dst, and then k_cpy_scalar overwrites a subset).
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 30-50% latency reduction for non-inplace set of small tensors (where launch overhead dominates). For large tensors, the improvement is smaller (~10-20%) since the memcpy and kernel already overlap on the GPU due to independent memory accesses.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Create a k_set_fused kernel that takes both src0 and src1 pointers, the offset, and src1's shape/strides. Each work-item processes one element of dst: if the element falls within the src1 view region, it copies from src1; otherwise, it copies from src0. The conditional branch is the same for all work-items processing the same row (no sub-group divergence for typical 2D/3D set operations). This kernel would be launched from set.cpp directly, bypassing cpy.cpp for the non-inplace case.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: The fused kernel must correctly handle the boundary between the src0 region and the src1 view region for arbitrary 4D offsets and strides. Edge cases: offset not aligned to element size (impossible per ggml constraints), src1 view exactly covers all of dst (set degenerates to cpy), src1 view is empty (ne == 0). Testing with all 12 existing test cases (3 dims x 2 inplace modes x 2 types) should cover correctness.

kernels.efficiency_notes: The set operation is a thin orchestration layer (42 lines, no dedicated kernel) that delegates to ggml_sycl_cpy(). The actual GPU work is: (1) a DMA memcpy for the base tensor copy (optimal — hardware DMA), and (2) a k_cpy_scalar kernel for the src1→view copy (suboptimal due to 8 int64 divisions per work-item and scalar loads, but work-group size of 256 is appropriate). The operation is near-identical to the CUDA implementation — no DPCT artifacts, no migration issues. Optimization potential is low because: (a) the set op is called infrequently during inference (primarily for KV cache updates, which are being replaced by set_rows in newer models), (b) the heavy lifting is in the cpy infrastructure (analyzed in sk_019), and (c) the inplace fast path avoids the memcpy entirely. Optimizations to cpy.cpp (int32 fast division, vectorization) benefit set transitively.

kernels.name: set_rows

launch_config.global_size_expression: ceil(ne_total / SYCL_SET_BLOCK_SIZE) * SYCL_SET_BLOCK_SIZE, where ne_total = ne00 * ne01 * ne02 * ne03
launch_config.notes: Uses nd_range<1> with SYCL_SET_BLOCK_SIZE=256 (from presets.hpp). Appropriate work-group size for Xe2. Single kernel function k_set_rows templated on <src_t, idx_t, dst_t>. Each work-item processes exactly one element. Dispatch: src0 always F32, src1 is I32 or I64 (index type), dst is F32/F16/BF16. Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]].

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: Source reads (src0_row[i00]) are coalesced when src0 rows are contiguous (nb01 == ne00*sizeof(float)), which is the common case. However, destination writes (dst_row_ptr[i00]) are scattered because each row maps to a different dst_row via the index tensor src1. Adjacent work-items within the same source row (same i01, i02, i03) write to the same destination row (coalesced), but work-items spanning different source rows write to arbitrary destination rows (scatter pattern). The degree of scatter depends on the index tensor contents.
strided_accesses: 5 int64 division/modulo operations per work-item for 4D index decomposition: i%ne00, (i/ne00)%ne01, (i/ne00*ne01)%ne02, i/(ne00*ne01*ne02)
2 additional int64 modulo ops for src1 index wrapping: i03%ne12, i02%ne11
Source row pointer computation: src0 + i01*s01 + i02*s02 + i03*s03 — strided if src0 is not row-contiguous
Index tensor read: src1 + i10*s10 + i11*s11 + i12*s12 — scattered read based on index structure
memory_patterns.notes: All loads/stores are scalar. Source reads are 4-byte float. Index reads are 4-byte (I32) or 8-byte (I64). Destination writes are 4-byte (F32), 2-byte (F16/BF16). No sycl::vec types used. The innermost dimension (i00) iterates across adjacent elements in both source and destination rows, making vectorization viable for the i00 dimension.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM used. Each work-item independently computes its own multi-dimensional index, reads one element from src0, reads one index from src1, and writes one element to dst. No data sharing between work-items.

reduction_pattern.notes: No reduction. set_rows is a pure scatter-write operation — each source element maps to exactly one destination location via the index tensor.

data_types.notes: SYCL supports F32, F16, BF16 destination types (src0 always F32). CUDA additionally supports 6 quantized dst types: Q4_0, Q4_1, Q5_0, Q5_1, Q8_0, IQ4_NL via a separate k_set_rows_quant kernel that quantizes F32→Qx inline. The type cast dst_row_ptr[i00] = (dst_t) src0_row[i00] is a simple truncation for F16/BF16. Index type supports both I32 and I64 via template.

math_functions.notes: No math functions. set_rows performs integer index computation and a type cast (F32→F16/BF16 truncation). Zero FLOPs per element.

loop_analysis.notes: No loops. Each work-item processes exactly one element with straight-line code: 7 int64 divisions/modulos for index decomposition, 3 multiply-add for src0 row address, 3 multiply-add for dst row address, 1 scattered index read, 1 source read, 1 type-cast store.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: For typical set_rows usage (token embedding scatter during inference), the kernel processes ne00*ne01*ne02*ne03 elements where ne00 is the embedding dimension (e.g., 4096) and ne01 is typically small (batch of tokens). With 7 expensive int64 divisions per work-item and zero useful FLOPs, the integer arithmetic for index decomposition dominates. CUDA avoids this entirely via fast_div_modulo with precomputed multiply-shift values — the SYCL common.hpp already has init_fastdiv_values() and fast_div_modulo() but set_rows.cpp does not use them. For large ne_total, the kernel becomes memory-bound (one scattered write per work-item, 0 FLOP/byte).
anti_patterns: 7 expensive int64 division/modulo operations per work-item for 4D index decomposition — CUDA uses precomputed fast_div_modulo (multiply-shift trick) for all 5 dimension decompositions; SYCL has this utility in common.hpp but set_rows.cpp does not use it

Missing quantized destination type support — CUDA has k_set_rows_quant with inline F32→Q4_0/Q4_1/Q5_0/Q5_1/Q8_0/IQ4_NL quantization; SYCL only supports F32/F16/BF16 destinations, forcing CPU fallback for quantized KV caches
No vectorized loads/stores — scalar 4-byte per work-item where vec4 could process 16 bytes for the contiguous innermost dimension (i00)
Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] attribute — compiler may select suboptimal sub-group size
Missing ROPE+VIEW+SET_ROWS kernel fusion that CUDA implements — SYCL requires 3 separate kernel launches (rope → view → set_rows) where CUDA fuses them into one kernel
supports_op restricts to F32/F16/BF16 only — CUDA's supports_op includes Q4_0/Q4_1/Q5_0/Q5_1/Q8_0/IQ4_NL, creating a functional parity gap

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace 7 expensive int64 division/modulo operations with fast_div_modulo using precomputed multiply-shift values. The SYCL codebase already has init_fastdiv_values() and fast_div_modulo() in common.hpp (used by solve_tri.cpp). CUDA's set-rows.cu passes 5 precomputed uint3 fast-division descriptors (ne00_fd, ne01_fd, ne02_fd, ne11_fd, ne12_fd) as kernel arguments. The SYCL kernel should do the same: compute init_fastdiv_values on the host for each dimension, pass as kernel arguments, and replace all % and / operations with fast_div_modulo calls.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 15-30% throughput improvement. The 7 int64 divisions are the dominant cost for this zero-FLOP kernel. fast_div_modulo replaces each division with one mul_hi + add + shift (3 int32 ops) — roughly 10-20x cheaper per division on Intel GPUs. The improvement is highest for small tensors where the arithmetic overhead is a larger fraction of total time.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: In set_rows_sycl launch helper: (1) compute ne00_fd = init_fastdiv_values(ne00), ne01_fd, ne02_fd, ne11_fd, ne12_fd on host. (2) Pass as kernel arguments (sycl::uint3 type). (3) In k_set_rows: replace 'i % ne00' with fast_div_modulo(i, ne00_fd).y(), replace '(i/ne00) % ne01' with sequential fast_div_modulo on the quotient, etc. (4) For i03%ne12 and i02%ne11 modular wrapping, use fastmodulo variant. The existing common.hpp utilities match CUDA's interface exactly.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Zero correctness risk — fast_div_modulo produces identical results to integer division for all uint32 inputs. The only constraint is ne00*ne01*ne02*ne03 < 2^32, which is true for all practical tensor shapes. The SYCL implementation in common.hpp is already proven in solve_tri.cpp.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add quantized destination type support (Q4_0, Q4_1, Q5_0, Q5_1, Q8_0, IQ4_NL) to match CUDA's k_set_rows_quant. This requires implementing inline F32→Qx quantization functions that quantize a block of qk elements at once. CUDA uses per-block quantize_f32_q4_0_block etc. functions. Without this, quantized KV cache models must fall back to CPU for set_rows, which is a significant performance cliff.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: Enables GPU execution path for quantized KV cache models — eliminates CPU fallback. No direct throughput improvement for existing supported types, but eliminates the host-device transfer bottleneck for quantized models. This is a critical functional gap.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Create k_set_rows_quant<idx_t, block_type, qk, quantize_func> kernel mirroring CUDA's approach: (1) Each work-item processes qk elements (one quantized block). (2) ne_total = (ne00*ne01*ne02*ne03)/qk. (3) i_base = i*qk for index decomposition. (4) Read qk consecutive F32 values from src0, quantize to one block_type, write to dst. (5) Need SYCL implementations of quantize_f32_q4_0_block etc. — check if these exist in the quantize infrastructure or port from CUDA cpy-utils.cuh. (6) Update supports_op to include the quantized types.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Requires implementing or porting per-block quantization device functions if they don't already exist in SYCL. Must ensure the quantized block boundary alignment (ne00 % qk == 0). Testing requires quantized KV cache model configurations.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add vectorized load/store path for the common case where the innermost dimension (ne00) is large and both source and destination are contiguous in the i00 dimension. Adjacent work-items with the same (i01, i02, i03) already access adjacent src0 and dst elements, so vec4 loads/stores (16 bytes per work-item for F32, 8 bytes for F16/BF16) would reduce memory transactions by 4x.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.5-2.5x throughput improvement when applicable. For typical LLM embedding dimensions (ne00=4096), this applies to >99% of work-items (only the tail 0-3 elements need scalar fallback). The improvement is bounded by memory bandwidth — the kernel is already memory-bound for large ne_total.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add a kernel variant k_set_rows_vec4 where each work-item processes 4 elements: global_id maps to element i*4 in the i00 dimension. Compute multi-dimensional index for element i*4, then load vec4 from src0, store vec4 to dst (with type conversion for F16/BF16). Launch condition: ne00 >= 4 && ne00 % 4 == 0 for the vectorized path, fallback to scalar for the remainder. For F16/BF16, use vec4 of sycl::half / sycl_bf16 (8 bytes per vec4 store).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Must handle ne00 not divisible by 4 with tail processing. Alignment of src0 and dst pointers must be verified (F32 is naturally 4-byte aligned, vec4 needs 16-byte alignment — use scalar fallback if misaligned).

optimization_opportunities.description: Implement ROPE+VIEW+SET_ROWS kernel fusion to match CUDA. CUDA fuses these 3 operations into a single kernel launch that applies rotary position embedding directly into the scattered destination rows, eliminating the intermediate buffer (rope output / view), the view operation, and the set_rows kernel — saving 2 kernel launches and 2 full read+write passes over the data. This fusion is triggered when rope→view→set_rows appears in the compute graph with compatible shapes.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 20-40% latency reduction for the combined rope+set_rows operation. For single-token inference (the dominant case), this eliminates 2 kernel launch overheads (~10μs each on Intel GPUs) and 2 memory passes (read+write of ne0*ne1*sizeof elements). For ne0=128, ne1=32, F16: saves 2 × 128*32*2 = 16KB of unnecessary memory traffic per attention head.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: This is a graph-level fusion that requires: (1) Pattern detection in ggml-sycl.cpp compute graph traversal (similar to CUDA's ggml_cuda_can_fuse). (2) A fused kernel that combines rope rotation (sin/cos application to element pairs) with scattered row writes. (3) The fused kernel reads rope input, applies rotation, converts to dst type (F32→F16), and writes directly to the scattered destination via index tensor. (4) Must handle both ROPE_TYPE_NORMAL and ROPE_TYPE_NEOX modes. (5) The SYCL backend currently lacks graph-level fusion infrastructure — this is a larger architectural change. This optimization was also identified for rope (sk_016, opt_016_001).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Graph-level fusion is a major architectural change. Requires: (a) compute graph pattern matching in SYCL backend (currently absent), (b) fused kernel correctness for all rope modes, (c) shape constraint validation matching CUDA's ggml_cuda_should_fuse_rope_set_rows checks. High implementation complexity but high reward for inference latency.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] attribute to the k_set_rows kernel to ensure optimal sub-group size on Intel GPUs. Without this attribute, the compiler may select SIMD8 or SIMD32, neither of which is optimal for Xe2 architecture.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 0-5% throughput improvement. Minor effect for this simple kernel but establishes correct baseline for Xe2.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add the attribute to the lambda in set_rows_sycl: stream.parallel_for(nd_range, [=](sycl::nd_item<1> item) [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] { ... });
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: No correctness risk. Standard Intel SYCL attribute.

kernels.efficiency_notes: The SYCL set_rows kernel is a clean manual port from CUDA with correct structure and appropriate WG size (256). However, it has two major gaps vs CUDA: (1) All 7 int64 division/modulo operations use expensive native division where CUDA uses precomputed fast_div_modulo — the SYCL infrastructure (init_fastdiv_values, fast_div_modulo in common.hpp) already exists but is not used. This is the biggest per-element inefficiency. (2) Missing quantized destination types (Q4_0, Q4_1, Q5_0, Q5_1, Q8_0, IQ4_NL) forces CPU fallback for quantized KV caches — a critical functional parity gap. (3) Missing ROPE+VIEW+SET_ROWS fusion (a graph-level optimization) costs 2 kernel launches and 2 memory passes per attention head per token. The kernel is used for KV cache scatter operations during inference (every attention layer), so medium optimization potential overall. Scalar loads/stores and missing reqd_sub_group_size are minor issues compared to the integer division and functional parity gaps.

kernels.name: count-equal

launch_config.global_size_expression: nblocks * WARP_SIZE, where nblocks = min(4*nsm, ceil(ne/SYCL_COUNT_EQUAL_CHUNK_SIZE)), nsm hardcoded to 64
launch_config.notes: Uses nd_range<1> with WG=WARP_SIZE (16 on Intel, 32 on NVIDIA). Each work-group is exactly 1 sub-group. This is a severely undersized work-group — only 16 threads per WG on Intel vs recommended 256. The kernel correctly specifies [[sycl::reqd_sub_group_size(WARP_SIZE)]]. SYCL_COUNT_EQUAL_CHUNK_SIZE=128 (from count-equal.hpp). The number of streaming multiprocessors (nsm) is hardcoded to 64 — should be queried from the device for optimal work distribution.

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: Both x[i] and y[i] reads are perfectly coalesced — adjacent threads in the sub-group read adjacent int32 elements (stride 4 bytes). The loop 'for (i = i0 + tid; i < i1; i += WARP_SIZE)' ensures coalesced access pattern. Each work-item processes dk/WARP_SIZE elements sequentially.
memory_patterns.notes: All loads are scalar int32 (4 bytes). No sycl::vec types. Each work-item reads one x[i] and one y[i] per loop iteration. With WARP_SIZE=16, the sub-group reads 16*4=64 bytes per iteration, which is one cache line. vec4 loads could quadruple this to 256 bytes per sub-group per iteration.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM used. The kernel is purely reduction-based: each thread accumulates a local count, then warp_reduce_sum aggregates across the sub-group, then atomic_ref aggregates across work-groups.

reduction_pattern.notes: Two-level reduction: (1) warp_reduce_sum(nequal) using sycl::reduce_over_group on the sub-group — correct and efficient for the int overload. (2) sycl::atomic_ref<int, relaxed, device, global_space> on dst[0] — each work-group atomically adds its sub-group sum. The atomic is on int (not int64) despite dst being I64 — the assert 'ne < (1 << 30)' guards against overflow. The reinterpret_cast<int*>(dst) is endianness-dependent but correct on little-endian x86/Intel GPUs.

data_types.notes: Source tensors are I32 (int), comparison produces int (0 or 1), reduction is int sum, atomic add is int, result stored in I64 tensor. The entire computation is integer. Only I32 source type is supported (same as CUDA).

math_functions.notes: No math functions. Pure integer comparison (==) and reduction (sum).

hot_loops.trip_count: dk/WARP_SIZE per work-item, where dk = GGML_PAD((ne + 4*nsm - 1) / (4*nsm), 128)
hot_loops.description: Main comparison loop: loads x[i] and y[i], compares, accumulates count

loop_analysis.notes: The hot loop processes dk/WARP_SIZE = ~128/16 = 8 elements per work-item for the typical case (ne ~ 32K-128K, nsm=64, nblocks=256). The loop is short enough that #pragma unroll would be beneficial. No unroll hint is present.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: count_equal is purely memory-bound with 0 useful FLOPs per byte (integer comparison is essentially free vs memory access cost). With WG=16 (1 sub-group), only 16 threads per EU, significantly underutilizing the hardware. The kernel reads 2 int32 arrays and produces 1 int64 scalar — arithmetic intensity is essentially 0. For typical tensor sizes in LLM inference (ne ~ 32K), the kernel completes in microseconds and launch overhead + atomic contention dominate. The stream.memset (zeroing dst) before the kernel adds an additional synchronization point.
anti_patterns: Work-group size = WARP_SIZE (16 on Intel) — far below recommended 256. Only 1 sub-group per work-group means no work-group level parallelism. Should use multiple sub-groups per WG (e.g., WG=256 = 16 sub-groups) with SLM-based inter-sub-group reduction before the final atomic
Hardcoded nsm=64 — should query device for actual number of compute units/execution units for optimal work distribution. Intel Arc Pro B60 has different EU count than the assumed 64 SMs
No vectorized loads — scalar int32 loads (4 bytes per thread) where vec4 loads (16 bytes per thread) would improve bandwidth utilization
Missing #pragma unroll on the hot comparison loop (typically ~8 iterations per work-item)
stream.memset for dst zeroing before kernel — could initialize dst inside the kernel (first atomic write could be a store instead of fetch_add, or use 0 as initial value via atomic exchange)

Atomic contention: all nblocks work-groups contend on a single atomic int — with 256 WGs each doing an atomic add, this is a serial bottleneck. Hierarchical reduction (WG-level → single atomic) would reduce contention

optimization_opportunities.description: Increase work-group size from WARP_SIZE (16) to 256 with 16 sub-groups per WG. Use SLM-based inter-sub-group reduction within the work-group, then a single atomic add per work-group to the global result. This reduces atomic contention by 16x (from nblocks atomics to nblocks/16 atomics) and improves EU occupancy by filling more hardware threads per execution unit.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 2-4x throughput improvement. The WG=16 configuration severely underutilizes hardware resources. With WG=256, each EU can schedule more concurrent threads, hiding memory latency better. Additionally, 16x reduction in atomic contention eliminates the serialization bottleneck.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Change local_range from WARP_SIZE to 256. Inside the kernel: (1) Each sub-group does warp_reduce_sum as before. (2) Sub-group leaders (lane 0) write their partial sum to SLM[sub_group_id]. (3) Barrier. (4) First sub-group reads SLM and does final warp_reduce_sum across 16 partial sums. (5) Thread 0 does atomic_add to global dst. Need sycl::local_accessor<int, 1> of size 16 (one per sub-group). Adjust nblocks calculation: divide by (256/WARP_SIZE) since each WG now processes 16x more data.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Standard multi-sub-group reduction pattern used in many other kernels (norm, softmax, sumrows). The SLM requirement is trivial (16 * 4 = 64 bytes).

optimization_opportunities.description: Use sycl::vec<int, 4> (vec4) loads for both x and y arrays to process 4 elements per loop iteration. Each comparison produces 4 int results that can be summed locally before the sub-group reduction. This quadruples the data processed per memory transaction.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.5-2x throughput improvement for the memory-bound comparison loop. Limited by the fact that the kernel is already bottlenecked on launch overhead and atomic contention for typical tensor sizes.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: In the hot loop: load sycl::vec<int,4> from x and y (requires 16-byte aligned addresses).
