Compare element-wise (vec4 == vec4 produces vec4 of 0/-1), sum the 4 comparison results into the accumulator. Handle tail elements (ne % 4 != 0) with scalar fallback. Must verify that src0->data and src1->data are 16-byte aligned (they are, per ggml allocator guarantees).
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Must handle non-multiple-of-4 element counts. Alignment is guaranteed by ggml allocator.

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace hardcoded nsm=64 with actual device compute unit count queried from ctx. The Intel Arc Pro B60 has a specific number of Xe-cores (20 Xe-cores / 160 XVEs) which may differ significantly from the assumed 64 CUDA SMs.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 0-10% improvement in work distribution. Wrong nsm leads to suboptimal chunk size (dk) and number of work-groups — either too many small work-groups (atomic contention) or too few large ones (underutilization). The impact depends on how far the actual EU count is from 64.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Query ctx.device().get_info<sycl::info::device::max_compute_units>() or use the SYCL backend's existing device info infrastructure. Set nsm = max_compute_units (or a fraction thereof, depending on how CUs map to the work distribution heuristic). The CUDA version uses ggml_cuda_info().devices[device].nsm which is the actual SM count.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: No correctness risk. The heuristic is purely about performance tuning.

kernels.efficiency_notes: The count_equal kernel is a clean CUDA port with correct sub-group reduction and atomic global accumulation. The main inefficiencies are: (1) WG=WARP_SIZE=16 on Intel — far below optimal 256, meaning poor EU occupancy and high atomic contention (one atomic per 16-thread WG vs one per 256-thread WG). (2) Hardcoded nsm=64 instead of querying device. (3) No vectorized loads. However, the overall optimization potential is LOW because count_equal is called extremely rarely during inference — it's used only for model accuracy evaluation (comparing predicted vs actual token IDs), not in the critical inference path. The kernel processes a single 1D tensor comparison, typically ne ~ vocab_size * batch_size, completing in microseconds. Optimizing WG size would improve efficiency but the absolute time savings are negligible in the context of end-to-end inference.

kernels.name: wkv

launch_config.global_size_expression: B * H * head_size, where head_size = C/H (64 or 128)
launch_config.notes: Uses nd_range<1> with local_range = head_size (SYCL_WKV_BLOCK_SIZE=64 or 128). Template parameter selects head_size at compile time. Each work-group processes one (batch, head) pair. WG size is 64 or 128 — below optimal 256 but architecturally constrained by head_size dimension. Each work-item maintains a private state vector of head_size floats and iterates over all sequence tokens. Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]]. 2 kernel variants: WKV6 (RWKV v5/v6) and WKV7 (RWKV v7) with different input tensors and state update equations.

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: Per-token SLM loads (_k[tid], _r[tid], etc.) are coalesced — adjacent threads load adjacent elements from contiguous tensor slices. Global v[t] load is also coalesced. State initialization reads state[i] with stride head_size across global memory (state[... + i * head_size + tid]) — this is strided by head_size elements, but since each thread reads head_size values sequentially, the access pattern is transposed. State writeback has the same pattern.
strided_accesses: State initialization: s[batch_i * state_size + head_i * head_size * head_size + i * head_size + tid] — inner loop over i produces stride-head_size global reads
State writeback: dst[T * C + ... + i * head_size + tid] — same stride-head_size pattern
WKV7 state init: s[... + tid * head_size + i] — stride-1 per inner loop iteration (contiguous per thread, but threads stride by head_size)
memory_patterns.notes: SYCL kernel uses scalar loads for all SLM and global accesses. CUDA uses float4& reinterpret casts on shared memory arrays for the inner loop (e.g., (float4&)(_k[j])) — this enables 128-bit SLM reads (4 floats per load). SYCL accesses SLM as _k[j+0], _k[j+1], _k[j+2], _k[j+3] — 4 separate 32-bit SLM reads vs 1 128-bit read. This is a significant difference for the hot inner loop.

slm_usage.slm_bytes: WKV6: 4 * head_size * 4 = 1024B (head_size=64) or 2048B (head_size=128). WKV7: 5 * head_size * 4 = 1280B or 2560B
slm_usage.notes: WKV6 caches 4 vectors in SLM: _k, _r, _tf, _td (each head_size floats). WKV7 caches 5 vectors: _r, _w, _k, _a, _b. The SLM usage is very modest (1-2.5KB out of 64KB available). The inner loop reads all head_size elements from each SLM array — with scalar access pattern, bank conflicts are possible when multiple threads in the same sub-group access the same SLM bank. CUDA's float4 access pattern naturally avoids this by reading 4 consecutive bank entries atomically.

reduction_pattern.notes: No inter-thread reduction. Each thread computes a local y value by accumulating over its private state and SLM-cached vectors. The final y value is directly written to dst[t]. The dot-product (y accumulation) is entirely thread-local. WKV7's sa (state-a dot product) is also thread-local — no sub-group reduction.

data_types.notes: All computation is FP32. RWKV models can potentially use FP16 for inference (state and activations), but the SYCL kernel only supports F32. CUDA is also F32-only. The inner loop performs head_size multiply-adds per token per thread — with head_size=64, that's 64*3 = 192 FLOPs per thread per token (for WKV6: kv=k*v, y+=r*(tf*kv+state), state=state*td+kv). Moderate compute intensity. Joint matrix is not applicable — the computation is element-wise state update, not matrix multiplication.

math_functions.notes: No transcendental math. All arithmetic is multiply-add on FP32 values. No exp, log, sin, cos etc.

hot_loops.trip_count: n_seq_tokens iterations over the time dimension
hot_loops.description: Outer time loop: iterates over all tokens in the sequence. Per iteration: barrier, load k/r/td to SLM, barrier, inner loop over head_size

hot_loops.location: wkv.cpp:53-68 (WKV6 inner), wkv.cpp:128-133 (WKV7 sa), wkv.cpp:137-152 (WKV7 state update)
hot_loops.description: Inner unrolled-by-4 loop: computes kv products, accumulates y, updates state. This is the computational hot spot — head_size/4 iterations of 12+ FLOPs each (WKV6) or 16+ FLOPs each (WKV7).

loop_analysis.notes: CRITICAL: CUDA uses #pragma unroll on the state init/writeback loops (head_size iterations) and the inner compute loop. SYCL has NO unroll hints on any loop. The inner loop is already manually unrolled by 4 (j += 4), but #pragma unroll would eliminate loop overhead and enable register allocation optimization for the 16/32-iteration inner loop. The state init/writeback loops (head_size iterations of strided global memory access) also benefit significantly from unrolling.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: Each work-item maintains a private state array of head_size floats: 64 floats = 256 bytes (head_size=64) or 128 floats = 512 bytes (head_size=128). With WG=64 and head_size=64: 64 * 256 = 16KB register file per WG. With WG=128 and head_size=128: 128 * 512 = 64KB register file per WG — this exceeds typical GPU register file capacity per execution unit, causing register spilling. The Xe2 architecture has ~128 registers per thread (512 bytes) — the head_size=128 variant exactly fits, but any additional temporaries will spill. The compute pattern within each time step is moderately compute-intensive (head_size multiply-adds), bounded by SLM bandwidth for the shared k/r/td vectors and register file bandwidth for the private state. The time loop has 2 barriers per iteration — serialization points. For long sequences, this kernel is compute-bound; for short sequences, launch overhead dominates.
anti_patterns: Missing #pragma unroll on state init loop (head_size iterations of strided global reads) — CUDA has this, SYCL does not
Missing #pragma unroll on state writeback loop (head_size iterations of strided global writes) — CUDA has this, SYCL does not

Scalar SLM loads in inner loop — SYCL reads _k[j+0], _k[j+1], _k[j+2], _k[j+3] as 4 separate 32-bit loads; CUDA uses (float4&)(_k[j]) for a single 128-bit SLM load. This 4x increase in SLM transactions may cause bank conflicts and reduce throughput
Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] — compiler may select suboptimal SIMD width
WG size 64 is below optimal 256 but architecturally constrained by head_size; the head_size=128 variant at WG=128 is better but still below 256
FP32-only — no FP16 variant for inference where reduced precision is acceptable (could halve register pressure and memory bandwidth)

optimization_opportunities.description: Add #pragma unroll to all loops matching CUDA behavior: (1) state initialization loop (head_size iterations), (2) state writeback loop (head_size iterations), (3) inner compute loop (head_size/4 iterations). CUDA explicitly uses #pragma unroll on state init/writeback and implicitly unrolls the inner loop. The inner loop is the computational hotspot — with trip count 16 or 32 (compile-time known via template), full unrolling eliminates loop overhead and enables the compiler to optimize register allocation for the accumulation chain.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% throughput improvement. The primary benefit is from unrolling the head_size/4 = 16/32 iteration inner compute loop, enabling the compiler to schedule multiply-add chains more efficiently. State init/writeback loops benefit from amortizing the loop control overhead over head_size iterations of strided memory access.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add '#pragma unroll' before: (1) 'for (int i = 0; i < head_size; i++)' at wkv.cpp:34,72,112,156. (2) 'for (int j = 0; j < head_size; j += 4)' at wkv.cpp:53,128,137. The inner loops have compile-time known trip counts (head_size is a template parameter), so the compiler CAN fully unroll them — but may not without the explicit hint.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: No correctness risk. #pragma unroll is a compiler hint that cannot change semantics. The only risk is code size increase for the head_size=128 variant (128/4 = 32 iterations fully unrolled), which is acceptable.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized SLM reads in the inner loop to match CUDA's float4 access pattern. Replace scalar _k[j+0], _k[j+1], _k[j+2], _k[j+3] with a single sycl::vec<float,4> load from SLM. CUDA uses (float4&)(_k[j]) for 128-bit SLM reads — this reduces SLM transactions by 4x and eliminates potential bank conflicts from 4 consecutive scalar reads to adjacent banks.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-20% throughput improvement for the inner loop. The benefit depends on whether the Intel compiler already vectorizes the scalar SLM loads. If the compiler does NOT coalesce them, the improvement could be significant (4x fewer SLM transactions). SLM bandwidth is often a bottleneck for kernels with high SLM read density like WKV.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: In the inner loops, replace scalar reads with: sycl::vec<float,4> k4 = *reinterpret_cast<const sycl::vec<float,4>*>(&_k[j]); Then access k4[0], k4[1], k4[2], k4[3] or k4.s0(), k4.s1() etc. Alternatively, use sycl::vec<float,4> as SLM element type. Must verify alignment (j is always multiple of 4, so the SLM pointer is 16-byte aligned). Apply to all SLM arrays: _k, _r, _tf/_w, _td/_a/_b.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Alignment is guaranteed since j increments by 4 and SLM arrays are float-aligned from index 0. reinterpret_cast on SLM accessor may need platform-specific validation. Alternative: use sycl::multi_ptr with alignment.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] to both kernel lambdas. With WG=64 (head_size=64), this gives 4 sub-groups per WG. With WG=128, this gives 8 sub-groups per WG. While the kernel doesn't use sub-group operations, specifying the sub-group size ensures the compiler selects SIMD16 execution width, which is optimal for Xe2 and prevents fallback to SIMD8 or SIMD32.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 0-5% throughput improvement. Minor for this kernel since there are no sub-group operations, but ensures correct SIMD width selection.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add the attribute to the parallel_for lambda: [=](sycl::nd_item<1> item) [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] { ... }
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: No correctness risk. Standard Intel attribute.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add FP16 kernel variant for inference where reduced precision is acceptable. This would halve register pressure (state array: 64 floats → 64 halfs = 128 bytes vs 256 bytes) and memory bandwidth requirements. RWKV models support FP16 inference. This is a larger optimization that also requires type dispatch in the host wrapper.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.5-2x throughput improvement from halved memory bandwidth and register pressure. The head_size=128 variant especially benefits — register pressure drops from near-limit to comfortable range.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Create rwkv_wkv6_f16_sycl and rwkv_wkv7_f16_sycl variants using sycl::half for state, SLM arrays, and intermediate computations. Keep accumulator y as float for precision. Need to check if ggml WKV ops can have F16 input tensors. This is a significant code change — add only if RWKV FP16 inference is actively used.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: FP16 state accumulation over long sequences may cause precision loss. RWKV's state update involves multiplication by decay factors (td/w) close to 1.0, which can amplify FP16 rounding errors. Need numerical validation against FP32 baseline.

kernels.efficiency_notes: The WKV kernels are clean CUDA ports with correct structure, proper SLM usage for shared vectors, and appropriate work-group sizing (constrained by head_size). The main inefficiencies vs CUDA are: (1) Missing #pragma unroll on all loops — CUDA explicitly unrolls state init/writeback and the compiler likely unrolls the inner loop. (2) Scalar SLM reads vs CUDA's float4 vectorized reads — 4x more SLM transactions in the compute hotspot. (3) Missing reqd_sub_group_size. (4) FP32-only. The kernel is moderately compute-intensive (each work-item does head_size*3 FLOPs per token per timestep) with high register pressure (head_size private floats). WKV is the core attention mechanism for RWKV models (v5/v6/v7), called once per layer — for RWKV models, this kernel is on the critical path. For non-RWKV models (the majority of LLM usage), this kernel is never called. Medium potential because the optimizations are straightforward (unroll + vectorized SLM) but the user base is limited to RWKV models.

kernels.name: gla

launch_config.global_size_expression: B * H * head_size, where head_size = C/H (64 or 128)
launch_config.notes: Structurally near-identical to WKV6 (sk_028). Uses nd_range<1> with local_range = head_size (64 or 128). Template parameter selects head_size at compile time. Each work-group processes one (batch, head) pair. WG=64 or 128 — below optimal 256 but constrained by head_size. Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]]. Single kernel variant: gated_linear_attn_f32.

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: Same as WKV6: per-token SLM loads (k[t], r[t], td[t]) are coalesced. State init/writeback has stride-head_size pattern through global memory.
strided_accesses: State initialization: s[... + i * head_size + tid] — stride-head_size global reads (same as WKV6)
State writeback: dst[T * C + ... + i * head_size + tid] — stride-head_size global writes
memory_patterns.notes: All SLM and global loads are scalar 32-bit. CUDA uses float4& reinterpret casts for 128-bit vectorized SLM reads in the inner loop. Same issue as WKV6.

slm_usage.notes: 3 SLM arrays: _k, _r, _td (each head_size floats). Even less SLM than WKV6 (which has 4 arrays). Scalar reads in inner loop may cause bank conflicts.

reduction_pattern.notes: No inter-thread reduction. y accumulation is thread-local (same as WKV6).

data_types.notes: FP32 only, same as CUDA. GLA models could potentially use FP16 for inference.

math_functions.notes: No transcendental math. Pure multiply-add + scale factor.

hot_loops.description: Outer time loop: barrier, load k/r/td to SLM, barrier, inner loop, write y*scale
Inner unrolled-by-4 loop: kv = k*v, state = state*td + kv, y += r*state. Computational hot spot.

loop_analysis.notes: CRITICAL: CUDA uses #pragma unroll on state init (line 19) and state writeback (line 58). SYCL has NO unroll hints. Same issue as WKV6.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: Same as WKV6: float state[head_size] per work-item (256 or 512 bytes). Moderate compute intensity (head_size multiply-adds per token per thread). 2 barriers per time step. For RWKV/linear attention models, GLA is called once per layer.
anti_patterns: Missing #pragma unroll on state init loop (CUDA has it) — head_size iterations of strided global reads
Missing #pragma unroll on state writeback loop (CUDA has it) — head_size iterations of strided global writes
Scalar SLM loads in inner loop — 4 separate 32-bit reads vs CUDA's single 128-bit float4& read per iteration
Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]]
FP32-only — no FP16 variant
Structurally identical to WKV6 — same optimization opportunities apply

optimization_opportunities.description: Add #pragma unroll to state init/writeback loops and inner compute loop, matching CUDA. Identical optimization as opt_028_001 for WKV6 — GLA shares the exact same code structure.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% throughput improvement. Same reasoning as WKV6.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add '#pragma unroll' before loops at gla.cpp:32 (state init), gla.cpp:47 (inner compute), and gla.cpp:66 (state writeback). All have compile-time known trip counts via template parameter.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: No correctness risk.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized 128-bit SLM reads (sycl::vec<float,4> or reinterpret_cast) in the inner loop to match CUDA's float4& pattern. Identical optimization as opt_028_002.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-20% throughput improvement. Same reasoning as WKV6.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace _k[j+0..3] scalar reads with *reinterpret_cast<const sycl::vec<float,4>*>(&_k[j]). Apply to _k, _r, _td arrays.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Alignment guaranteed since j is always multiple of 4.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] attribute to the kernel lambda.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 0-5% throughput improvement.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add attribute to the parallel_for lambda.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Standard Intel attribute.

kernels.efficiency_notes: GLA is structurally near-identical to WKV6 (sk_028) — same code pattern (SLM-cached shared vectors, private state array, outer time loop, inner unrolled-by-4 compute loop). Same anti-patterns: missing #pragma unroll, scalar SLM reads vs CUDA's float4, missing reqd_sub_group_size, FP32-only. GLA is the core attention mechanism for gated linear attention models (e.g., RetNet, GLA architectures). For these models, it's on the critical path; for standard transformer models, it's never called. Medium potential because the optimizations are straightforward and identical to WKV6, but the user base is limited to GLA/linear attention models.

kernels.name: tsembd

launch_config.global_size_expression: nd_range<2>(global_range(ne00, num_blocks_x * 256), local_range(1, 256))
launch_config.notes: nd_range<2> with local_range(1, 256): dim0 is degenerate (1 thread per batch element via group index), dim1 is the actual work dimension over half_ceil embedding positions. WG=256 appropriate for Xe2. ne00 is batch size (typically 1-4 for diffusion). Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]]. Near-identical to CUDA grid(num_blocks, ne00, 1) with blockDim=256.

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: Adjacent threads write adjacent embedding positions: embed_data[j] and embed_data[j+half]. Both writes are coalesced within a WG. Read is a single scalar broadcast: src0_d[i] (same timestep value for all threads in a WG row).
memory_patterns.notes: Each work-item reads 1 float (timestep), writes 2 floats (cos, sin) at offset j and j+half. The two writes are half apart so vectorization is not straightforward. Total bandwidth per work-item: 4B read + 8B write = 12B. Very light memory footprint.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM used. Each work-item operates independently.

reduction_pattern.notes: No reduction. Embarrassingly parallel — each work-item computes one (cos, sin) pair independently.

data_types.notes: FP32 only (same as CUDA). Embedding precision matters for downstream diffusion model accuracy, so FP16 is not advisable here.

math_functions.notes: 4 transcendental functions per work-item. CUDA uses expf/logf/cosf/sinf (fast single-precision). SYCL uses full-precision sycl::exp/log/cos/sin. Could use sycl::native::exp/log/cos/sin for ~2-3x faster transcendentals with slightly reduced precision (sufficient for embedding generation). The exp(-log(max_period)*j/half) could also be precomputed as pow(max_period, -j/half) or computed via a single exp with combined argument.

loop_analysis.notes: No loops in the kernel body. Each work-item is a straight-line computation: 1 read, 4 transcendentals, 2 writes. The 'loop' is over threads in the nd_range.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: 4 transcendental functions (exp, log, cos, sin) per work-item dominate execution time. Memory footprint is trivial (12 bytes per work-item). Arithmetic intensity is high (4 transcendentals / 12 bytes). However, the kernel is called extremely rarely (once per diffusion step) and processes small tensors (dim is typically 320-1280), so absolute runtime is negligible.
anti_patterns: Missing [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]]
Full-precision sycl::exp/log/cos/sin instead of sycl::native:: variants (CUDA uses fast single-precision expf/logf/cosf/sinf)
nd_range<2> with degenerate dim0 local_range(1,...) — works but the batch dimension uses groups not threads

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace sycl::exp/log/cos/sin with sycl::native::exp/log/cos/sin for ~2-3x faster transcendentals. CUDA's expf/logf/cosf/sinf map to fast hardware intrinsics; SYCL's full-precision variants do not. For embedding generation, native precision (roughly 2^-11 relative error) is more than sufficient.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 2-3x faster kernel execution from native transcendentals. However, absolute impact is negligible because the kernel processes tiny tensors (dim=320-1280) and is called once per diffusion step.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Replace sycl::exp with sycl::native::exp, sycl::log with sycl::native::log, sycl::cos with sycl::native::cos, sycl::sin with sycl::native::sin. Alternatively, combine: float arg = timestep * sycl::native::exp(sycl::native::log((float)max_period) * (-j_over_half));
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Native math has reduced precision (~2^-11 relative error) but this is acceptable for sinusoidal embeddings. CUDA already uses fast-math equivalents.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add [[intel::reqd_sub_group_size(16)]] to ensure optimal SIMD16 execution on Xe2.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 0-5% throughput improvement. Mostly a correctness/consistency attribute.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add the attribute to the parallel_for lambda.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: No correctness risk. Standard Intel attribute.

kernels.efficiency_notes: The timestep embedding kernel is a near-perfect 1:1 CUDA port. Embarrassingly parallel with no reduction, no SLM, no synchronization, and trivial memory footprint. The only meaningful inefficiency is full-precision transcendentals vs CUDA's fast-math intrinsics. The kernel processes tiny tensors (dim=320-1280 for typical diffusion models) and is called only once per diffusion inference step. Even with 2-3x speedup from native math, the absolute time saved is sub-microsecond. Low potential because: (1) kernel is already well-structured, (2) called extremely rarely, (3) processes small data, (4) only used by diffusion models (not LLMs). The main value of optimization here is code consistency (using native math everywhere).

kernels.name: roll

launch_config.global_size_expression: nd_range<1>(num_blocks * SYCL_ROLL_BLOCK_SIZE, SYCL_ROLL_BLOCK_SIZE) where num_blocks = ceil(n_elements / 256)
launch_config.notes: Correct nd_range<1> with WG=256 (SYCL_ROLL_BLOCK_SIZE). Matches CUDA's CUDA_ROLL_BLOCK_SIZE=256. 1D dispatch over all elements in a flat 4D tensor. No reqd_sub_group_size — acceptable since kernel has no sub-group-level operations. Clean and idiomatic.

memory_patterns.coalesced_notes: Destination writes are perfectly coalesced: dst[idx] since the flat output index equals the global thread ID. Source reads are mostly coalesced: consecutive threads read consecutive d0 values (d0 = wrap_index(i0 - s0, ne00)) except at the wrap boundary where one thread in a sub-group may jump to a distant address. This is a minor effect (1 wrap per ne00 elements).
memory_patterns.notes: Each work-item reads 1 float and writes 1 float. No vectorized loads (sycl::vec, float4). Scalar 4-byte load/store. Same as CUDA original.

slm_usage.notes: No SLM used. Appropriate — this is a simple 1:1 element copy with index remapping, no data reuse.

reduction_pattern.notes: No reduction. Embarrassingly parallel — each work-item independently reads one element and writes one element.

data_types.notes: FP32 only. Host wrapper asserts src0->type == GGML_TYPE_F32. No F16/BF16 support (same as CUDA). The roll operation is a pure copy — data type does not affect compute, only bandwidth.

math_functions.notes: No transcendental math. All computation is integer arithmetic for 4D index decomposition and wrap_index (comparison + add/subtract). The kernel performs zero floating-point computation — it's a pure data movement kernel.

loop_analysis.notes: No loops in the kernel body. Each work-item executes straight-line code: decompose flat index to 4D, apply wrap_index per dimension, compute source flat index, copy one float. No unrolling needed.

current_analysis.bottleneck_notes: Pure memory-bound kernel with zero floating-point computation: 4 bytes read + 4 bytes written = 8 bytes per work-item, 0 FLOPs (only integer index math). Arithmetic intensity is exactly 0 ops/byte for floating-point, far below the 27 ops/byte compute threshold. Performance is limited entirely by memory bandwidth. The 4 int64 division/modulo operations for index decomposition add some integer compute overhead but this is secondary to memory latency.
anti_patterns: Expensive 64-bit integer division/modulo for 4D index decomposition (4 divisions per work-item) — all dimension values likely fit in int32, and could use multiply-shift trick (fast_div) for further speedup
No vectorized loads/stores — could process 4 floats per work-item with sycl::vec<float,4> for simple roll along dim0 only
FP32-only — no F16/BF16 support for half-precision tensors (same limitation as CUDA)
Redundant destination index computation: dst[i3*(...)+i2*(...)+i1*ne00+i0] is identical to dst[idx] since idx = i0 + i1*ne00 + i2*(ne00*ne01) + i3*(ne00*ne01*ne02)

optimization_opportunities.description: Replace expensive 64-bit integer division/modulo for 4D index decomposition with 32-bit arithmetic or multiply-shift fast division. Each work-item performs 4 int64 divisions (%, /) to decompose a flat index into (i0, i1, i2, i3). Since tensor dimensions (ne00, ne01, ne02, ne03) are typically < 2^31, int32 arithmetic suffices. Furthermore, the common.hpp fast_div_modulo or precomputed reciprocals could eliminate division entirely.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 5-15% throughput improvement from cheaper integer index decomposition. Int64 division on GPU is multi-cycle; int32 division is faster, and multiply-shift avoids division entirely.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Option A (simple): Cast ne00/ne01/ne02/ne03 to int32 and use int32 %, /. Option B (advanced): Use fast_div_modulo from common.hpp (init_fastdiv_values + __fast_div). Option C: Use 3D or 4D nd_range to decompose indices via the hardware grid, eliminating division entirely. Option C would require restructuring the launch to nd_range<3> with local_range(1,1,256) and computing i0/i1/i2/i3 from group and local IDs.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Integer optimization with no floating-point changes. Same mathematical result. Int32 truncation risk only for tensors with > 2^31 elements in a single dimension, which is extremely unlikely.

optimization_opportunities.description: Use vectorized 16-byte loads/stores (sycl::vec<float,4>) when the roll shift is only along dimensions >= 1 (i.e., s0 == 0 and ne00 is a multiple of 4). When rolling only along outer dimensions, consecutive elements in dim0 map to consecutive source elements with the same shift, enabling 4-wide vector copies. This would reduce memory transactions by 4x for the common case.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 1.5-2x throughput improvement for the s0==0 case (vec4 loads/stores). No improvement when s0 != 0 since consecutive elements in dim0 may wrap to non-contiguous source addresses. Most practical roll operations shift along a single dimension, so the fast path would be hit frequently.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Add a fast path: if (s0 == 0 && ne00 % 4 == 0) { process 4 elements per work-item using sycl::vec<float,4> }. Adjust global range to n_elements/4 for the fast path. Fall back to scalar for s0 != 0 or ne00 % 4 != 0.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Conditional fast path — scalar fallback ensures correctness for all cases. 16-byte alignment of float arrays is guaranteed by the allocator.

optimization_opportunities.description: Add F16/BF16 support via template to match potential future CUDA expansion. Currently both CUDA and SYCL only support F32. For models using half-precision tensors, the roll operation would need to convert F16→F32→roll→F32→F16, which wastes bandwidth. A templated kernel processing sycl::half directly would halve the bandwidth requirement.
optimization_opportunities.expected_improvement: 2x bandwidth improvement when processing F16 tensors (2 bytes vs 4 bytes per element). However, this is only useful if the upstream model uses F16 tensors, which is not the current default.
optimization_opportunities.implementation_notes: Template the kernel on data type: template<typename T> roll_sycl(const T* src, T* dst, ...). Instantiate for float, sycl::half, sycl::ext::oneapi::bfloat16. Update the host wrapper to dispatch based on src0->type.
optimization_opportunities.risk_notes: Pure code expansion — no algorithmic changes. The roll operation is a copy, so there are no precision concerns with F16/BF16.

kernels.efficiency_notes: The roll kernel is a near-perfect 1:1 CUDA port. Clean hand-written SYCL (no DPCT artifacts), correct nd_range<1> with WG=256, proper bounds checking. Embarrassingly parallel with zero floating-point computation — a pure memory-bound data movement kernel. Writes are perfectly coalesced; reads are mostly coalesced except at wrap boundaries. The only inefficiencies are: (1) expensive int64 division for index decomposition, (2) scalar 1-element-per-thread processing where vec4 could be used for the common s0==0 case. Low potential because: (1) roll is called infrequently in LLM inference, (2) the kernel is already well-structured, (3) absolute time per call is small for typical tensor sizes. The primary optimization value is in integer arithmetic (fast_div) which would benefit many similar kernels.
